Preliminary measurements have been performed with the CUPID VSTT (Vertical Slice Test Tower), a prototype tower designed to test the detectors' response and the apparatus' mechanical and thermal stability. In addition, a key objective was to demonstrate the improved performance of germanium-based cryogenic light detectors. In CUPID, light detection is used for both particle identification and pile-up rejection. Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ is a scintillating crystal, enabling particle identification by exploiting the dependence of light yield on particle type. This requires collecting the Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ scintillation light, peaking at $\sim$600 nm, with a $\sim$300 $μ$m-thick high-purity germanium wafer placed next to the crystal. The wafer is also equipped with concentric Al electrodes biased at a few tens of volts. This bias improves the signal-to-noise ratio by an order of magnitude thanks to the Neganov-Trofimov-Luke effect. This work presents preliminary results on the performance of the VSTT light detectors and of its Optical Injection System.

items.title: Laser-induced damage threshold of periodic plasmonic metasurfaces
items.summary: Plasmonic metasurfaces enable strong nonlinear optical responses due to sub-wavelength field confinement, yet their performance is fundamentally limited by low laser-induced damage thresholds (LIDT). Here, we present a comprehensive experimental and numerical study of the interplay between surface lattice resonances (SLRs), second-harmonic generation (SHG), and LIDT in periodic gold nanobar metasurfaces. Angle-resolved measurements reveal that excitation of SLRs at the fundamental wavelength strongly enhances SHG efficiency while simultaneously reducing the LIDT. In contrast, excitation of an SLR at the second-harmonic wavelength does not affect the damage threshold, allowing the SHG signal to be maximized. Our findings establish a fundamental trade-off between nonlinear efficiency and optical robustness and provide design guidelines for optimizing periodic plasmonic metasurfaces for high-power nonlinear applications.

items.title: AI4Plasma II: Geometry-Aware Surrogate Modeling for Variable Electrode Gap GEC Plasmas
items.summary: Industrial plasma process development requires broad exploration of operating and geometric parameters. Geometric parameters, particularly electrode spacing, affect discharge structure and processing uniformity. Exploring these parameter spaces through repeated high-fidelity simulations can be computationally expensive. Surrogate models can offer rapid predictions, but geometric variation complicates their application because the computational domain and discretization may change across samples. In this work, six geometry-aware surrogate models based on prescribed and learned geometry mappings, extended-domain representation, continuous coordinates, and geometry-native discretizations are compared in terms of their data requirements for accurate predictions of full plasma fields and ion density profiles near the wafer. The simulation dataset spans pressure, voltage, frequency, and electrode gap, with each reference case requiring an average simulation cost of 5.32 CPU h. To achieve a 2% mean error across the four plasma fields, prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO and Transolver require 100 training cases, compared with 250-1000 for the other models. Predicting ion density profiles near the wafer is more demanding and reveals larger differences among models, with prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO requiring the fewest training cases for the profile accuracy targets considered. To further reduce the data required for accurate predictions near the wafer, we introduce charge-separation weighting into the training loss, which reduces the prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO's minimum tested training requirement for a 5% profile error from 1000 to 100 cases. These results support prescribed-mapping Geo-FNO as a practical starting point for the variable-gap problem studied here when a suitable geometry mapping is available, while Transolver achieves the highest prediction accuracy with sufficient training data.

items.title: Quantum-logic detection of rotationally inelastic collisions of single molecules
items.summary: Collisions between molecules govern chemical reactions and energy transfer across a range of different environments from interstellar space to the Earth's atmosphere. Despite their fundamental importance, molecular collisions have traditionally been studied through ensemble-averaged experiments which obscure the dynamics of individual scattering events on the quantum level. Probing single molecular collisions with quantum-state resolution has thus far remained a major experimental challenge. Here, we demonstrate a method for detecting individual rotationally inelastic collisions of single molecular ions with neutral atoms using quantum-logic techniques. We prepare individual trapped N$_2^+$ ions in their rotational ground state, subject them to a beam of helium atoms and detect isolated collision events through their effects on the motion of the trapped ions. Quantum-logic-spectroscopic measurements reveal changes of the molecular state upon collision enabling the determination of the probability of rotationally inelastic scattering. The experiments are analysed by comparison with quantum and classical scattering calculations yielding detailed insights into the underlying collision dynamics. By combining single-collision detection with non-destructive readout of the molecular quantum state, our approach establishes a new experimental framework for investigating molecular scattering beyond conventional ensemble measurements. It opens a route towards investigating state-to-state scattering in individual molecules and exploring molecular interactions at the level of single quantum-state resolved events.

items.title: Bare and stretched string tyre models with distributed FrBD dynamics
items.summary: This paper presents a novel class of string tyre models with FrBD friction dynamics. By modelling the distributed carcass and tread deformations with string-like equations, the resulting formulation leads to a system of semilinear parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs) that describe the evolution of the tyre states without explicitly distinguishing between stick and slip regimes. Rigorous stability and passivity analyses are also conducted using a Lyapunov-based approach, establishing boundedness of the distributed states and energy dissipation during rolling contact. The proposed Lyapunov function admits a clear physical interpretation as the total elastic energy stored in the tyre, enabling a direct link between mechanical energy storage and frictional dissipation due to slip losses. The steady-state and transient behaviours of the model are investigated both numerically and experimentally, revealing that the new formulation can satisfactorily reproduce nonlinear relaxation phenomena excited by step slip inputs. The resulting model provides a physically interpretable, mathematically well-posed, and computationally efficient basis for advanced vehicle dynamics simulations and control-oriented applications.

items.title: Mechanisms of Zener diode and ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction: A novel explanation in terms of impurity-photovoltaic-effect resulting from infrared self-emission at room-temperature
items.summary: In textbooks, a quantum-mechanical tunneling mechanism based on electron-wavefunction is used to explain Zener diode as well as ohmic contact resulting from a heavily doped p-n junction. In this study, an attempt in particle description is made to explain these devices. Any object at room-temperature emits infrared (IR) photons. The process of heavy doping can cause many defects. The self-absorption of the IR emission could be achieved through sub-band-gap excitations due to defects, creating carriers. In a heavily doped p-n junction device, some of the IR-generated carriers diffuse into the junction which has a built-in field. The built-in field sweeps out the carriers, creating IR photocurrent. The reverse leakage current of the p-n junction is regarded as the IR photocurrent according to a precedent where impurity-photovoltaic-effect is used to explain circuit devices (arXiv:2510.18226). Heavy doping results in not only a great many IR-generated carriers but also an avalanche effect at low voltage, producing Zener breakdown. Additionally, the impurity-photovoltaic-effect can make a reasonable contribution to explaining the temperature dependence of Zener breakdown. If the doping is very heavy, the heavily doped p-n junction can be altered to create an ohmic contact, which can also be explained in terms of impurity-photovoltaic-effect. Not only quantum mechanics, but also this photovoltaic mechanism in particle description can explain the above devices. Considering the wave-particle duality, the combination of quantum-mechanical and photovoltaic mechanisms is suggested to explain these devices. Each mechanism plays a big or small role in the explanation.

items.title: Evidence for MeV Radiation from a Large-Amplitude Crystalline Undulator
items.summary: We report evidence for MeV radiation from a large-amplitude crystalline undulator in which 35 GeV/c positrons channel along periodically bent Si(110) planes. Si$_3$N$_4$ stressors produce ten periods with $λ_u = 334~μ$m and midplane amplitude $A_u \simeq 1.85$ nm (XRD-validated modeling). Under planar alignment, the energy-loss spectrum shows an excess over the misaligned case peaking at $6.8 \pm 0.3$ MeV ($4.05σ$), in agreement with simulations and the 7.2 MeV analytical estimate. Simulations for 20 GeV FCC-ee injector positrons predict a peak brilliance of $1.8\times10^{21}$ photons/(s mm$^2$ mrad$^2$ 0.1% BW).

items.title: The physical design of the superfluid helium-4 UCN source at CSNS
items.summary: Ultracold neutrons (UCN) play a crucial role in fundamental physics research, enabling investigations into new sources of CP violation, neutron lifetime measurements, and the exploration of non-Newtonian forces. However, these experiments are often limited by the intensity of UCN sources. The China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS) is developing a UCN source utilizing superfluid helium-4 at Beamline 12. This paper focuses on enhancing UCN density and total UCN number by analyzing various parameters that impact the UCN system, including the influence of different wavelengths of cold neutrons, incident beam size, converter length, wall and reflector materials, extraction method, extraction guide radius, and guide material composition. A preliminary design of the UCN source at CSNS is presented based on this analysis. For a Be-coated converter, the predicted saturated UCN density is 315 UCN/cm^3, with a UCN production rate of 12,055 UCN/s and an extraction efficiency of 84%, yielding approximately 1.3 x 10^6 extracted UCNs per cycle in accumulation mode. The UCN source design presented in this study forms part of the overall physical design of the Neutron Physics and Application Spectrometer at CSNS, which successfully passed its physical design review on March 25, 2025.

items.title: Ultrahigh-speed digital holography reveals blood flow beneath the skin
items.summary: Laser Doppler holography (LDH) leverages ultrahigh-speed digital holography to reveal blood-flow signals in vessels beneath the skin of the closed eyelid and around the eye. We demonstrate this in one volunteer using recordings acquired at approximately 16,000 frames/s under 10~mW of diffuse near-infrared illumination. Numerical Fresnel reconstruction and principal-component filtering reveal branching vascular patterns. These results extend an ocular imaging system to blood-flow visualization beneath the skin without requiring elaborate immobilization procedures.

items.title: Potential for helicity-mediated reverse intersystem crossing in boron--nitrogen-substituted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons with inverted singlet-triplet gaps
items.summary: The prospect of exothermic reverse intersystem crossing (rISC) in organic chromophores with inverted singlet-triplet (INVEST) excited states has stimulated considerable interest in next-generation emitters. However, realizing efficient spin conversion remains challenging because energetic inversion does not necessarily imply the appreciable spin-orbit coupling (SOC) required for rISC. Here, we investigate direct ${\rm S}_1-{\rm T}_1$ SOC in 85 INVEST candidates comprising 32 azaphenalenes, 7 non-alternant hydrocarbons, and 46 boron-nitrogen-substituted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (BNPAHs), all previously predicted to exhibit negative singlet-triplet gaps using a correlated wavefunction method at reliably optimized molecular geometries. While the azaphenalenes and non-alternant hydrocarbons exhibit negligible direct SOC, 28 of the 46 BNPAHs display finite coupling. Analysis of molecular geometries and natural transition orbitals suggests that SOC variations depend on molecular topology, orbital orientation, and electronic-state symmetry rather than nonplanarity or excited-state character alone. We estimate direct-rISC rates with a Marcus model, identifying selected BNPAHs with rates approaching $10^7\,{\rm s}^{-1}$.

items.title: Chaos without Local Spectral Instability in a Kicked Oscillator
items.summary: A damped harmonic oscillator kicked by a pulsed periodic potential can be chaotic although every local Jacobian has eigenvalues inside the unit circle. Damped rotation between kicks lets non-normal shears of opposite curvature compound, so ordered products of contracting Jacobians amplify perturbations. We derive the exact joint spectral radius of the Jacobian family and an exact Lyapunov-exponent decomposition showing how this geometric pumping overcomes dissipation. The proposed mechanism can be realized with laser-cooled trapped ions in a pulsed optical lattice.

items.title: SFQED Cascade Saturation and Laser Depletion Dynamics In CP Rotating Laser Standing Waves
items.summary: Multi-petawatt laser facilities are approaching the regime where colliding laser pulses can spontaneously ignite self-sustained QED cascades, converting laser energy into dense electron-positron plasmas. Using 1D PIC-QED simulations of a circularly polarized standing wave, we characterize the complete lifecycle of seeded cascades from exponential growth through relativistic opacity and macroscopic laser depletion. We show that cascade saturation is governed by the competition between pair creation and longitudinal lepton migration out of the magnetic nodes. The overdense plasma reflects the driving laser, disrupting the standing wave and triggering secondary cascades in adjacent nodes, driving an apparent spatial expansion whose velocity scales linearly with the cascade growth rate. Finally, we generalize an analytical laser absorption model to realistic time-dependent pulse envelopes, accurately reproducing the simulated conversion efficiency of laser energy into gamma-ray photons and electron-positron pairs.

items.title: Generalized Discrete Fractal Dimensions of Graph Families
items.summary: We study generalized discrete fractal dimensions of sequences of finite connected graphs whose diameters tend to infinity. Using normalized shortest-path metrics and a general scale function, we define regularized energy dimensions for vertex probability measures and their optimized versions. We then establish a variational principle that identifies the optimized energy dimension with the supremum of ball-mass concentration dimensions. We also establish monotonicity in the moment order, stability under uniformly comparable measures, and upper bounds in terms of Rényi entropy growth and the upper mass dimension. Cluster estimates and explicit graph constructions show that local vertex concentration can lower the uniform energy dimension without changing the mass dimension. Finally, for uniformly Ahlfors-regular graph families, we obtain an integral criterion for energy boundedness and explicit formulas for the critical dimensions. These results clarify how global growth, local distance distributions, and the choice of scale function jointly determine discrete fractal dimensions.

items.title: From Models To Experiments: Shallow Recurrent Decoder Networks on the DYNASTY Experimental Facility
items.summary: The Shallow Recurrent Decoder networks are a novel paradigm recently introduced for state estimation, combining sparse observations with high-dimensional model data. This architecture features important advantages compared to standard data-driven methods including: the ability to use only three sensors (even randomly selected) for reconstructing the entire dynamics of a physical system; the ability to train on compressed data spanned by a reduced basis; the ability to measure a single field variable (easy to measure) and reconstruct coupled spatio-temporal fields that are not observable and minimal hyper-parameter tuning. This approach has been verified on different test cases within different fields including nuclear reactors, even though an application to a real experimental facility, adopting the employment of in-situ observed quantities, is missing. This work aims to fill this gap by applying the Shallow Recurrent Decoder architecture to the DYNASTY facility, built at Politecnico di Milano, which studies the natural circulation established by internally heated fluids for Generation IV applications, especially in the case of Circulating Fuel reactors. The RELAP5 code is used to generate the high-fidelity data, and temperature measurements extracted by the facility are used as input for the state estimation. The results of this work will provide a validation of the Shallow Recurrent Decoder architecture to engineering systems, showing the capabilities of this approach to provide and accurate state estimation.

items.title: Exact Solution of the Direct and Inverse Quasi-stationary Dynamo Problem in the Expanding Plasma Ball
items.summary: It is shown that differential equation of the quasi-stationary dynamo effect (i.e., generation of the electric fields and currents) in a uniformly-expanding plasma ball with strongly anisotropic conductivity possesses the unique mathematical property: namely, the spectrum of its eigenvalues is universal and independent of physical parameters of the medium. As a result, it becomes possible to introduce a special set of eigenfunctions - which we called the generalized spherical functions - that can be used to solve the dynamo problem in exactly the same way as ordinary spherical functions are used to solve the Laplace equation. The corresponding exact solutions should be especially valuable for treating the inverse dynamo problem, i.e., determination of the plasma parameters from the experimentally measured electric fields and currents.

items.title: Sparse, admissible and interpretable: discovery of isotropic limit surfaces with extended invariant libraries, physically gated mixtures of experts, and end-to-end structural identification
items.summary: Choosing and fitting a limit surface, a yield or failure criterion, to multiaxial strength tests is a model-selection problem with physical side conditions. The equivalent stress concept provides a catalogue of criteria with admissibility conditions: convexity, a unique surface definition, explicit solvability, and bounds on inelastic Poisson ratios. We recast the task as sparse, constrained, differentiable model discovery and compare three representations. The first is a library of invariant monomials I1^a q^m r3^c containing classical criteria as sparse members. The second extends this library by trigonometric Lode-angle terms, restricted by isotropy to cosine modes, and Podgorski-Bigoni-Piccolroaz (PBP) atoms with learnable shape parameters. The third is a mixture of convex gauge experts using either a competition (smooth-maximum) or direction gate with hard-concrete and Gumbel-softmax sparsity. A ray-wise first-root definition gives explicit solvability and an exactly differentiable objective. Convexity and absence of re-entrant branches are differentiable penalties for the libraries and hold by construction for the competition gate. That gate acts as a physically motivated regime selector between mechanisms. Under stated assumptions its responsibilities are the share of failure probability in Weibull statistics, the share of dissipation in Koiter's multi-surface flow rule, and a Boltzmann weight in Gibbs principles. In synthetic benchmarks, the extended library recovers truths like Mohr-Coulomb and PBP surfaces within 1% error. We analyse five experimental datasets: two PMI foams, PA6, concrete, and TSSA in Hencky-strain space. A sharp Lode function matters more than many terms. With PBP atoms, concrete data are fitted with a fourfold lower error. End-to-end identification from notched-bar loads via differentiable finite elements removes nominal-stress mapping bias.

items.title: Divergent Interfacial Lifetimes without Bulk Criticality in Fully Miscible Fluids
items.summary: A fully miscible interface must disappear at equilibrium, but its lifetime need not be governed by a bulk instability. We construct a spatially resolved, dissipative two-field model in which a prepared correlation-excited interface undergoes a localized saddle-node while its homogeneous excited surroundings remain metastable and the relaxed mixture is strictly one phase. The interfacial soft mode produces a deterministic first-passage time that grows as the inverse square root of the distance from the fold and couples directly to the evolving concentration-profile width. The quartic structural potential admits an exact reduction from competing positive harmonic energies on a constrained configuration manifold; sixth- and eighth-order examples provide additional numerical robustness tests. The result is an interface-specific kinetic singularity without equilibrium bulk criticality, subject to explicitly stated microscopic and continuum limits.

items.title: Sphere-based test cases for open boundary simulations in electrostatics and magnetostatics
items.summary: This paper presents a library of sphere-based test cases for verifying the correctness of open boundary simulations in electrostatics and magnetostatics for computational physics and engineering applications. While the energy in the fields of a single sphere is computed for various source configurations, the energy, force and torque (when applicable) are also computed for a pair of spheres. An extension to electromagnetic momentum is also given for the single sphere, demonstrating its use as a benchmarking metric. Analytical expressions are provided for each test case, from which the validity of a simulation environment can be assessed. The finite element method is used as the example context, and four different open boundary methods are evaluated. Once verified, the simulation is used to visualize the Poynting vector field associated with an electric charge placed near a permanent magnet, a configuration for which no analytical expression is available. Simulation files are made available and all numerical experiments are reproducible with the ONELAB open source software.

items.title: The infrared vacuum reduces the laser energy needed to break molecular bonds of simple molecules
items.summary: Vibrational strong coupling within a few molecules has recently been demonstrated in infrared nanocavities at room temperature, opening new alternatives to explore chemical reactions assisted by the confined electromagnetic vacuum. However, the intrinsic mechanisms of how the quantized electromagnetic mode modifies reactivity are not fully understood. We study infrared photodissociation of a single molecule strongly coupled to a resonant infrared nanocavity mode. The coupled system is driven by a monochromatic infrared laser that vibrationally excites the molecule directly or injects photons into the nanocavity field. We compare the intracavity dynamics of CO2 and H2O molecules and demonstrate that the driving energy required for dissociation is up to three orders of magnitude lower inside the cavity by injecting photons into the nanocavity than by driving the molecule directly. We show that photodissociation enhancements are due to the interplay between nuclear anharmonicity, stronglight-mattercoupling, and vacuum field polarisation according to the dipolar nature of the molecular bond. Our results provide the conceptual and numerical tools for understanding how to control chemical processes and to design nanophotonics experiments at the few-molecule level within a cavity quantum electrodynamics perspective.

items.title: Reinforcement learning to design near-perfect acoustic absorbers
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is proposed as a strategy for the multi-objective design of Helmholtz resonators with near-perfect acoustic absorption. The approach formulates resonator design as a sequential decision-making problem in which geometrical parameters are iteratively updated to balance competing objectives, including resonator volume, resonance frequency, and acoustic reflection. A Q-learning algorithm based on a neural network is developed to explore the design space and identify non-dominated solutions, providing a Pareto front of optimal configurations. The acoustic response is evaluated using a transfer matrix method that incorporates viscothermal losses and acoustic end corrections. Three representative designs are subsequently investigated using full-wave finite element simulations, showing good agreement in their absorption and reflection spectra and validating the accuracy of the reduced-order model. Finally, one optimized resonator is fabricated by three-dimensional printing and experimentally characterized in an impedance tube. The measured absorption coefficient reaches approximately 95\% near the resonance frequency, in agreement with the numerical predictions. These results demonstrate the potential of reinforcement learning for the automated design of compact acoustic absorbers and establish a computationally efficient framework combining multi-objective optimization, numerical modelling, and experimental validation.

items.title: Advancing global water cycle science with the upcoming MAGIC satellite mission through data assimilation
items.summary: The GRACE and GRACE-FO missions provide unique global measurements of terrestrial water storage anomalies (TWSA) from space since 2003. However, in order to spatially downscale the GRACE/-FO resolution of 300 km further, and to vertically disaggregate TWSA into soil moisture, groundwater and other contributions, the TWSA observations were assimilated into hydrological and land surface models in the past while improving the realism of the models. With the upcoming MAGIC (Mass Change and Geosciences International Constellation) constellation consisting of two satellite pairs (NASA/DLR GRACE-C and ESA NGGM), significant advancements are expected for the monitoring of water mass changes, with improved temporal and spatial resolution, reduced latency, and with lower noise levels. In this study, we reviewed the capabilities and limitations of existing GRACE/-FO data assimilation systems. We then investigated the benefit of including data from the upcoming MAGIC constellation into existing assimilation frameworks to improve not only data sets for water and carbon cycle science but also in view of operational applications, within a closed-loop simulation. For example, we extended a global 17 years GRACE/-FO assimilation era to a long time series of 33 years with synthetic MAGIC data assimilated and show reductions in groundwater trends errors and errors in identifying hydrological extreme events. We further showed for Europe that both storage and river runoff simulations benefit from more frequent assimilation, which the integration of MAGIC data will enable due to the foreseen 5-daily (instead of monthly) TWSA product. Finally, we demonstrated for the Iberian Peninsula and for Eastern Europe that MAGIC TWSA data assimilation also improved simulated carbon cycle variables via coupling in the land surface model, especially in water-limited regions.

items.title: The amplifier effect of artificial agents in social contagion
items.summary: Individuals and organizations increasingly consider delegating decision-making to AI agents, which may significantly alter social contagion dynamics. We ask whether artificial agents exhibit different adoption thresholds from those of human subjects when making decisions and, if so, how such differences may affect the spread of social contagions. To answer these questions, we conduct two choice experiments - recently administered to human participants - with artificial agents powered by large language models (LLMs). Across two domains and five LLMs, artificial agents exhibit systematically lower adoption thresholds than human subjects. Simulations of diffusion calibrated with the experimental findings show that, holding network structure fixed, even a modest share of artificial agents leads to higher total adoption. Our findings suggest that the presence of artificial agents in social networks can alter diffusion.

items.title: EQUIP-RPT: A framework for objective evaluation of quantitative imaging methods in radiopharmaceutical therapies
items.summary: Quantitative imaging (QI) provides a non-invasive approach for dosimetry and quantitative response assessment in radiopharmaceutical therapies (RPTs). QI methods are being developed for instrumentation, acquisition, reconstruction, and image analysis. However, a key barrier to routine adoption of these methods is that evidence demonstrating reliable performance of QI methods on clinically relevant quantification tasks in RPTs remains limited. Our goal is to outline the Evaluation of Quantitative Imaging Performance in Radiopharmaceutical Therapy (EQUIP-RPT) framework, a structured approach for objective, task-based evaluation of QI methods for RPTs. We outline the EQUIP-RPT framework based on image-science and task-based image-quality evaluation methodology, practical considerations, and recent literature. The framework is organized around four linked design steps: (i) specification of the quantification task, (ii) design of the study population and imaging protocol, (iii) task-specific information extraction, and (iv) selection of figures of merit (FoMs). The EQUIP-RPT framework is presented in the context of four quantification tasks in RPT: activity uptake, absorbed dose, volumetric tumor burden, and lesion-level longitudinal quantifications. The framework distinguishes two paradigms for task-specific information extraction and organizes FoMs according to the performance attributes they characterize. We describe key elements to apply the EQUIP-RPT framework in simulation, physical phantom, and clinical studies. Finally, we show how EQUIP-RPT can be used to generate a quantitative claim based on the evaluation study. The EQUIP-RPT framework is designed to provide a structured approach for objective task-based evaluation of QI methods in RPTs, thereby facilitating clinical translation of these methods.

items.title: Shannon observables: A scalable approach to information decomposition
items.summary: Distributed systems, such as biological and artificial neural networks, process information via complex interactions engaging multiple subsystems, resulting in high-order structure of the information within the system with distinct properties across scales. Investigating how these systems process information remains challenging due to difficulties in defining appropriate multivariate metrics and ensuring their scalability to large systems. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework based on what we call "Shannon observables": quantities that capture essential properties of high-order information processing, yet can be computed directly from Shannon entropies and scale efficiently to large systems. Our theoretical results demonstrate how Shannon observables can be used to resolve long-standing ambiguities regarding the interpretation of widely used multivariate information-theoretic measures. On the practical side, we demonstrate the framework's versatility across several domains. An analytical study of error-correcting codes shows how Shannon observables trace out distinct encoding regimes as channel noise varies; analyses of deep classifiers and convolutional autoencoders reveal characteristic information-processing signatures across layers and over training; and applied to magnetoencephalography recordings from the human brain, the framework yields a cortical atlas exposing pronounced regional structure in directed information transfer. Overall, our framework resolves fundamental limitations in analysing high-order information phenomena and offers broad opportunities for theoretical developments and empirical analyses.

items.title: Block-Fitness Modeling of the Global Air Mobility Network
items.summary: Accurate representations of the World Air Transportation Network (WAN) are fundamental inputs to models of global mobility, epidemic risk, and infrastructure planning. However, high-resolution, real-time data on the WAN are largely commercial and proprietary, therefore often inaccessible to the research community. Here we introduce a generative model of the WAN that treats air travel as a stochastic process within a maximum-entropy framework. The model uses airport-level passenger flows to probabilistically generate connections while preserving traffic volumes across geographic regions. The resulting reconstructed networks reproduce key structural properties of the WAN and enable simulations of dynamic spreading that closely match those obtained using the real network. Our approach provides a scalable, interpretable, and computationally efficient framework for forecasting and policy design in global mobility systems.

items.title: An Analytical Model for Fast Design Optimization and Performance Studies of nuSTORM
items.summary: The concept of generating neutrino beams from stored muons (nuSTORM) has been explored for several decades. A few nuSTORM facilities have been designed for GeV muons, and a design of a sub-GeV nuSTORM, proposed for the European Spallation Source, is now underway. At low energy, the much larger beam divergence can significantly reduce the neutrino flux reaching the detector. Therefore, optimization of facility parameters is essential to avoid additional flux losses. This optimization, however, is not trivial due to the interdependency of the parameters. In this paper, we derive an analytical expression for the absolute neutrino flux incident on the detector front face and show how it can guide the optimization of a nuSTORM facility. The analytical expression is furthermore validated with published data and Monte Carlo simulations from five separate cases. In addition, we show how it can be extended to also predict the neutrino energy distribution at the detector, thus offering a convenient method to estimate the facility performance without time-consuming Monte Carlo simulations of particle transport and decay.
authors: J. P. A. M. de André

items.title: A Magnetic Neuroevolution Potential for Large Scale Spin-Lattice Simulations
items.summary: Accurately describing magnetic order, lattice vibrations, and their coupling at finite temperatures within a unified framework remains a major challenge in atomistic simulations of magnetic materials. In this work, we develop a magnetic neuroevolution potential that explicitly incorporates magnetic degrees of freedom, establishing a potential-energy description jointly determined by atomic structures and magnetic configurations and enabling unified predictions of atomic forces and magnetic energy gradients. Using CrN, Fe, and FeGe with collinear or noncollinear magnetic configurations as representative systems, we demonstrate that the model outperforms standard neuroevolution potentials without magnetic descriptors in predicting energies, atomic forces, and virials, while yielding equilibrium lattice constants consistent with experimental values. Phonon calculations for different magnetic states show that the model captures lattice vibrational responses to changes in magnetic order. Finite-temperature spin-lattice dynamics simulations further reveal the temperature dependence of magnetic excitation spectra, while calculations of the average atomic magnetic moment versus temperature demonstrate the influence of spin-lattice coupling on magnetic transition temperatures and system-size convergence. For Fe, explicitly including spin-lattice coupling brings the predicted magnetic transition temperature closer to experiment, whereas the difference in FeGe is smaller. Performance benchmarks demonstrate that the method enables coupled dynamics simulations of over two million atoms on a single consumer-grade GPU. By combining magnetic-configuration resolution with high computational efficiency, the framework provides an efficient tool for investigating finite-temperature dynamics and spin-lattice coupling in large-scale magnetic systems.

items.title: Hydrogen-Bond Donor-Acceptor Imbalance in Low-Frequency Terahertz Water Spectra
items.summary: The low-frequency dielectric response of liquid water is commonly described by a dominant Debye relaxation together with additional faster contributions whose microscopic origin remains debated. Here we show that the dielectric function of water between 0.14 and 1.21 THz can be represented by a collective Debye relaxation plus a Drude-Smith term constrained to the zero-dc-conductivity limit. The Drude-Smith spectral weight increases upon heating pure H2O from 20 C to 50 C and decreases upon isotopic substitution (D2O at 20 C vs. H2O at 20 C). Molecular dynamics simulations including nuclear quantum effects show correlated changes in the population of water molecules with unequal numbers of donated and accepted hydrogen-bonds. Ab-initio-based spectra calculations further indicate that the ~0.1-1 THz response contains both nuclear-motion and explicit electronic-polarisation/charge-redistribution contributions. We therefore interpret the excess low-frequency THz response as a localised, mixed nuclear-electronic dielectric response correlated with transient donor-acceptor imbalance in the hydrogen-bond network.

items.title: Impurity turbulent transport and its role in driving zonal flows in tokamak plasmas
items.summary: The driving mechanisms of zonal flows (ZFs) in multi-ion-species tokamak plasmas are investigated by using gyrokinetic theory and simulations. For deuterium plasmas containing either helium ash with a steep density gradient or lithium impurity at a high charge concentration, the magnitude of impurity turbulent energy flux (TEF) can be comparable to, or even stronger than, that of the main-ion TEF. Moreover, the impurity TEF significantly drives ZFs. Both the impurity and main-ion turbulent poloidal Reynolds stress (PRS) drives are significant for the case with a high lithium charge concentration. The shielding timescale of the turbulent PRS drive is found to be the damping time of geodesic acoustic mode, which is significantly shorter than one ion bounce period.

items.title: A novel model-based equation for size dependent mean recovery coefficients for spheres and other shapes
items.summary: Background: In NM-imaging, theoretical curves for the recovery coefficient (RC) of the signal maximum and mean are known for spheres and cubes, if a 3D Gaussian PSF is assumed. The RC of the maximum is also known for cylinders. For these and other shapes empirical equations with one or two fit-parameters have been utilized. Methods: An equation for the RC for large objects of arbitrary shape is derived and generalized into an empirical equation for smaller objects, which is verified by numerical simulations. The proposed equation is compared to published results on SPECT kidney phantom measurements and to PET measurements on the NEMA IEC PET body phantom with six spheres. Results: The signal loss (1-RC) for large spheres is inversely proportional to the radius, where the slope is proportional to the FWHM of the spatial resolution. For non-spherical shapes the generalized instead of the volume equivalent radius should be utilized. For smaller objects, an equation with one added empirical fit-parameter is presented. It is demonstrated that the EANM-guidelines' two-parameter logistic function results in a poor fit if the theoretical slope and inverse proportionality are forced and it gives a suboptimal fit when both parameters are fitted. Conclusions: A novel model-based equation for the mean RC-curve is derived. It can be used for arbitrary shapes as long as the sphericity is taken into account and it is accurate down to RC=10%. One parameter is directly related to the spatial resolution, while the other is a shape depending fit-parameter.

items.title: Ultrafast Optical Probing of Laser Processing
items.summary: Laser treatment has emerged into a cornerstone of industrial manufacturing. This creates the demand to understand in detail the involved physical processes and their dynamics, to control the process, and to keep guard in-situ the laser manufacturing steps. Given the contactless interaction of light with matter, particularly optical methods appear most suitable for probing laser processing. This chapter reviews the current scientific and technological state of analyzing laser-based material processing by short and ultrashort optical pulses. For that, sequential passive interrogation of material properties (via reflection, absorption, scattering, diffraction, interference, or specific nonlinear responses) can be employed through so-called pump-probe techniques (where the time-resolution is not given by the detector response time but by the duration of an electromagnetic probe pulse that is interrogating the transient scenery at a controlled delay (typ. fs to μs) with respect to the arrival of the pump laser pulse). These approaches are capable to analyze on microscopic to macroscopic scales a plethora of different processes involved in laser processing, such as heating, melting, ablation, plasma- and shockwave-formation, optical breakdown in surrounding liquids and gases, shielding and accumulation effects, surface solidification and restructuring, etc. A special focus is set on the variety of ultrafast optical imaging schemes for visualizing the dynamics of laser processing at the surface and in the bulk of the irradiated materials, including photography and microscopy, holography, tomography, ptychography, and coherent diffractive imaging. The chapter provides a historic survey, highlights important scientific and technological developments and breakthroughs, discusses selected applications, explores the requirements and current limitations, and sheds light on emerging future trends.

items.title: Track fitting at the full LHC collision rate
items.summary: The LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider underwent a major upgrade before the LHC Run 3 data-taking period, employing an all-software approach in its trigger system. Here we present a fast implementation of a Kalman filter, used in the first trigger stage since the 2025 data-taking period, allowing to determine parameter estimates of charged-particle trajectories at the full LHCb collision frequency of 30 MHz. This approach replaces computationally expensive magnetic field map lookups and numerical integration methods with fast analytical parameterisations while maintaining the mathematical framework of Kalman filtering. Implemented on approximately 500 GPUs within the first-level trigger, the algorithm has replaced the previous partial track fitting algorithm in the real-time trigger environment at the cost of a 2% increase in processing time. Compared to the previous fitter this parameterised Kalman filter shows a significantly improved momentum resolution, resulting in a factor of two improvement in the invariant mass resolutions for reconstructed D0 and J/ψ hadrons. It additionally demonstrates greater robustness against detector misalignment effects and substantially sharpens the discrimination between genuine particle trajectories and accidental background, more than doubling the rejection of the latter at no cost to genuine-track efficiency, for a standard selection working point.

items.title: Imaging performance of a Single-Plane Readout Compton Camera
items.summary: This work presents the design, development, and characterization of a compact Compton camera employing a novel single-plane readout architecture. The proposed concept simplifies conventional multilayer Compton cameras by optically coupling the scatterer and absorber into a single compact detector element using a light guide, enabling readout exclusively from one side with silicon photomultipliers. The system was validated through Monte Carlo simulations, prototype construction, and experimental characterization using standard gamma-ray sources. Detector performance for 511~keV and 662~keV photons was optimized using simulations based on the Geant4 framework, by guiding event selection strategy. Event reconstruction relied on coincidence detection consistent with Compton scattering kinematics, while image reconstruction was performed using maximum likelihood expectation maximization algorithm. The prototype comprises 64 detector elements arranged in an $8\times8$ matrix, read out by an $8\times8$ silicon photomultiplier array. Each element consists of two GAGG:Ce scintillators coupled by a 20 mm long light guide. Measured energy resolutions were $8.9\%\pm1.9\%$ and $10.8\%\pm1.6\%$ for the front and back layers, respectively. Successful gamma-ray imaging was demonstrated for Na-22 and Cs-137 sources, achieving angular resolutions of $12.4^\circ$--$14.3^\circ$ at 511~keV and $14.3^\circ$--$16.8^\circ$ at 662~keV, confirming the feasibility of the proposed single-plane architecture for compact and cost-effective gamma-ray imaging applications.

items.title: Quantum Beam-Splitter Cooling and Thermometry in Large Trapped-Ion Crystals
items.summary: We propose and characterize a protocol for rapid near-ground state cooling of the center-of-mass (c.m.) mode of a large trapped ion crystal. When the initial mean thermal occupation of the mode $\bar{n}_i$ is small compared to the number of ions $N$ ($\bar{n}_i \ll N$), a red sideband drive implements a beam-splitter type state exchange (SWAP operation) between the mode and the collective spin of the $N$ ions, with the latter effectively serving as a quantum harmonic oscillator. Subsequently, a reset of the spins removes the entropy, leading to near-ground state cooling of the c.m. mode. We term this protocol as quantum beam-splitter cooling (QBSC). We analyze the impact of several practical imperfections on the final temperature achievable under QBSC, including finite ion number, off-resonant carrier and blue-sideband contributions, the sideband drives arising from spectator modes, and spatially inhomogeneous driving across the crystal. We outline practical strategies to eliminate the carrier drive. We extend our analysis to multiple cycles of QBSC and also generalize the analysis to demonstrate the cooling of non-c.m. modes using this protocol. Furthermore, we show that measuring the population statistics of the ions at the end of the SWAP operation can enable near-optimal quantum beam-splitter thermometry (QBST), with the classical Fisher information approaching the quantum Fisher information of a thermal state. We discuss the connection of QBSC with continuous sideband cooling and compare QBST with a recently proposed rapid adiabatic passage-based thermometry scheme. Our work constitutes an example of harnessing many-body effects to open new routes to laser cooling and thermometry in large trapped ion crystals.

items.title: On the statistical reliability of chaotic simulations at reduced precision
items.summary: Reduced-precision arithmetic is increasingly used to accelerate scientific simulation, while AI workloads are driving its growing prominence in hardware design. Yet small arithmetic errors do not necessarily imply accurate statistics. Finite representation limits spatial resolution, while rounding can merge trajectories that should separate in chaotic systems, progressively concentrating probability on a shrinking collection of computer states. This redistribution can distort statistical averages well before periodicity becomes apparent; furthermore, disjoint computational basins can induce an initialisation bias, even when the intended equilibrium statistics are independent of the initial ensemble. We use functional graphs and their transfer operators to connect these pathologies to bounds on statistical bias, the duration of accurate averaging, and the effect of reducing precision. Exhaustive numerical experiments on four chaotic maps, with 1-24 significand bits and the 24-bit endpoint matching IEEE FP32, show how initially accurate ensembles drift towards incorrect statistics, with lower precision often bringing this deterioration forward. Stochastic rounding substantially extends some useful averaging windows but leaves others severely biased. Longer computed trajectories can therefore worsen inferred statistics, and a finite average can outperform the "infinite-time" computer average by orders of magnitude. This exposes a risk of statistically biased inference at reduced precision and provides a further motivation for collecting statistics from ensembles of shorter trajectories.

items.title: No prior over nuisance parameters is required for credible intervals and Bayes factors
items.summary: This work shows that there are procedures that maintain the subjective Bayesian property of coherently informing decision making under uncertainty (i.e., if they tell you to take a certain bet, you should) without needing to assign a prior distribution over nuisance parameters, only over the parameter(s) of interest. We first carefully define this sense of 'credibility', and show that within this framework one can condition on any statistic of choice rather than only on the full dataset. This relaxation of credibility is a natural middle ground between Bayesian and frequentist statistics in the following sense: To a p% Bayesian credible set we should assign a p% belief after observing both the dataset and the interval, to p% frequentist sets we can generally only assign a p% belief before observing either the data or the interval, while to the statistical sets proposed here we can assign a p% belief after observing the set, but not necessarily after inspecting the full dataset ourselves. We then show that choosing a conditioning statistic whose distribution we know, or can bound, for each value of the parameter of interest leads to prior-free Bayes factors even for composite hypotheses, and to non-parametric credible sets with priors only over the parameter of interest. We derive such procedures for several (groups of) statistical problems. Particularly noteworthy is that any frequentist test gives a Bayes factor of the power over the size of the test, and that anytime-validity of E-process-based tests can be carried over to this Bayes factor.

items.title: Influence of Assortativity on the SICP Spreading Process in Hypergraphs
items.summary: Many real-world systems involve group interactions that cannot be captured by pairwise graphs. They can be better represented by hypergraphs where each hyperedge could connect an arbitrary number of nodes. The Susceptible-Infected Contact Process (SICP) has been proposed to model the spreading of information and epidemics on hypergraphs. However, how higher-order topological properties of a hypergraph influence the SICP spreading process remains understudied. In this paper, we examine the impact of hypergraph assortativity based on the Neighborhood Coefficient (NC)-the average size of hyperedges incident to a node-on the SICP spreading process. By introducing a low-complexity measure of hypergraph assortativity grounded in analysis of variance, we apply hyperdegree-preserving rewirings to real-world networks and synthetic hypergraph models to tune their assortativity. We find and explain why lower NC assortativity yields higher average epidemic prevalence and lower prevalence variance across different seed selections. This phenomenon is evident when hyperdegree-preserving rewirings are applied to real-world networks with heterogeneous topological structures, but it is largely absent when comparing synthetic random hypergraphs to their rewired counterparts.

items.title: Directed Domain Wall Motion by Radio-Frequency Currents
items.summary: Magnetic domain walls (DWs) are central to emerging spintronic technologies for memory, logic and neuromorphic computing, where their controlled displacement is a key functionality. While current-induced DW motion driven by spin-orbit torques is well established under direct currents, it remains unclear how radio-frequency (RF) currents couple to DWs and whether they can generate directed motion under a symmetric periodic drive. Here we show that RF currents drive DW oscillations, which can be rectified into directed motion through symmetry breaking. Using time-resolved and static magneto-optical Kerr microscopy, we demonstrate that RF spin-orbit torques efficiently excite low-frequency DW oscillations well below the ferromagnetic resonance frequency. Whereas these oscillations remain symmetric in the absence of perturbations, symmetry breaking by a transverse magnetic field produces self-propulsion, while symmetry breaking by an initial current pulse gives rise to sustained DW motion. We further show that in initially uniform magnetic states, RF-driven expansion of a pulse-generated edge domain ultimately results in efficient RF-assisted magnetic switching. Together, these results establish a general framework for understanding how RF-driven DW oscillations are rectified into directed motion, providing new opportunities for their high-frequency control.

items.title: Role of Metastable Dicationic Intermediates in the Breakup of CH$_4^{2+}$
items.summary: We investigate the fragmentation dynamics of methane dication (CH$_4^{2+}$) produced in collisions with 50-MeV C$^{6+}$ ions using the COLTRIMS technique. The method provides complete three-dimensional momentum vectors of the charged fragments, enabling full kinematic reconstruction of the fragmentation process. The dynamics are analyzed using Dalitz plots, Newton diagrams, and the native-frame method to distinguish between concerted and sequential dissociation mechanisms. The data indicate the presence of sequential fragmentation pathways for the CH$_4^{2+}$ $\rightarrow$ CH$_2^+$ + H$^+$ + H, CH$_4^{2+}$ $\rightarrow$ CH$^+$ + H$^+$ + 2H, and CH$_4^{2+}$ $\rightarrow$ C$^+$ + H$^+$ + 3H channels, consistent with dissociation via short-lived dicationic intermediates CH$_3^{2+}$, CH$_2^{2+}$, and CH$^{2+}$, respectively. From the Newton-diagram momentum distributions, we estimate half-rotational periods of approximately 180~fs, 71~fs, and 44~fs for the $\mathrm{CH_3^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{CH_2^{2+}}$, and $\mathrm{CH^{2+}}$ intermediates, respectively, providing characteristic lower-limit timescales for their survival prior to fragmentation. The experimental observations are further supported by comparisons with calculated potential-energy curves.

items.title: Cross-channel amplification of frequency-distinct scattered waves in multibeam stimulated Brillouin scattering
items.summary: Multibeam stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS) can be amplified when one side-scattered wave draws energy from several pumps, each through a separate ion-acoustic-wave (IAW) branch. This is not common-daughter-wave coupling: scattered waves from different parent pumps may occupy nearly the same wave-vector region yet remain distinct optical modes because their frequencies differ. We examine this process with local-growth and finite-width-gain models, three-dimensional coupled-mode calculations and two-dimensional particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations. Adding the extra branches increases temporal growth and spatial gain across the tested crossing angles. In three dimensions, direct branches alone give weak, localized side scatter; with the cross branches present, a strong field fills much of the interaction region even though the incident beams, direct channels and initial seed are unchanged. The distinction persists at fixed total power. The coupled response remains strong as the power per beam falls, whereas the direct-only response drops rapidly. PIC spectra contain nearby scattered-light features accompanied by several pump-specific IAW branches, and the fixed-power scans yield a strong, non-monotonic response. These results support cross-channel feedback through separate IAWs as a multibeam SBS amplification mechanism that may help predict and control SBS losses in laser-fusion plasmas.

items.title: Hypersonic Flow Over an Axisymmetric Open Cavity: Effects of Segmentation Angle and Reynolds Number
items.summary: This study investigates the influence of cavity segmentation angle ($φ$) on the flow characteristics of a cavity mounted on a cone under Mach 6 freestream conditions in a Ludwieg tunnel. Four segmentation configurations, corresponding to $φ= 360^\circ$, $48^\circ$, $32^\circ$, and $16^\circ$, are examined for cavity length-to-depth ratios ($L/D$) of 1 and 6 over a range of Reynolds numbers ($Re_D = 23000$--$74000$). The flow field is characterized using surface pressure and heat flux measurements, complemented by planar laser Rayleigh scattering visualization. The results indicate that, for $L/D = 1$, the downstream Strouhal number ($St$) and mean pressure remain largely unaffected by the segmentation angle and closely agree with those of the axisymmetric configuration. In contrast, the flow parameters within the cavity are larger than in the axisymmetric case, which is attributed to the three-dimensional bounding effect. For $L/D = 6$, the mean pressure distribution exhibits a similar trend across the segmentation angles, whereas the downstream $St$ increases with increasing $φ$, approaching the axisymmetric value. Flow-mode transitions are observed across all segmentation angles, consistent with the axisymmetric configuration. However, both the transition Reynolds numbers and the corresponding flow modes vary with the segmentation angle.

items.title: Extension of the Renard-Deck Drag Decomposition to Compressible Rough-Wall Turbulent Boundary Layers
items.summary: A generalized Renard-Deck (RD) drag decomposition is developed for spatially developing compressible turbulent boundary layers over rough surfaces. Derived from the locally resolved, time-averaged momentum equations, the formulation accounts for both viscous friction and pressure drag without requiring spatial averaging at the roughness-element scale. Eight direct numerical simulations are considered at freestream Mach numbers of 2.5 and 5.86, comparing smooth walls and two-dimensional transverse square ribs ($λ_x/k=8$) under adiabatic and cold-wall conditions. The decomposition reconstructs the total drag with errors below 5%. Mean-flow viscous dissipation and turbulent kinetic-energy production together account for approximately 90% of the drag work. While their contributions are comparable over smooth walls, turbulent production dominates over rough walls, contributing approximately 80%. More importantly, roughness substantially alters the wall-normal distributions of both contributions. Viscous dissipation becomes concentrated near the roughness crest, whereas turbulent production peaks above the crest, with both contributions decaying more gradually into the outer layer than over smooth walls. The resulting differences in their cumulative contributions persist across a substantial fraction of the boundary layer, demonstrating that the energetic influence of surface roughness extends well beyond the roughness sublayer.

items.title: DaYu-TC: a global-regional nested AI system for tropical cyclone forecasting
items.summary: Accurate tropical cyclone intensity forecasts are essential for disaster preparedness, yet persistent intensity underestimation limits the value of artificial intelligence (AI) weather models for predicting these destructive storms. Here we present DaYu-TC, a global-regional nested system that links the preservation of strong-wind and low-pressure signals with high-resolution regional prediction. Its global and regional models share an architecture and extreme-aware training objectives. The regional model combines evolving local states with global forecasts valid at each target time, connecting large-scale environmental information with finer-scale cyclone evolution. In an independent evaluation of 16 western North Pacific tropical cyclones in 2023, the global model retains competitive conventional forecast skill while reducing five-day maximum-wind root-mean-square error (RMSE) by 6-22% relative to other evaluated global AI models. Relative to the global model, regional nesting reduces maximum-wind RMSE by 22.0-33.1% and minimum-pressure RMSE by 28.6-39.8% across 12-120 h. The complete system outperforms concurrent operational high-resolution forecasts from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts for minimum pressure at 12-120 h and maximum wind speed at 48-96 h, with respective RMSE reductions of 26% and 12% at 72 h. Without retraining, the same regional model enhances three other global AI models, reducing overall maximum-wind RMSE by 22.6-28.6%. Five-day forecasts take under one minute on a single GPU. These results establish a transferable multiscale approach to reducing cyclone intensity underestimation, extending advances in AI weather forecasting towards more accurate prediction of high-impact weather events.

items.title: An energy-stable and accuracy-preserving finite volume scheme for wall-distance computations
items.summary: The distance to the nearest wall provides a length scale in models of wall-bounded turbulence. Computing this distance accurately on highly stretched meshes is challenging because small near-wall cells restrict explicit pseudo-time steps and geometric singularities can induce spurious oscillations. To address these challenges, this paper presents a semi-implicit finite-volume scheme based on a scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) for solving the pseudo-time Eikonal equation on unstructured meshes. An upwind weighted least-squares reconstruction supplies the gradients used to evaluate the cell-averaged Eikonal residuals. The artificial-viscosity term is discretized using a two-point face flux whose coefficient vanishes as the regularized residuals in both adjacent cells tend to zero. The SAV update advances the semi-discrete system in pseudo-time by evaluating the residuals and viscosity coefficients explicitly and coupling the wall-distance averages and auxiliary variables implicitly. The analysis establishes unconditional energy stability under homogeneous Dirichlet conditions, permitting a grid-independent global pseudo-time step. The system's M-matrix structure guarantees nonnegative cell averages of the physical wall distance under a separate step restriction, while residual regularization and artificial viscosity preserve the formal order of spatial accuracy. Numerical tests confirm second-order spatial convergence for the quarter-cylinder case and demonstrate robust wall-distance computation on highly stretched meshes typical of Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes simulations. The SAV formulation is independent of the reconstruction scheme, providing a basis for extensions to higher-order finite-volume methods and other nonconservative scalar equations.

items.title: Crystal Nucleation Driven by Microjets from Hydrodynamically Interacting Thermocavitation Bubbles
items.summary: Primary nucleation predominantly dictates the physicochemical, optical and mechanical properties of crystals emerging from solution. Here, we reveal a previously unrecognized nucleation mechanism arising from bubble-bubble hydrodynamic interactions using laser-induced thermocavitation bubble pairs. Under confinement, antiphase generation of two bubbles produces a micron-scale, high-speed liquid jet. Upon impact with the surrounding supersaturated liquid, this microjet generates intense localized shear, thereby inducing crystallization of the model inorganic salt, potassium permanganate. Under identical laser energies and supersaturation levels, crystallization was not observed in single-bubble experiments, in which no microjet was present. We show that the crystallization probability increases with microjet velocity. Boundary integral simulations reveal how experimental parameters such as confinement, bubble spacing, and laser energy govern microjet formation and velocity. We quantify the relationship between jet velocity and the observed enhancement in crystal nucleation kinetics by incorporating shear into the kinetic prefactor in classical nucleation theory. By combining experiments, theory, and simulations, we establish how microjets emerging from bubble-bubble hydrodynamic interactions may influence crystallization kinetics, opening new opportunities for the manufacture of crystalline materials.

items.title: Interface Energy and Phase Transformations: A Comparative Analysis of Cahn-Hilliard and CALPHAD-based Models in Ternary Substitutional Alloys
items.summary: Diffusional phase transformations in alloys are modeled either by phase-field methods of Cahn-Hilliard type, in which a double-well free energy and a gradient term impose an interface energy, or by reactive diffusion models, in which the driving forces follow from the CALPHAD methodology, the convex hull of the molar free energy, and the interface carries no energy. Their numerical schemes are tied to their free energies: phase-field schemes break down when the interface energy is set to zero, and reactive diffusion codes rely on finite differences. We derive, from the thermodynamic extremal principle, a single finite element scheme that covers both limits: the stationarity of the Rayleighian functional (free energy rate plus one half of the dissipation, with mass conservation imposed by multipliers) with respect to the rates, fluxes and multipliers at a frozen state. Fluxes and chemical affinities are primary unknowns, so no derivative of the affinity is required. The time-discrete scheme is the corresponding incremental minimization; it conserves mass exactly and satisfies a discrete energy-dissipation inequality for every convex molar free energy, including the convex hull without regularization. We make explicit that this last case is a degenerate parabolic problem of Stefan type, whose degeneracy can be removed, without altering the free energy, only by a moving mesh; since our aim is the coupling to continuum mechanics and damage on a fixed mesh, we operate at the boundary of degeneracy and show that mass conservation, the energy balance and the second law remain intact there. Thermodynamic consistency is proved for multi-component systems, a scheme relating Onsager and diffusion coefficients is proposed, and the role of interface energy is studied in binary and ternary examples, the latter with vacancies as a non-conserved component.

items.title: Multi-dimensional kinetic modeling of laser-plasma instabilities by a Vlasov-Maxwell system
items.summary: We present PLAW-EM2d (Two-Dimensional PLAsmaWave ElectroMagnetic Simulation), a two-dimensional Vlasov-Maxwell code for kinetic studies of laser-plasma interactions. The code combines a hybrid electrostatic- TEz field decomposition with an Eulerian 2d2v Vlasov solver for the electron distribution function and a cold closure for the out-of-plane response. Vacuum propagation, Landau damping, and a homogeneousplasma comparison with PIC simulations benchmark the coupled solver. We then consider two representative SRS problems. In an inhomogeneous plasma, the code reproduces convective SRS backscatter with a reflectivity consistent with the Rosenbluth estimate. In a transversely extended target, it captures SRS side scattering in a self-consistent two-dimensional Vlasov simulation, resolving oblique electromagnetic and Langmuir waves that satisfy the resonance conditions. These calculations show that PLAW-EM2d can describe both conventional SRS backscatter and a two-dimensional side-scattering channel relevant to laser-plasma interactions in ICF.

items.title: Demonstration of Flying-Focus-Enhanced Relativistic Thomson Scattering
items.summary: We report the experimental demonstration of a spatiotemporally engineered "flying-focus" laser pulse for enhanced X-ray generation via relativistic Thomson scattering. By combining longitudinal chromatic aberration, angular dispersion, and group delay dispersion, we create a relativistically intense laser pulse whose focal point propagates with an independently tunable velocity vector, enabling control of both its speed and propagation angle. Precise tuning of the focal-point trajectory is used to match the motion of a near-counterpropagating ultrarelativistic electron bunch generated by a laser wakefield accelerator. This spatiotemporal velocity matching extends the interaction length while mitigating nonlinear scattering effects, resulting in an enhanced X-ray yield. Simulations indicate that this approach can increase the spectral density and brightness of Thomson-scattered X-ray beams by orders of magnitude relative to equivalent focusing without spatiotemporal control. The technique provides a new degree of freedom for high-intensity laser-matter interactions, allowing dynamic intensity structures with programmable two-dimensional motion and opening a route to enhanced laser-particle interactions and next-generation ultrabright radiation sources.

items.title: Boundary-layer detachment and infinite-Reynolds limit of two-dimensional wall-bounded flows
items.summary: Understanding boundary-layer detachment and its consequences for the infinite-Reynolds-number limit remains a major challenge in fluid mechanics. Here, direct numerical simulations of incompressible flow in a two-dimensional periodic channel with no-slip walls are used to investigate this problem. Reynolds-number-dependent initial conditions are constructed with a boundary layer of Prandtl thickness that converge in the energy norm to an analytic, stationary Euler flow, while the associated Prandtl system develops a finite-time singularity. Highly resolved simulations show boundary-layer detachment and departures from Prandtl scaling, yet provide numerical evidence that the Navier--Stokes solutions continue to converge to the Euler flow over the simulated time interval. In particular, the squared energy norm of the velocity difference and the time-averaged energy dissipation both scale approximately as $Re^{-1/2}$, consistently with established convergence criteria. Although the detached vortices become more numerous and intense as the Reynolds number increases, their characteristic size and occupied area appear to decrease. These observations suggest how boundary-layer detachment and the breakdown of the Prandtl description can coexist with convergence to a smooth Euler flow.

items.title: Hybrid Machine Learning for Physically Consistent Prediction of Mutual Diffusion Coefficients in Binary Liquid Mixtures
items.summary: Experimental data on mutual diffusion coefficients in liquid mixtures are scarce, and existing prediction methods are unreliable for non-ideal mixtures. Building on HADES, our hybrid model for self-diffusion coefficients, we introduce the Enhanced Vignes Equation (EVE), which augments the Vignes equation with a deep-set model. Its inputs are molecular descriptors derived from SMILES and activity-coefficient information from HANNA, a machine-learning model for activity coefficients. EVE predicts Maxwell--Stefan diffusion coefficients; the corresponding Fickian coefficients follow from the thermodynamic factor, likewise obtained from HANNA. Trained and evaluated on 2106 experimental data points for 123 binary mixtures, EVE outperforms all available semi-empirical models, halving the mean absolute relative error for mixtures without experimental infinite-dilution diffusion data. Combined with HADES, EVE yields the complete set of self- and mutual diffusion coefficients of a binary mixture from SMILES and pure-component viscosities alone. EVE and HADES are available at https://ml-prop.mv.rptu.de/, and the code is fully disclosed.

items.title: Improvements in Tropical Cyclone Representation in JRA-3Q over ERA5
items.summary: Reanalysis products are widely used for long-term tropical cyclone (TC) studies, yet the fidelity of their TC representation is not fully established. We evaluate TC representation in the recently released JRA-3Q reanalysis against the higher-resolution ERA5 using the SyCLoPS tracker. JRA-3Q achieves substantially higher detection skill, with a hit rate of 90% and a false alarm rate of 6% during 1979-2024. Unlike ERA5, which exhibits markedly degraded detection skill during the pre-satellite era, JRA-3Q maintains stable performance over time. We analyze false alarms and missed TCs in the North Indian basin, TC vortex evolution following TC bogussing, and the spatial variance of column-integrated moist static energy, showing that JRA-3Q's improvements stem from both reduced model biases and a more effective and consistently applied TC bogus scheme. A decomposition of TC representation errors into contributions from tracking algorithm, reanalysis, and best-track uncertainty helps explain the sources of these biases.

items.title: When optimized geometries are not optimal: Implications for inverted singlet-triplet gap predictions
items.summary: Pseudo-Jahn-Teller distortions can substantially alter singlet-triplet gaps, potentially reversing the predicted excited-state ordering in molecules proposed to exhibit inverted singlet-triplet (INVEST) gaps. In this study, we benchmark geometry optimization methods for 13 azaphenalenes against CCSD(T)-quality reference geometries, assessing their ability to reproduce symmetry lowering and its consequences for singlet-triplet gaps. Among the methods examined, $ω$B97M-D4 reliably describes the distorted geometries and corresponding gaps, whereas the commonly used methods B3LYP and MP2 retain high-symmetry structures, potentially leading to false-positive INVEST assignments. We further assess $ω$B97M-D4 geometries across 337 molecules comprising azaphenalenes, boron/nitrogen-substituted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and non-alternant hydrocarbons. Subsequent L-CC2/aug-cc-pVDZ calculations predict negative singlet-triplet gaps for 85 molecules and identify discrepancies with previously reported INVEST assignments. These findings demonstrate that the choice of geometry optimization method is crucial for reliable INVEST screening, particularly in systems susceptible to symmetry-breaking distortions.

items.title: Rotational covariance, continuous spectrum and non-modal growth of three-dimensional planar weak viscous shock layers
items.summary: Three-dimensional linear stability of a weak shock layer is analyzed with exact Reynolds-number-independent base-flow and stability equations, written in shock viscous scales. For any base flow depending on the shock-normal coordinate alone, with zero transverse velocity, the eigenvalue problem is proved covariant under rotation of the transverse wavenumber vector. Its eigenvalues depend only on the magnitude of this vector, and every eigenmode decouples exactly into an in-plane acoustic-entropy branch, which carries all dilatation and thermodynamic coupling, and an out-of-plane vortical branch, governed by a single shear-diffusion equation. The continuous spectra are obtained using the Grosch-Salwen far-field companion matrices and, independently, closed-form dispersion relations. The two agree to machine precision. The vortical continuous spectrum retreats from the real axis exactly as the square of the transverse wavenumber, while the acoustic-entropy continuous spectrum is strictly damped and, numerically, its least-damped point does not increase with this wavenumber. Three-dimensional disturbances are therefore damped at least as strongly as their two-dimensional counterparts with the same in-plane wavenumber, as measured by the least-damped point of the spectrum, exactly for the vortical branch and numerically otherwise, making the reduction the exact, Reynolds-free counterpart of Squire's transformation, in which the wavenumber magnitude plays the role of the Reynolds number. Planar oblique shock stability results are obtained from normal-shock results by a Doppler shift. Non-modal growth, measured in the Euclidean norm, is far stronger in the post-shock than in the pre-shock gas. Linear optimal disturbances of the shock-layer ripple the post-shock density field without displacing the shock front.

items.title: Analytic T-Matrix Formalism for Helmholtz Resonators
items.summary: We develop an analytic T-matrix formalism for two-dimensional circular acoustic Helmholtz resonators with thin rigid walls. The central idea is to use an aperture projection operator to obtain a compact expression for the T-matrix with explicit coefficients describing coupling and decoupling between external fields and cavity resonances. An equivalent formulation providing much faster convergence uses an aperture-to-Fourier map and an edge-adapted basis for the aperture flux. The method extends directly to multiple apertures of arbitrary angular widths and positions. The calculated scattering spectra agree with full-wave numerical simulations. For single- and double-aperture resonators, we decompose the T-matrix into even and odd parts under inversion to identify the channels associated with Willis coupling. We show how internal losses enable direction-dependent scattering and absorption when inversion symmetry is broken, while reciprocity ensures equal extinction for opposite incidence. Finally, we show how shifting the expansion origin redistributes radiation among multipole channels, enabling more compact T-matrix representations.

items.title: Transient CFD simulation of a linear start-up of a variable speed reversible pump-turbine
items.summary: The integration of intermittent energy sources has led to a growing demand for fast response and partial-load operation of hydraulic turbines, making variable speed units increasingly important. In hydraulic turbines, frequent start-stop cycles generate the highest loads under normal operating conditions. Although historically infrequent and often neglected in turbine design, the growing occurrence of these cycles now necessitates particular consideration due to their contribution to fatigue loading and reduced runner lifetime. Experimental investigations of turbine start-up are costly and cannot be conducted during early design stages. While start-up sequences have been simulated with CFD for fixed speed turbines, each approach has had notable limitations. Some studies have lacked experimental validation. Some studies have used reduced geometrical domains, making it unclear whether inaccuracies stem from geometry simplification or turbulence modelling, and others employ hybrid LES/RANS models, at a very high computational cost, making them unfeasible for use during the design phase.
