items.summary: Crypto agility maturity models aim to support organizations in preparing for cryptographic transitions, such as migrating to post-quantum cryptography. Recognizing the importance of measurable maturity, NIST references several such models in its guidance. Given NIST's influence on cybersecurity practice, these models may shape organizational planning and governance mechanisms. However, their design quality has not been systematically evaluated. In this work, we assess three industry-driven maturity models against established design principles. Our analysis reveals recurring weaknesses, particularly the lack of measurable, reproducible assessment criteria and limited prescriptive guidance for improving crypto agility. At the same time, we highlight individual strengths that can assist practitioners in choosing among the models and derive concrete recommendations for strengthening future crypto agility maturity models.

items.title: It Was Better Not to Know: Digital Recognition, Family Authority, and Postpartum Mental Health in Bangladesh
items.summary: Postpartum mental distress affects roughly one in five mothers in low- and lower-middle-income countries, yet recognition and support remain limited where formal mental-health care is scarce, and family relationships govern health decisions. We report a five-month interview study with 20 mothers in urban, urban slum, and rural Bangladesh who had given birth within the previous two years. Mothers encountered the concept of postpartum depression incidentally, through Facebook and YouTube recommendations rather than deliberate search or clinical guidance, and then used these platforms for private sensemaking without disclosing. Recognition, however, rarely traveled beyond the self: mothers could identify their distress while families dismissed it, leaving them with knowledge but no authority to act. Participants sought validation as a precondition for support and described recovery as relational rather than clinical or digital. We argue that postpartum technologies should engage partners, families, and community health workers rather than placing recognition solely on mothers.

items.title: Robust Amortized Simulation-Based Inference via Learned Error Models
items.summary: Recent advances in neural density estimation have enabled amortized Bayesian inference for complex stochastic simulators. However, these methods rely on simulators accurately reflecting the true data-generating process and can degrade significantly under model misspecification. We consider the setting where multiple unlabeled observations are available and introduce robust variational neural posterior estimation (RVNP), an amortized Bayesian inference method that uses an importance-weighted autoencoder to jointly learn a misspecification-robust posterior proxy and an explicit error model that captures the simulation-to-reality gap. Our results show that RVNP can recover robust posterior inference in a data-driven and interpretable manner, outperforming previous methods on multiple metrics across misspecified benchmarks.

items.title: AnalogLayoutWorld: An Open Benchmark for Agentic Analog Layout Design
items.summary: Coding agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in software development, yet their ability to tackle long-horizon engineering tasks governed by physical constraints remains less understood. We study this question through analog circuit layout, which demands domain knowledge, geometric reasoning, and iterative interaction with design and verification tools. We introduce \textbf{AnalogLayoutWorld}, an open-source agent benchmark with 40 expert-reviewed tasks for end-to-end layout generation from fixed transistor-level netlists. It combines an integrated design environment with independent physical and post-layout electrical verification, as well as objective layout quality metrics co-designed with analog layout experts. Across 13 model--harness configurations, 91.1\% of attempts produce GDS layouts, but only 23.0\% satisfy the benchmark's acceptance criteria. We also evaluate Novara, an internally developed agent system, which achieves the highest reported aggregate score. Our analysis links performance differences to test-time scaling under fixed budgets, suggesting that reasoning efficiency and effective use of verification feedback help sustain design quality as task complexity grows.

items.title: Fairness-Aware Federated Learning with Trajectory Shapley Value
items.summary: Federated learning is an emerging distributed paradigm that addresses the challenges posed by heterogeneous, privacy-sensitive data. It enables multiple clients to train a model collaboratively by aggregating their local updates at a server. However, conventional aggregation schemes typically use fixed weights that fail to reflect unequal and time-varying client contributions, leading to biased and unstable learning. To improve fairness and stability, we propose the Trajectory Shapley Value (TSV), a contribution metric that evaluates how each client influences the optimization trajectory of the global model using a validation-based, temporally consistent utility. Building on TSV, we design FedTSV, an adaptive aggregation method that converts per-round evaluations into dynamic client weights, allowing the server to respond to heterogeneous and adversarial participation in real time. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that FedTSV accelerates convergence, improves robustness, and yields more equitable contribution assessments, thereby providing a principled foundation for fairness-aware federated optimization. The source code is available at https://github.com/DCN-FAU-AvH/FedTSV.

items.title: Primer: An AI Framework for Instructor-Centered Educational Simulation Creation
items.summary: Educational simulations are a well-established pedagogical technique that gives learners opportunities to apply knowledge, respond to challenges, and reflect on their performance. High-quality simulations, however, are difficult to build, requiring instructor input, scenario design, character development, scaffolding, technical implementation, and repeated revision. This paper presents Primer, an open-source, LLM-agnostic AI-supported system that helps educators create adaptive educational simulations. Educators contribute their knowledge of the subject, lesson, and students, while generative AI produces responsive variations of practice for students. Primer uses a multi-agent system centered around executing educator's instructional intent through the entire learning experience. We hope that by releasing Primer as an open-source system, including its prompts and GitHub repository, we provide a foundation for development and research on educator-in-the-loop AI authoring, multi-agent educational workflows, and simulation-based pedagogy. Further, by allowing the use of various AI models, including local and open source models, we provide the opportunity for implementation under varied governance regimes. Primer points toward a model of educational AI in which instructors can create locally grounded practice opportunities based on their own materials, goals, examples, and knowledge of students.

items.title: ElasticDino: Dense Semantic Features Using Elastic Deformations
items.summary: Vision transformers (ViTs) serve as the backbone for countless vision tasks, including dense prediction tasks, such as segmentation and depth estimation, even though the quadratic complexity of self-attention severely limits feature resolution and induces spatial artifacts. In this work, we introduce ElasticDino, a lightweight adapter which produces high-resolution feature maps, adhering to the fine details of the input image. As a key insight, we observe the consistency of artifacts across channels, and simultaneously resolve them to match the input image structure. Using a slim architecture based on spatial deformations, ElasticDino produces pixel-aligned, high-resolution feature maps efficiently. Leveraging deformations allows strictly preserving sharp semantics, and thereby avoiding the smoothness biases inherent to alternative approaches. Due to the absence of ground truth, we employ pixel-level semantic segmentation and depth estimation with linear heads to predict a set of downstream dense tasks, guiding the deformation process without leaking task-specific semantics into the model. We demonstrate superior accuracy over current methods on a range of popular dense task benchmarks, with better computational performance.

items.title: Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents: Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games
items.summary: Weight-space programming (WSP) uses language models to construct neural network weights without training. We test whether known game mechanics can be compiled into compact agents that generalise to held-out levels, renderings and start states within a game family. Writers receive simulator source with held-out level data removed for 20 privately authored, unpublished ARC-AGI-3-style game families. With a fixed 57k-parameter recurrent architecture, the strongest writer reaches 56% held-out-level success with feedback, while the four main writers' Python players reach 97-100%. An exploratory free-architecture condition reaches 68-90%. Learning from support-level examples transfers much less well, but these learners lack the source information given to writers. Written networks have a program-like structure: 93% of parameters are zero, and 90% of the rest are small integers or powers of two. NumPy players under comparable computation caps reach 91%, versus the networks' 79%. Training the strongest writer's architectures from scratch yields about 1% success within our budget. Written fixed-network weights are fragile, and standard PPO removes most of their success. Prompts for noise robustness increase tolerance by about four orders of magnitude for two of three writers, but PPO makes larger updates and still removes most success. These results demonstrate rule-to-network compilation in this setting, while showing limited benefits over Python programs and no successful combination with the tested PPO fine-tuning.

items.title: Disambiguating 2D-3D Correspondences in Gaussian Splatting-based Feature Fields for Visual Localization
items.summary: While Gaussian Splatting-based Feature Fields (GSFFs) have shown promise for visual localization, this paper highlights that photometrically optimized GSFFs are inherently not suitable for 2D-3D matching. The volumetric extent of each Gaussian induces many-to-one pixel-to-point mappings that destabilize PnP-based pose estimation, while photometric optimization gives rise to superfluous Gaussians devoid of multi-view consistency. To address these issues, we propose SplitGS-Loc, a GSFFs construction framework for localization, which disambiguates 2D-3D correspondences by exploiting Gaussian attributes. Our key design, Mixture-of-Gaussians-based splitting, decomposes each Gaussian into smaller Gaussians, replacing ambiguous many-to-one with precise one-to-one correspondences. In parallel, we exploit composition weights from GS rasterization to select Gaussians that significantly and consistently contribute across multiple views and aggregate discriminative features through strong pixel-Gaussian associations. The resulting compact yet discriminative feature fields enable stable PnP convergence, achieving competitive performance on localization benchmarks. Extensive experiments validate that SplitGS-Loc extends the utility of photometric GSFFs to accurate and efficient localization by exploiting Gaussian attributes, without per-scene training for feature fields or iterative pose refinement. The code is available at: https://github.com/misoleekr/SplitGS-Loc.

items.title: Efficient Multi-Organ Segmentation Using SpatialConfiguration-Net with Low GPU Memory Requirements
items.summary: Even though many semantic segmentation methods exist that are able to perform well on many medical datasets, they are often not designed for direct use in clinical practice. The two main concerns are generalization to unseen data with a different visual appearance, e.g., images acquired using a different scanner, and efficiency in terms of computation time and required Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) memory. In this work, we employ a multi-organ segmentation model based on the SpatialConfiguration-Net (SCN), which integrates prior knowledge of the spatial configuration among the labelled organs to resolve spurious responses in the network outputs. Furthermore, we modified the architecture of the segmentation model to reduce its memory footprint as much as possible without drastically impacting the quality of the predictions. Lastly, we implemented a minimal inference script for which we optimized both execution time and required GPU memory.

items.title: Morphological Simplification in Alzheimer's Disease: Computational Analysis and Identification From Connected Speech
items.summary: Purpose: Morphology is often regarded as relatively spared in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and is rarely modeled in connected speech. This study asked which morphological features distinguish speakers with AD from healthy controls, how well morphology classifies AD compared with other linguistic levels and BERT-based models, and whether the signal exceeds transcript length and vocabulary. Method: Fifty-five automatic measures in eight families, seven of them new and theory-motivated, were computed from participant speech in the ADReSS Cookie Theft descriptions (78 AD, 78 controls) and analyzed with group comparisons, equivalence tests, SHAP, family ablation, likelihood-ratio tests, feature-selection classifiers, and BERT-based models. The automatic measures were validated manually, and models were transferred to two other corpora. Results: Nineteen of 38 measures differed between groups: speakers with AD produced fewer suffixed and inflected words, shorter verbs and nouns, and fewer present-progressive but more past-tense forms (largest effect r = -0.42), whereas errors were rare and statistically equivalent between groups. Eight measures survived adjustment for length and lexical frequency. With test-set feature selection, morphology reached a macro-F1 of 0.85, on par with syntax and above fine-tuned BERT (0.80 over five seeds); fully cross-validated selection gave 0.62. Adding morphology to BERT improved AUC (0.91 vs. 0.89) but not macro-F1. Transfer was limited, although two thirds of the effects kept their direction in mild cognitive impairment. Conclusions: AD connected speech shows morphological simplification and temporal reanchoring rather than breakdown. Morphology is more informative than its reputation suggests. Keywords: Alzheimer's disease; morphology; connected speech; ADReSS; inflection; tense and aspect; SHAP; machine learning; BERT

items.title: CLASP: A Cluster-Level Autonomous Selective Picking Robot with a Soft Rolling-Band Gripper for Fresh-Market Blueberry Harvesting
items.summary: Fresh-market blueberries require selective, gentle picking, which is labor-intensive and expensive. Over-the-row machine harvesters are fast but non-selective, bruising mixed-ripeness fruit and limiting yield to the processing market. Selective robotic harvesters typically target individual fruits rather than fruit clusters, which limits harvesting efficiency for small, densely clustered blueberries. This paper presents CLASP, a Cluster-Level Autonomous Selective Picking robot with a Soft Active Rolling-Band Gripper (SARB-Gripper). Two compliant bands envelop the cluster and roll against the fruit, drawing mature berries off in sequence, while closed-loop regulation of the pulling force keeps the applied load below the immature detachment threshold. A global-to-local perception pipeline pairs an eye-to-hand camera for global cluster detection and target selection with an eye-in-hand camera for local localization and cluster orientation estimation. Field measurements confirm a clear detachment-force separation between mature and immature fruit, and the SARB-Gripper reproduces a commanded pulling force to within \SI{3.7}{\percent}, enabling selective harvesting at the cluster level. In end-to-end field trials, CLASP autonomously grasped 23 of 25 presented clusters (\SI{92}{\percent}). With the component cost of approximately \$3326 per unit, CLASP offers a scalable approach to selective cluster-level harvesting for fresh-market blueberries.

items.title: A PTAS for Constraint Satisfaction Problems on Interval Graphs and Bounded Rank-Width Graphs
items.summary: We present a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for all Boolean arity-two maximum constraint satisfaction problems (Boolean Max-2-CSP) where the constraint graph is either interval or has bounded rank-width. This class of problems includes, for example, Max-Cut, Max-DiCut, Max-2-Lin(2), and Max-2-SAT. In particular, this settles the approximability of Max-Cut on interval graphs. To achieve these results, we show the following. 1. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, there is an $n^{\mathcal O(r \varepsilon^{-2})}$-time $(1 - \varepsilon$)-approximation for Boolean Max-2-CSP on graphs of rank-width at most $r$. 2. There is a polynomial-time algorithm that, for any interval graph $G = (V, E)$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, finds a subgraph $H = (V, F)$ of $G$ such that $|F| \geq (1 - \varepsilon) |E|$ and $H$ has rank-width at most $\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon^{-1})$. Our techniques additionally extend to all bounded-alphabet arity-two max CSPs.

items.title: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models
items.summary: Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. \emph{Rather than deciding how much to think}, we explore a different paradigm, \emph{zero-or-$T$ thinking}: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of $T$ tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a \emph{hybrid decision model} (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight \emph{self-routing block} chooses between them. The block estimates the \emph{value of thinking}, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price $λ$ set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce \emph{Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation} (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores $0.857$ against Jev's $0.851$ ($+0.7\%$) at a median $0.179$\,s against $0.652$ ($-72.5\%$). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by $80.1\%$.

items.title: Lara Mini Base: Language Diversity as a Resource, Not a Trade-off
items.summary: General-purpose language models are trained mostly on English: over open models we review, at most, non-English pretraining data makes up only a 12% share. Models built for European languages give them far more, but score well below general-purpose models of the same size. A common concern is that, in small models, languages compete for capacity. We present Lara Mini base, a model trained from scratch on 6T tokens in English and 44 other languages, which together cover all 24 official languages of the European Union. As training progresses, the 44 other languages together come to outweigh English. To give these languages enough capacity at low cost, Lara Mini base uses a mixture of experts architecture with 7.2B total and 0.6B active parameters. Among open base models with up to 2B active parameters, it achieves the highest average score across standard English, multilingual, math, and code benchmarks, ahead of models trained on 4 to 6 times as many tokens. Its margin is largest on multilingual benchmarks in the languages it supports and on math benchmarks. It supports contexts of up to 128k tokens. We find that our MoE architecture reduces capacity competition between languages. For a single user on one GPU, without quantization, it generates text at least 1.8 times faster than any model with a higher average score. We release the weights of Lara Mini base under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. In addition, we will release T-HellaSwag, a higher-quality machine translation of the commonsense reasoning benchmark HellaSwag into 110 language variants.
authors: Andrea Fernandez Tostado Ro. Diego Andrea

items.title: A Disease-specific Retinal Aging Biomarker for Predicting Progression to Late Age-related Macular Degeneration
items.summary: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a leading cause of irreversible vision loss in older adults. While chronological age is a primary risk factor, it inadequately reflects individual variations in retinal aging, limiting effective AMD risk stratification and timely intervention. Here, we propose and validate fundus-based AMD age (FAA), which quantifies disease-specific retinal aging in AMD and captures accelerated AMD-related retinal aging, thereby improving prognostic precision over chronological age. Trained on 36,782 images from 2,192 participants in the Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) dataset and validated across AREDS and AREDS2 cohorts, our model demonstrates significant improvements over traditional chronological age-based approaches. Specifically, integrating the proposed FAA into Cox proportional-hazards models significantly enhances prediction performance. FAA improved the C-index from 0.836 to 0.888 and reduced the 5-year Brier score from 0.050 to 0.046 in AREDS, with consistent gains observed in AREDS2 (C-index 0.715 to 0.756; 2-year Brier 0.078 to 0.076). FAA showed improved prognostic performance across the two datasets and under different phenotype definitions (reading center-defined vs. specialist-defined grading), supporting its potential utility for AMD risk stratification. These findings highlight the advantage of incorporating FAA into AMD risk prediction frameworks, supporting further evaluation of FAA for AMD risk stratification.

items.title: On Designing Diffusion Autoencoders for Efficient Generation and Representation Learning
items.summary: Diffusion autoencoders (DAs) are variants of diffusion models that use an input-dependent latent variable to capture representations alongside the diffusion process. The latent variable is typically used for tasks such as downstream classification, controllable generation, and interpolation. However, the latent variable has an effect on unconditional generation, with performance strongly dependent on how this variable is modelled and learnt and how it is used in the denoising process. Here, we draw a connection between DAs and a particular class of improved diffusion models---those that learn their forward (noising) process---to argue that DAs have unrealised potential as generative models. We develop a variant of DAs, termed diffusion models with $z$ (DMZ), to show that the adoption of certain design decisions, such as the choice of latent variables and conditioning method, can help realise this generative potential. Through extensive experiments and ablations, we show DMZ converges in fewer iterations, generates high-quality samples with fewer denoising steps, and learns effective latent representations for downstream tasks like classification and domain transfer.

items.title: Will It Survive? Deciphering the Fate of AI Agent-Authored Code in Open Source
items.summary: AI coding agents such as GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex and Devin now open pull requests (PRs) that are merged into open-source projects. Industry reports suggest that AI-assisted code is revised or reverted soon after it is written, which raises the concern that agent code is "disposable". However, little is known about what happens to agent code after it is merged. Knowing how long this code survives, and why it is changed, can help maintainers decide how much review it needs. We performed a survival analysis of the 648,959 lines that 2,794 merged PRs added outside vendored and generated paths in 215 open-source repositories from the AIDev dataset, comparing agent-attributed and human code within the same repositories. Agent-attributed code is not modified sooner than human code. When each PR is weighted equally, agent-attributed lines are modified later (HR = 0.83, 95% CI [0.75, 0.93]). This difference comes from the supervised assistants, mainly Copilot and Codex (HR = 0.76). Code from Devin does not differ from human code over the whole period (HR = 0.95), but among PRs merged after mid-May 2025, code from both the supervised assistants and Devin is modified later. Without PR weighting, the difference is not statistically significant. When agent-attributed code is modified, the intent of the change is similar to that of human code (Cramer's V = 0.080). A file's size and recent changes predict whether agent-attributed code will be modified better than its code tokens do (AUC-ROC 0.78 vs. 0.70), and process features predict when it will be modified only weakly (Macro F1 of 0.31 against 0.25 for a random guess). Our findings suggest that agent code is not disposable, but whether it survives longer than human code depends on the agent, on when the code was merged and on how the comparison is computed.

items.title: SignalAudit-QD: A Reproducible Audit Resource for External Signals in AI-Query Forecasting
items.summary: SignalAudit-QD is a reproducible audit resource for testing whether a dated public signal adds information beyond query history in a fixed 20-term U.S. AI panel. It aligns two archived Google Trends extractions with eight USPTO AI-patent publication streams and releases origin-indexed predictions, paired losses, provenance, executable tests, and tamper-evident run manifests. Both inputs are retrospective reconstructions obtained after the modeled 2020--2023 origins; the task is therefore a pseudo-origin assay within frozen measurement vintages, not a historical deployment simulation. In the designated one-month comparison, adding a two-component patent block to a level ridge changes macro mean absolute error by +0.0012 Trends points, with conditional 95% moving-block interval [-0.0363,+0.0387]. This establishes neither aggregate benefit nor equivalence. Alternative dimensions, semantic mapping, patent definitions, a second extraction, and a three-month horizon remain unresolved; persistence-anchored and nonlinear hosts instead show model-specific worsening, tiny for the anchored fit. Matched timing controls expose availability assumptions, while a planted-signal assay detects only the largest tested injection. A within-query high-interest alert demonstrates the released interface but not online utility. The contribution is a bounded negative case study and an extensible evidence schema for auditing external-signal claims in temporal information retrieval.

items.title: Accurate predictions of properties of energetic materials with tabular foundation models
items.summary: We use TabPFN, a recently developed tabular foundation model, to predict three properties of energetic materials: impact sensitivity, decomposition temperature and crystal density. Without any hyperparameter tuning, TabPFN outperforms the best published models for all three properties. It also substantially outperforms a wide range of established machine-learning models, including tuned gradient boosting (XGBoost), random forests and Gaussian processes. This holds both when the models are given hand-crafted molecular descriptors and when they are given learned representations from Chemprop's message-passing neural network. In particular, for all three properties, TabPFN applied to Chemprop's own embedding is more accurate than Chemprop's predictions. TabPFN is also among the fastest models we consider, more than an order of magnitude faster than XGBoost. As TabPFN predicts the entire distribution of the target rather than just a single value, it offers built-in uncertainty quantification, which we compare with the empirical distributions of compounds with repeated measurements. Finally, we interpret the predictions using Shapley values, which rank the features by their importance.

items.title: Data Center Governance Under AI Expansion Pressures
items.summary: The promised benefits of data centers are global, but their negative impacts are very much local, affecting the energy bills, aquifers and living environments of citizens across the United States. While governments and authorities have historically provided data centers with incentives such as tax credits and exemptions, AI's aggressive growth in scale has changed this dynamic, and recent months have seen them issue bills and file lawsuits in order to ensure that data centers remain a net positive influence on their legislatures. Existing pieces of federal legislation -- such as the Public Trust Doctrine, the Pollution Prevention, Clean Air and Safe Drinking Water Acts -- exist to manage natural resources, but their scope remains contested, and the current federal government's stance on competitiveness and growth of AI has put the onus on regional governments to endeavor to protect local resources. There are also state- and regional laws and regulations that are relevant for building and operating data centers since, in practice, they require substantial land, electricity, water, and infrastructure at a local level. Given this situation, communities are currently provided with the opportunity to raise their concerns regarding the potential negative impacts of how data centers are built and operated, and have existing regulations that can be used to put pressure on data center operators.

items.title: S1-Evo: Experience-Guided Evidence Competition Attacks on Typed System-1 Decision Models
items.summary: Typed System-1 (S1) decision models are increasingly deployed in LLM agents for routing, moderation, and authorization to cut inference cost, yet untrusted context can still manipulate typed outputs and alter execution branches. Unlike autoregressive System-2 (S2) models, S1 interfaces score dynamic rules and options without token-by-token decoding, mismatching attacks targeting text continuation or explicit override commands. We propose S1-Evo, a self-evolving framework tailored to S1's contract-based option competition and margin feedback. S1-Evo perturbs untrusted fields via contract-aware evidence channels to induce \emph{evidence competition} with original task evidence while preserving fact invariance. Offline on seed tasks, it optimizes candidates via feedback search guided by directional margins and re-verification, distilling verified flips into experience cards. At test time, S1-Evo retrieves relevant cards to construct perturbations for unseen tasks. Across four benchmarks and three S1 models, S1-Evo reaches 71.99\% mean ASR and 57.47\% high-confidence ASR on \texttt{jev-1.14}, and causes up to 24.00\% E2E agent violations.

items.title: Universal Infectious Disease Forecasting with Mantis 2
items.summary: Public health agencies need to anticipate how outbreaks will unfold, when they will peak, and how long demand on health services will remain elevated. We previously developed a foundation model, Mantis, which was trained entirely on simulated outbreaks---enabling us to generate the diversity and scale of training data needed to support forecasting across diseases. However, our previous work left unresolved when simulation improves predictions and how it should complement observational data. Here, we varied the balance of simulated and observed training data while holding forecasting tasks fixed and varying the available surveillance history. We found that simulation-rich training was particularly valuable with limited local history, and its relative advantage diminished as more observations became available. We also found that simulation-based training reduced exceptionally large forecast errors, suggesting that mechanistic knowledge can help compensate for limited local evidence. Building on these findings, we developed Mantis 2, which combines simulated and observational training to jointly forecast up to six variables sixteen weeks ahead. Across 30 forecasting tasks, Mantis 2 achieved the best aggregate probabilistic accuracy over short, medium, and long horizons among the machine learning, statistical, and baseline models evaluated. It missed roughly 30\% fewer outbreak peaks than the strongest comparison model, with successfully anticipated peaks identified more than six weeks in advance on average. We publicly release Mantis 2, enabling public health agencies and researchers to forecast disease outcomes without developing a separate model for each disease or location.

items.title: Time Flies When You Parallelise: Pareto-efficient Time Series Foundation Models with Linear Recurrences
items.summary: Time series foundation models have demonstrated strong zero-shot forecasting performance, but computational efficiency remains a central architectural challenge. Temporal self-attention incurs quadratic cost in the number of temporal tokens, while nonlinear recurrent state transitions restrict parallel computation along the temporal dimension. We introduce ci-proto, a family of time series foundation models based on Mamba-3, whose linear state recurrences support chunk-wise parallel-in-time computation during training, and inference costs that scale linearly with sequence length. The architecture alternates recurrent temporal processing with cross-variate attention, supporting multivariate probabilistic forecasting with past-only and future-known covariates. Across fev-bench's 100 forecasting tasks, ci-proto XL sets a new state of the art among time series foundation models. The five ci-proto variants also make up the entire Pareto frontier for mean scaled quantile loss and mean absolute scaled error against both parameter count and median runtime.

items.title: Kezek: Splitting Mono Two-Person Conversations into Per-Speaker Tracks for Full-Duplex Dialogue Data
items.summary: Full-duplex spoken dialogue models learn turn-taking, overlaps and backchannels from conversations recorded with one channel per speaker, but most available conversational audio is a single mono mix. We present Kezek, a model that turns a mono recording of exactly two people into one track per person with the original length and timing; overlaps and short replies ("yeah", "mm-hm") stay on the track of the person who said them. Kezek decides who speaks when and who is who once for the whole recording (stage 1: a two-voice activity model guided by a speaker fingerprint trained to be insensitive to phase), and a conditioned time-domain separator only carries out that decision (stage 2), with outputs that always sum to the input. Standard separation metrics miss the failures that matter for dialogue data, so we report short-reply retention, leakage onto the other person's solo, channel swaps and coverage. Against the open pipeline pyannote -> DialogueSidon on the same recordings, Kezek keeps more short replies (0.83 vs. 0.69 on Open Yap test; 0.80 vs. 0.71 over the other's speech on unseen telephone speech from CallHome English), mostly because it returns the whole recording while the external pipeline drops part of it (on the audio both return, reply retention is about the same: 0.859 vs. 0.865 on Open Yap); it also leaks less, swaps channels less often, and runs 4-5 times faster (about 230 hours of audio per GPU-hour). We also report negative results and an ideal-mask ceiling that locate the remaining gap: quiet replies under a louder voice. Code and weights are released under permissive licences.

items.title: Beyond Curiosity: Habit and Organizational Learning Capability as Predictors of Shadow AI
items.summary: Generative AI has entered the workplace faster than organizations can govern it. A large share of employees now use AI tools their employer has not sanctioned, and many actively conceal that use, but the psychology of this covert technology behavior remains poorly understood. A common assumption, in popular accounts and early commentary, treats unauthorized (shadow) AI use as curiosity-driven exploration by adventurous individuals. We test this against a competing account grounded in the psychology of habitual technology use, in which automaticity rather than exploratory disposition sustains the behavior. Using survey data from 510 employed generative AI users across multiple countries, we adjudicated among individual and contextual predictors (workplace curiosity, habit, technology-acceptance beliefs, and organizational learning capability) with hierarchical regression, relative weights analysis with bootstrap confidence intervals, and full-subset dominance analysis. Habit was the strongest predictor, accounting for 28.3% of explained variance, and completely dominated joyous exploration, the curiosity dimension most aligned with the exploration account, across all 512 possible predictor subsets. Joyous exploration contributed 3.4% (95% CI [1.6, 7.4]) and fell to nonsignificance once use behavior and habit were modeled. Learning-supportive organizational conditions accounted for a further 24.1% and operated additively rather than by moderating dispositions. Parallel models decomposing the outcome showed the same dominance pattern for unauthorized use and concealment, and perceived social support for AI use was protective specifically against concealment. These findings reframe shadow AI as a habit-and-environment phenomenon rather than an individual-exploration phenomenon. The cross-sectional design means causal claims are exploratory.

items.title: SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection
items.summary: The easy access to Large Language Models (LLMs) has made AI-generated texts on the web increasingly ubiquitous, making AI-text detection a crucial task. Prompts greatly influence the generation process, but existing detectors focus solely on the generated texts --- supervised methods learn from labeled texts only, and zero-shot methods rely on the text's probability distributions --- ignoring the underlying generation process, which limits their robustness in open-world scenarios. We introduce SPADE: Soft Prompts for Ai-text DEtection, a novel framework for detecting AI-generated text that transfers better across datasets. Specifically, we measure the prompt's influence and use it as a discriminative signal. We characterize the prompt's influence by introducing a Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) term that captures how much a prompt explains a text. Based on this quantity, SPADE trains one soft prompt per class to amplify the separation, and predicts the class whose prompt best explains the candidate text. Extensive experiments on several benchmarks against various detectors demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our method, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets.

items.title: STEALTH: Steganographic Text Encoding Agnostic to Low-Level Tensor Hardware
items.summary: Provably secure linguistic steganography hides a message inside text sampled from a language model, so that without the key, a stegotext is computationally indistinguishable from an honest model sample. Nearly every such scheme assumes the receiver can recompute the sender's token probabilities exactly bit for bit. We show this assumption is fragile: across three model families, bit-exact schemes decode almost none of our messages once the receiver's floating-point precision, quantization, or GPU architecture differs from the sender's, or even when the receiver merely scores a text in parallel versus one token at a time, with the same model, precision, and hardware held fixed. We present STEALTH, a scheme built for exactly this setting. The sender draws each token with an exponential race driven by keyed pseudorandom noise, so a receiver's probability mismatch flips a token only when the race is close; a rateless spinal code, decoded by beam search, absorbs the resulting flips without the sender and receiver ever agreeing on a single distribution. We prove stegotexts remain indistinguishable from honest samples under this construction. Empirically, STEALTH decodes every message we sent for every receiver in the sender's model family, at every precision and quantization level, on smaller models, and on a different GPU architecture. STEALTH is even robust across different model families with separate vocabularies and tokenizers, decoding every message we tested. Our approach carries far more payload per token than prior robust schemes, and trained steganalyzers and a targeted statistical test both fail to distinguish its stegotexts from honest model output.

items.title: Report of the 8th LSVOS Challenge: Mobile Unified Multimodal Understanding
items.summary: This report summarizes the Mobile Unified Multimodal Understanding (MUMU) track of the 8th Large-scale Video Object Segmentation (LSVOS) Challenge, held in conjunction with ECCV 2026. MUMU asks for a single unified model that jointly performs multi-concept image tagging over quality, scene, and event vocabularies, open-vocabulary object detection, and concise image captioning, within a budget of 0.5B parameters and 8 GB of peak inference memory. Submissions are ranked by a weighted task score scaled by an efficiency factor. We describe the tasks, rules, and evaluation protocol, report the final results, and review the methods of the top three teams. All three leading solutions build on the compact Florence-2-base model, but extend it in different ways: lightweight tagging heads with cross-task inference refinement, a shared low-rank adapter trained on coverage-aware multi-source data with task-dependent decoding, and a training-free pipeline that maps captions to tags and applies detection test-time augmentation. The results show that a compact prompt-based vision-language model can serve all three outputs when supervision, decoding, and cross-task cues are designed for each task, while open-vocabulary detection on novel categories remains the main bottleneck.

items.title: FrOGS: Discrete Neural Sampler for Independent Alloy Configurations Across Chemical Conditions
items.summary: Predicting the thermodynamic properties of an alloy requires sampling its configurations across many chemical conditions and recovering free energies on a common absolute scale. Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is the standard tool, but it requires separate simulations at different conditions, and auxiliary free-energy methods such as thermodynamic integration are used to place results on a common absolute scale. Modern discrete neural samplers typically use reverse KL divergence as the objective and can be mode-seeking or biased. We present Free energy Offering Generative Sampler (FrOGS), a hybrid discrete neural sampler that couples an autoregressive model to a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) to be trained jointly under a single shared loss. FrOGS draws i.i.d. configurations, returns an unbiased estimate of the partition function, and gives consistent estimates of thermodynamic observables. We train a single model across a wide range of chemical conditions to produce estimates on a common absolute free-energy scale. FrOGS matches exact finite-size results on the 2D Ising model and reference phase diagrams for AgPd and CuAu, without mode collapse. We additionally compare to SEGAL, a published autoregressive baseline, and find that only FrOGS recovers the stability range of the CuAu$_3$ phase.

items.title: Scentree: a framework for generating scenario trees for multistage stochastic programming
items.summary: We present scentree, an open-source Python package for constructing scenario trees for multistage stochastic programming models using either historical data or samples drawn from a probability distribution. It combines machine learning and multivariate time series models to obtain a scenario fan that captures dependencies in the stochastic processes. This scenario fan is subsequently reduced into a scenario tree that preserves representativeness of the stochastic process, providing a flexible and extensible framework for uncertainty modeling in stochastic programming problems. The framework can also be naturally applied to two-stage stochastic programming problems. Key contributions are the joint modeling of the stochastic process, preserving correlations between all random variables, and the automation of the complete workflow, including forecasting model selection, parameter estimation, scenario fan generation, and scenario tree construction. In addition, scentree does not assume any underlying data distribution, reducing the statistical expertise required to produce a scenario tree, and is modular by design, allowing external forecasts and other partial executions of the workflow.

items.title: Batch, Pack, and Prove: More Efficient Verifiable Computation for CKKS
items.summary: An important challenge in homomorphic encryption (HE) is ensuring the integrity of the encrypted computations. Although verifiable computation can address this in theory, making it practical is far from trivial. [Cascudo et al. CRYPTO 2025] recently proposed a solution to this problem for the CKKS scheme. In particular, they propose new succinct arguments that efficiently prove arithmetic circuits and range checks over the ring $R_q = \mathbb{Z}_q[Y]/(Y^N+1)$, and combine them to prove computations on CKKS ciphertexts. Despite the important progress, their work faces scalability challenges: the size of the polynomial commitment proofs, a large $O(N)$ overhead in range proofs, and the lack of an explicit method for efficient -- sublinear in circuit size -- verification. In this paper we present new techniques that remove all these bottlenecks. First, we provide a more efficient arithmetization of CKKS computations. Second, we introduce BatchFold, a new polynomial commitment for $R_q$ that supports batched evaluations and achieves shorter proofs. Third, we design packing, a novel algebraic technique that eliminates the need to commit to massive polynomials and removes the $O(N)$ overhead in range proofs. Finally, we introduce SparsePack, an efficient protocol for proving the evaluations of sparse, circuit-dependent polynomials, leveraging both packing and batched evaluations. We evaluate the efficiency of our solution on a generic neural network architecture, achieving proofs several orders of magnitude smaller and faster than prior approaches.

items.title: Beyond Word Error Rate: A Failure Taxonomy of Streaming Dictation ASR
items.summary: Speech recognition (ASR) systems are usually compared by word error rate (WER) on recorded files, after punctuation, capital letters and number format are removed. In dictation, the audio is streamed live and the text goes into the user's message as written, so what matters is which mistakes the user has to fix. The test set, streamed to eleven ASR systems, comprises 106 scripted English dictations from one speaker (read in a quiet room, with a fan on, and whispered), 20 clips in each of eleven other language and dialect sets, and 400 recordings that join clips in two languages. Every error was sorted by a fixed rule into four levels: recognition, output formatting, language handling and, for the self-hosted models, audio dropped before the model. Systems with similar WER failed in different ways. Zoom Scribe and OpenAI's GPT-Live-Transcribe have almost the same WER on quiet English (7.4% and 7.3%), but 34.7% and 8.8% on whispered English. Zoom and both AssemblyAI models left out 26-28% of whispered words, and still 21-26% with their end-of-turn detection relaxed or off; seven other systems left out at most 3%. Qwen3-ASR's 32% came from the speech detection in our own deployment (6% when relaxed). Across 107 EARS speakers, the same four systems lost 7-31% of whispered words, while six others lost under 2%. With only English selected, Gemini, Deepgram and our self-hosted Whisper lost the non-English part of a two-language recording in 86-99% of recordings, against 33-46% with both languages selected, while GPT-Live-Transcribe, OpenAI's realtime Whisper and Meta lost it in at most 20%. Running Whisper behind a Silero voice activity detector that drops audio judged to be silence raised whispered WER from 10.1% to 51.4%. Most English results come from one read speaker. The code, the recordings, both references and every transcript are released.

items.title: CT-SGAL-LIO: Causal Continuous Time Refinement of Discrete LiDAR Inertial Odometry
items.summary: State-of-the-art LiDAR-inertial odometry methods, including those on richer state manifolds, achieve strong global accuracy, yet their pose stream alternates between propagation and correction and can oscillate over short horizons even when globally accurate. Most existing methods follow these approaches: they either modify the filter to enable faster updates or estimate a continuous-time trajectory from raw LiDAR and inertial data. The latter involves extra optimization, delaying state updates and becoming less robust during rapid rotations or accelerations. We propose CT-SGAL-LIO, a continuous-time refinement module that smooths the posterior pose stream of a discrete SGal(3) estimator without modifying the estimator itself. The key novelty is to perform continuous-time trajectory refinement directly on the projected SGal(3) posterior: we fit a cubic trajectory over a bounded window of recent poses and evaluate it at a small fixed lag. This places the query time within the observed interval, so the refined pose is obtained by interpolation rather than extrapolation, while preserving causal operation. CT-SGAL-LIO improves relative trajectory accuracy on 17 sequences from three public benchmarks. Across 17 sequences from GRAND-TOUR, MCD, and GEODE, CT-SGAL-LIO improves short-term motion accuracy while largely preserving global accuracy. RTE improves by up to 70% on GRAND-TOUR and on all seven GEODE sequences, with 9.9-51.1% reductions. A 19.5-min R-Campus run also reduces posterior jumps by 85.4% with only a 4.7 mm change in the end-to-start gap. We plan to release our source code and results to support community validation and reproducibility.

items.title: CauProphet: Teaching Agents to Develop Causal Cognition like Humans
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly support long-horizon tasks by leveraging external memory and past experience. However, existing agents mainly retrieve records or summaries, lacking the ability to form and refine causal understanding of the world. Inspired by human causal cognition, we introduce CauProphet, an agent that develops and updates causal knowledge within its Causal Cognition. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge in Causal Cognition with current evidence to construct a Causal Belief, a structured belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions. It uses this belief for decision-making and continuously updates both the belief and Causal Cognition as new observations emerge, enabling causal knowledge that persists beyond individual experiences. Evaluations demonstrate that CauProphet progressively acquires causal knowledge and transfers it to future decision-making. In financial research, CauProphet leverages prior discoveries to improve downstream analyses and outperforms all baselines in mean rank correlation with next-day returns, achieving a 25.4% improvement over a baseline agent. It also improves prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Further experiments validate its ability to perform reliable causal analysis and action selection across scientific and everyday tasks, demonstrating the potential of causal experience learning for next-generation LLM agents. The project repository is available at https://github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauProphet.

items.title: CADET: Construction of PCB Routing Instances with Executable Demonstrations
items.summary: Printed circuit board (PCB) routing is the stage of physical layout that finds paths connecting the placed pads of each net. Public datasets in this domain are few, and most contain only the final states of routed boards, not demonstrations of the electronic design automation (EDA) engine actions that produce them. To close this gap, we propose CADET (Constructing executAble Demonstrations for Engine-grounded Training), which jointly generates synthetic boards and demonstrations built from EDA engine actions. The resulting RouteDemos provides 100,000 synthetic boards routed with zero design rule violations (DRVs), together with their demonstrations. Their distributions over 17 statistics resemble those of 142 real reference boards. CADET trains a routing policy on these demonstrations with behavior cloning and fine-tunes it with reinforcement learning (RL). On real test boards, the policy raised the rate of complete DRV-free routing from 38.0% to 67.2% over an RL-only baseline. This rate was comparable to that of the open-source autorouter FreeRouting and exceeded those of the other baselines, including GPT-6 Astra. We release the dataset and its generation code as open source at https://github.com/LGAI-Research/CADET.

items.title: Scaling limit of the Random Language Model
items.summary: We develop a quantitative theory of the Random Language Model (RLM), an ensemble of stochastic context-free grammars, in a scaling limit where the number of hidden symbols $N \to \infty$ while the grammar temperature $\tildeε_d \to 0$ at fixed $x = \tildeε_d \log N$. In this limit, the model admits a controlled description based on a large-deviation principle over rule-usage patterns. A semi-annealed approximation maps the problem to a class of Random Energy Models with nontrivial combinatorics. We show that the RLM exhibits a freezing transition at a critical value $x_c=1/8$, below which rule usage condenses on a subset of preferred rules and language statistics acquire a nontrivial dependence on corpus length. A second characteristic scale at $x=1/2$, associated with the breakdown of Gaussian fluctuations, separates transition and babbling regimes. Across regimes, we derive explicit scaling laws for the number of distinct rules, entropy, and energy, identifying distinct frozen and critical regimes controlled by the interplay of grammar size, corpus length, and temperature. The theory resolves previous ambiguities regarding the existence of a thermodynamic transition and explains the slow approach to the large-$N$ limit as a consequence of the dependence on $\log N$. It further provides a unified framework in which universal statistical properties of language emerge from typical realizations of generative grammars, with implications for both natural language statistics and the behavior of large language models. Heaps' law and Zipf's law are both derived, and the dependence of predictive entropy on context length is rationalized. Comparison with empirical measurements of Heaps' and Zipf's laws yields parameter estimates for real languages.

items.title: SAGAS: Semantic-Aware Graph-Assisted Stitching for Offline Temporal Logic Planning
items.summary: Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) provides a rigorous framework for specifying long-horizon robotic tasks, yet existing approaches face a trade-off: model-based synthesis relies on accurate labeled transition systems, whereas learning-based methods often require online interaction, task-specific rewards, or specification-conditioned training. We study LTL-specified robotic planning and execution in an offline, model-free setting, where the agent is given only fixed, task-agnostic trajectory fragments, with no dynamics model, task demonstrations, or online data collection. To address this setting, we propose SAGAS, a framework that combines the compositionality of symbolic synthesis with the data-driven reachability structure learned from offline trajectories. SAGAS first learns a reusable latent reachability graph and a frozen goal-conditioned executor from fragmented offline data. For each new LTL formula, it performs task-time semantic graph augmentation to ground state-defined propositions on the learned graph and applies Büchi product search to synthesize a cost-aware accepting prefix--suffix waypoint plan executed by the frozen executor. This separation of learning and planning enables zero-shot generalization to unseen LTL formulas and new predicates supported by the offline data, without task-specific rewards, additional data collection, or policy retraining. Experiments on LTL task suites constructed from OGBench locomotion domains show that SAGAS achieves higher success rates and lower execution costs than baselines on diverse unseen tasks, with further evaluation in OGBench Scene demonstrating its applicability to robotic manipulation.

items.title: Automated PD-L1 Tumor Proportion Scoring with Uncertainty-Guided Triage in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
items.summary: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) tumor proportion score (TPS) informs immunotherapy selection in non-small cell lung cancer. Near the 1% and 50% cutoffs, the score should also indicate when closer review is warranted. We designed a three-stage framework to follow the sequence of TPS assessment. Stage 1 identifies tumor regions and excludes macrophage-rich patches. Stage 2, a dual-branch cell counting network (D2Count-Net), counts PD-L1-positive and PD-L1-negative tumor cells in these regions to calculate TPS. Stage 3, TPS-Guard, an uncertainty-guided triage mechanism, reports model uncertainty as the disagreement among independently trained models, refers the most uncertain slides, and flags scores near the 1% or 50% cutoff when model estimates disagree across that cutoff. Flags state the reason for referral or alert the pathologist to possible scoring errors on auto-reported slides. In a retrospective, single-center study, 154 whole-slide images were scored by three pathologists, and the model and each pathologist were compared in turn with the mean of the other two. On the 114 slides unseen in training, model mean absolute error (MAE) was 6.96 percentage points, within the range of the three pathologists (4.24 to 8.29), and model uncertainty correlated with absolute TPS error (Spearman rho = 0.77) and inter-pathologist disagreement (rho = 0.71). After referral of the 15% most uncertain slides, model and pathologist MAE both decreased. Applied without retraining to an external, publicly available dataset, TPS-Guard still directed review to higher-error cases, and referring more uncertain cases raised sensitivity at the 50% cutoff. TPS-Guard provides reasons for reviewing individual automated scores and identifies slides that also produce greater disagreement among pathologists. Prospective reader studies should assess TPS-Guard's effect on TPS reporting.

items.title: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP
items.summary: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam

items.title: Uncertainty-aware quantum machine learning based on Dempster-Shafer theory
items.summary: A large body of work in quantum machine learning has centered on characterizing the expressivity and performance of quantum models. In contrast, little attention has been paid to the reliability of predictions beyond average performance measures such as accuracy. In this work, we introduce an uncertainty-aware quantum classification framework based on Dempster-Shafer theory. This theory allows to express uncertainty through weights assigned not only to individual classification labels but to sets of labels. We introduce a training strategy that enables parameterized quantum circuits to learn such assignments directly from data. This provides an efficient way to prepare the corresponding quantum states and enables the application of different post-processing strategies. In particular, it offers a practical setting for quantum Dempster-Shafer fusion procedures with polynomial resource requirements, even when the corresponding mass functions are defined over exponentially many subsets. Overall, our work represents a step toward enabling quantum models to express uncertainty about their predictions, thereby extending the evaluation of quantum models beyond predictive performance alone.

items.title: Non-Functional Requirements to Hyperparameter Translation for Quantum Software via LLMs
items.summary: Quantum software engineering (QSE) lacks validated approaches for translating natural-language non-functional requirements (NFRs) into execution parameters such as shots and transpiler optimization levels. Existing methods emphasize semantic similarity rather than execution outcomes. We evaluate seven large language models (LLMs) against a deterministic heuristic baseline using 540 synthetic and 18 real-world user stories. We assess semantic accuracy and execution outcomes, including time, cost, top-state probability, and two-qubit gate exposure, through Qiskit/Aer simulations. All LLMs significantly outperformed the heuristic in semantic accuracy, achieving 55.6 to 83.3 percent on real-world stories compared to 16.7 percent for the heuristic. However, no LLM demonstrated statistically significant superiority over others on the real-world dataset. Speed- and cost-oriented configurations reduced execution time and cost, but fidelity improvements were not supported. Some failures resulted from provider safety refusals rather than translation errors. Our findings demonstrate the potential of LLMs as middleware for NFR-to-configuration translation in QSE, while emphasizing execution-based validation, human oversight, and careful interpretation of model differences.

items.title: TokenStream: Multi-Subject Personalized Video Generation with Token-wise LoRA and Guided Attention
items.summary: We introduce TokenStream, an optimization-based framework that composes independently learned subject identities in text-to-video generation without a reference-video training dataset or joint optimization of each new subject combination. Learning from a single reference image makes subject appearance difficult to separate from static-image bias, while merging independently trained adapters can mix identities. Token-wise LoRA (ToRA) restricts low-rank updates to the cross-attention value projections of subject-associated text tokens, providing a separate adaptation path for each subject. A T2V-guided stream copies queries and keys from the frozen base model during early denoising to reuse its layout and motion priors while retaining personalized values. We also introduce Multi-DB, a 30-subject, 122-prompt benchmark with appearance-free prompts and varied interactions. On Multi-DB at 1.3B, TokenStream improves identity preservation from 0.422 for DreamBooth to 0.467 and textual alignment from 0.652 to 0.688.

items.title: Human or Synthetic? What a Fixed Budget Buys for Post-Training
items.summary: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.

items.title: Look It Up: Multi-bit LLM Watermarking via Codebook Search
items.summary: Attributing short LLM-generated texts to a specific source remains challenging for existing multi-bit watermarking methods, which often require long generations or costly decoding to recover payloads reliably. We propose a codebook-based watermarking scheme that maps an $n$-bit payload to a longer $u$-bit codeword and embeds it during generation through token-level logit biasing. During extraction, the received bit sequence is matched to the nearest codeword in a precomputed secret codebook using Hamming or Levenshtein distance. Experiments show that our method achieves near-perfect recovery for 16-24 bit payloads on 200-token generations and strong performance on 127-token generations for base models. Results are weaker on some instruction-tuned models with very short texts, where low-entropy output distributions reduce embedding reliability. We also study a BCH-based variant that avoids codebook storage but generally reduces robustness. The Levenshtein variant improves resilience to deletions and light paraphrasing, while insertions and stronger rewrites remain challenging. We analyze collision probability, codeword separation, extraction time, tokenization consistency, and text quality, highlighting both the practicality and limitations of codebook-based watermarking for short-form attribution.

items.title: Control-Flow Profiling for Workload Representativeness
items.summary: Workload characterization in performance engineering often replaces expensive target executions with lower-cost proxies, including reduced datasets, miniapps, and training inputs. Such substitutions require empirical verification that the proxy faithfully exercises the target's dynamic execution behavior. This paper presents an address-keyed control-flow profiling methodology and tool suite designed to evaluate workload representativeness directly from compiled, unmodified binaries. We pair time-ordered basic-block vector (BBV) recurrence analysis with exp-branchprof, an experimental Valgrind tool that captures five orthogonal structural profile families spanning branch direction bias, four-bit global history contexts, dynamic indirect targets, function call transitions, and intraprocedural CFG edges. Our method compares weighted event distributions from two executions of the same binary. It reports support coverage, reference event-mass coverage, distribution distance, entropy-derived quantities, and phase structure, rather than claiming that a single similarity score certifies a proxy. We validate the tool with exact-oracle microbenchmarks across AArch64 and x86-64, covering conditional and inverted exits, calls, returns, direct and indirect jumps, and forked processes. We then apply the workflow to SPEC CPU2017 and CPU2026 train/reference pairs and seven refrate/refspeed pairs. The corpus contains both close matches and cases where a shorter execution reaches much of the same code but misses substantial target, callgraph, CFG, or BBV event mass. The accompanying artifact supports the same analysis for proprietary workload/proxy pairs without requiring raw PC-level profiles to leave the collection environment.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Verification in Dafny
items.summary: Formal verification of complex algorithms requires expertise in program specification, invariant construction, mathematical proof, and the management of automated theorem provers. Although large language models (LLMs) can generate program code and proof fragments, reliably developing complete machine-checked verifications remains challenging: it requires an iterative process of constructing and validating specifications and invariants, building proofs, diagnosing solver failures, and optimizing verification performance. This paper presents a systematic ten-step workflow for LLM-assisted verification of scientific algorithms using the Dafny verification system. The workflow integrates algorithm formalization, contract development, empirical invariant validation, proof construction, bottleneck profiling, and resource-driven proof optimization. We applied the workflow using Antrhopic's Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 models, combining LLM-driven development with automated testing and verification feedback, while retaining human oversight for correctness-critical decisions and strategic interventions. We evaluate the approach on 37 complex algorithms from graph theory and labelled transition systems. Notably, we verified the Hopfcroft-Tarjan triconnectivity test, demonstrating that even highly challenging algorithmic verification tasks can be carried out through a structured LLM-assisted workflow. Many of our machine-checked verifications were obtained within hours to a few days of interactive development. Our results suggest that LLM-assisted workflows can shift the role of the human verifier from detailed proof construction toward supervision, specification review, and strategic guidance.

items.title: How Hard Is It to Rig a Benchmark? A Social Choice Analysis of Leaderboard Robustness
items.summary: Multi-task benchmarks have become a central pillar of machine learning research, yet their growing influence has incentivised benchmark gaming -- strategic actions taken to improve the leaderboard rank of a specific model. Treating datasets as voters and models as candidates, we consider benchmark-specific training -- the inclusion of benchmark data in training -- as a form of election manipulation. For any ordinal benchmark, the problem of choosing datasets to train on so that a target model becomes top-ranked corresponds to shift bribery, a class of manipulation problems from computational social choice. Leveraging this identification, we show that the benchmark-specific training problem is NP-hard under Borda count and mean win rate. Complementing this worst-case perspective, we introduce the instance-level robustness, the minimum number of datasets a model developer must include in training to top a given leaderboard, and derive expressions for it under arithmetic mean, median, mean win rate and pairwise majority. We evaluate these expressions on MMLU under HELM and on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) under the Open LLM Leaderboard. Across both suites, mean win rate is hardest to manipulate: this gap is clear on BBH (24 tasks, 4507 models), where its median robustness is 22 tasks (92%), compared with 13 (54%) under arithmetic mean and 12 (50%) under median and pairwise majority.

items.title: Collision-Resilient All-to-All Broadcast Scheduling in Underwater Acoustic Networks
items.summary: This paper studies all-to-all broadcast scheduling for underwater swarms with collision-resilient physical layers that can decode asynchronously overlapping packets. Propagation-aware collision-free schedulers coordinate packet arrivals but do not account for this reception capability. We first design a data-driven neural reception model that captures per-interferer power and timing effects. The model improves prediction accuracy over SINR baselines while admitting an exact mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation. The resulting neural-network-embedded MILP (NN-MILP) optimizes transmission times while explicitly encoding schedule-dependent overlaps and the predictor's inference, enabling globally optimal scheduling for small-scale instances. For larger networks, a two-stage ant colony optimization (ACO) heuristic combines low-cost transmission-order search with neural-aware timing refinement. Simulation results show that ACO shortens broadcast rounds compared with existing schedulers. It approaches the NN-MILP optimum on small-scale instances while supporting larger networks at substantially lower computational cost.

items.title: Beyond Co-Movement: Locality by Exposures Enables a Joint Factor-Graph Framework for Portfolio Diversification
items.summary: Current portfolio construction methods are either agnostic to the effects of idiosyncratic shocks (standard factor models) or to the latent data structure driving systematic returns (recent graph-based approaches). This presents an opportunity to combine the complementary market aspects captured by the factor and graph domains, allowing asset allocations to operate directly on the underlying market structure, rather than on its observed co-movement or its finite-sample artefacts. In this work, we introduce the Mutually-INformed Graph-Locality and Exposures framework (MINGLE), which mutually regularises the factor and graph domains by redefining graph locality through systematic factor exposure profiles, rather than via observed co-movements. This is formalised through a unified Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) framework that jointly learns a latent factor representation and its induced graph topology directly from market returns. The resulting exposure-similarity graph aligns more closely with established economic sectors than conventional correlation-based graphs. Portfolios constructed from this representation are shown to consistently outperform their correlation-based counterparts across a range of volatility regimes and transaction cost levels. For rigour, paired statistical testing confirms that these gains stem from the reconciliation of the graph and factor domains.

items.title: Pretraining Data Statistics Shape the Phases of Learning Entity Comparison in Language Models
items.summary: How does data shape language model (LM) behavior throughout pretraining? We investigate this question through a case study on entity comparison, e.g., Between France and Brazil, which country is larger?, across nine comparison tasks spanning five entity types. We begin with controlled experiments in which we train small LMs (163M parameters) on mixtures of natural text from pretraining corpora and synthetic task data. Our analysis identifies three distinct phases of learning: (1) an early phase where the LM selects entities by frequency, (2) a middle phase where the LM selects entities by position in the prompt (first vs. last mentioned entity), and (3) a late phase where the LM selects the entity that is the correct answer. We show that the emergence of these three phases is causally determined by statistical properties of the training data. With small amounts of task-specific synthetic data, we observe only the first two phases and the model fails to learn the task; with large amounts, the model jumps directly from the frequency-based heuristic to solving the task correctly. Moreover, changing the entity frequency distribution from a naturally occurring Zipfian distribution (a small number of entities are very common and the vast majority are rare) to a uniform one weakens the frequency phase and speeds up learning of the task. Lastly, we show that the three phases of training dynamics from our controlled experiments appear in the open source model OLMo-2 32B. Together, our findings demonstrate that properties of pretraining data are causal drivers of heuristic learning and show that small-scale synthetic experiments can predict training dynamics at larger scales.

items.title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
items.summary: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.

items.title: Read, Parse, Describe: Unified Document Parsing with Visual Element Description Generation
items.summary: Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading-order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page-level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation.
