Chem-PerturBridge therefore supports both diagnostic evaluation of cross-dataset signature agreement and model-oriented reuse of heterogeneous perturbation transcriptomic data.

items.title: LEMON-ZEST: Evolution-Informed Tokenization for Efficient Protein Language Modeling
items.summary: Protein Language Models (PLMs) have made remarkable progress following scaling laws established in natural language processing across sequence- and structure-based tasks, yet the potential of tokenization remains underexploited. Unlike human language, proteins preserve structure despite extensive sequence variation, a property standard tokenization strategies fundamentally fail to capture. We introduce ZEST (Zoned Encoding of Sequence Traits), an evolution-informed vocabulary derived from conserved regions of multiple sequence alignments. ZEST allows embedding domain-level biological priors directly at the tokenization stage rather than learning them implicitly through scale. ZEST natively compresses sequences to an average token length of 3.3 residues, enabling our model to process $\geq3380$ residues within a standard 1024-token context window. Building on this, we present LEMON (Layered Extraction of Molecular Ordering from Nature), a compact 200M-parameter sequence-based model for detection of remote homology between protein sequences trained on a single H100 GPU for one week. Despite its modest size, LEMON outperforms models of 600M to 3B parameters and is on-par with TM-Vec. Our results demonstrate that evolution-informed tokenization can substitute for massive parameter scaling, opening a new direction for efficient, biologically-grounded protein representation learning. All code and model weights are publicly available (at \href{https://github.com/LDWLab/ZEST}{github.com/LDWLab/ZEST}) under the MIT license.

items.title: Pixels over Symbols: Sensory Realism Improves Behavioral Alignment in Models of Cognition
items.summary: Computational models of cognition have traditionally relied on abstract symbolic inputs that approximate sensory experiences with simplified vector representations. This simplification reflects historical computational constraints and a long-held assumption that the details of sensory realism are incidental to the study of cognitive processes. Recent advances have enabled the development of sensory-realistic models capable of performing diverse cognitive tasks, yet whether sensory realism meaningfully shapes cognition has not been formally established. We address this gap through a large-scale empirical comparison of abstract and sensory-realistic neural network models trained on a battery of memory-dependent decision-making tasks. Our results show that sensory-realistic models mirror human behavioral response patterns significantly more than their abstract counterparts, though a substantial gap to human internal behavioral consistency remains even for the best tested models. By analyzing the internal dynamics of these systems, we find that the learned recurrent weights are not the main source of this divergence. In fact, frozen abstract-trained weights driven by sensory-realistic inputs recover the human consistency of sensory-realistic models. The resulting dynamics are also within the seed-to-seed variability of sensory-realistic models. Together, our findings argue that across a broad set of visual working-memory tasks, sensory realism accounts for a substantial portion of the model-human behavioral agreement, more than the choice of sequence architecture and comparable to the choice of vision encoder. These results suggest that findings obtained from abstract task models in neuroscience should be more carefully interpreted in light of their potential behavioral limitations.

items.title: The DynaCell Evaluation Suite for Dynamic 3D Virtual Staining of Live Cells
items.summary: Understanding how cells respond to perturbations over time is central to cell biology and drug discovery. Live-cell imaging captures the dynamics of perturbation-induced phenotypes in individual cells. While fluorescence imaging can visualize specific molecular phenotypes, labeling and repeated illumination often affect cell health. Virtual staining offers an alternative by predicting these fluorescence images from images acquired without fluorescent labels. Although many virtual staining models have been developed, their performance on volumetric time-lapse data remains poorly characterized. We address this gap with an evaluation suite for 3D time-lapse virtual staining of live cells. The suite combines paired 3D time-lapse images acquired with and without fluorescent labels, a set of baseline models, and three metric tiers measuring pixel-level fidelity, organelle segmentation performance, and single-cell phenotype similarity. Using this evaluation suite, we study metric and model behavior across 3 cell types, 2 microscopes, 4 organelles, and 3 perturbation states. We find that regression baselines better predict the spatial localization of target organelles, whereas the generative baseline better captures the distribution of phenotypes across cells. These differences expose trade-offs between structural and phenotypic fidelity that are obscured by single-metric evaluation and suggest how virtual staining models can be developed for diverse downstream tasks such as localization, segmentation, tracking, and phenotypic profiling. We release the curated datasets, baseline checkpoints, and evaluation code as part of DynaCell, a broader framework for image-based profiling of cell-state dynamics.

items.title: Learning Reusable Behavioral Motifs for Continuous Animal Behavior Modeling
items.summary: Natural behavior evolves continuously and often reuses movement structure across contexts, but existing behavioral segmentation methods typically assign a single discrete syllable at each time point or impose restrictive generative assumptions. We introduce Motif-based Continuous Dynamics (MCD), a computational framework that models behavior as time-varying combinations of reusable behavioral motifs. MCD learns motifs as latent behavior-level features from transition dynamics, through spectral representation learning within a reinforcement learning framework. MCD then infers policies that combine these motifs across time or context, through offline imitation learning. This formulation avoids hard behavioral boundaries while capturing continuity and compositionality. Across simulated gridworld and continuous-control tasks, mouse maze navigation and pose data, MCD identifies reusable motifs that explain task and temporal variation. MCD therefore provides a flexible and interpretable framework for computational behavior analysis. Code is available in https://github.com/G1NO3/MCD.

items.title: Prospective Coding Improves Learning in Deep Continuous-Time Recurrent Networks
items.summary: Temporal integration gives continuous-time recurrent networks memory, but in deep stacks it also delays bottom-up signals and attenuates top-down errors. We compensate for this delay by making each layer's bottom-up input prospective, and we develop Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), biologically motivated temporal band-pass filters that are a special case of diagonal state-space models (SSMs). Starting from an energy model, we derive the RQF dynamics and show that each RQF is a band-pass filter whose learnable parameters control its tuning frequency and bandwidth. We then make each layer's bottom-up input prospective using a parameter-free two-tap update that leaves the recurrent transition and parallel scan unchanged. We extend this correction to general diagonal SSMs and show that it mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation when temporal gradients are truncated, i.e., spatial-only backpropagation. We evaluate the performance of RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs (a nonlinear gated RNN with built-in attentional modulation and recurrent normalization) trained using full backpropagation through time (BPTT) and spatial-only backpropagation. Under full BPTT, the prospective variants of these models match or outperform their non-prospective controls in every configuration. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF achieves 96.09% accuracy on raw-audio Speech Commands with 31.9k parameters; a width-64 six-layer RQF achieves 83.36% on the 16,384-step Path-X task. We also introduce selective RQFs (sRQFs), which make each filter's input gain and, optionally, its bandwidth and tuning frequency input-dependent while retaining the parallel scan. With the input gain alone, the same six-layer model achieves 86.31% on Path-X; with all three input-dependent, a four-layer prospective sRQF solves Selective Copying (99.83%).

items.title: Efficient and Accurate Zero Shot Generation of Symmetric Protein Complexes
items.summary: Symmetric organization is a fundamental principle of biomolecular complex assembly. The same principle underlies engineered applications, from vaccine platforms to nanomaterials, making symmetric de novo generation a core capability for computational protein design. We establish a theoretical foundation equating generation of an assembly with underlying symmetry group $G$ to generation within a quotient space over $G$. This directly allows $\mathrm{SE}(3)$-equivariant models to generate symmetric structures with minimal distribution shift. With this insight we introduce ZeUS ($\textbf{Ze}$ro-shot $\textbf{U}$nified $\textbf{S}$ymmetrization), a framework that converts any pretrained $\mathrm{SE}(3)$-equivariant backbone generative model into an efficient generator of symmetric assemblies with no retraining. ZeUS operates on a single $\textit{canonical subunit}$ and utilizes $\textit{phantom subunits}$ to preserve internal model operations, reducing memory and runtime cost by $\mathcal{O}(|G|)$ for finite groups $G$, compared to a full-complex forward pass. We implement ZeUS for IPA-based models (FrameDiff, FoldFlow) and axial-attention-based RFdiffusion, showing high generation efficiency with minimal degradation to generation quality. We then apply ZeUS to generate symmetric complexes of over $10{,}000$ residues with exact, untruncated attention, a scale previously intractable with any model.

items.title: Burstiness and interpersonal foraging between human infants and caregivers in the vocal domain
items.summary: Adult caregiver vocal responses are believed to promote more frequent and more advanced infant vocalizations. However, the inherent hierarchical temporal clustering of infant and caregiver vocal interactions over the course of a day creates a confound for reliably measuring immediate turn-by-turn effects of social vocal input within real-world vocal behavior. We first quantify temporal clustering in infant and caregiver vocalization events in daylong naturalistic infant-centered (ages 3, 6, 9, and 18 months) audio recordings using positive correlations between successive inter-event intervals (IEIs). Informed by flight time analyses in foraging studies, we develop an analytical framework to assess the effect of social input on the timing of subsequent infant and caregiver vocalizations after controlling for endogenous temporal dynamics as quantified by positive IEI-to-IEI correlations. For both infants and adults, receiving a social response predicts a shorter subsequent inter-event interval (IEI) than would be expected in the absence of a response. These results support a conceptualization of infant-caregiver vocal interactions as an `interpersonal foraging' process with inherent multiscale dynamics wherein social responses serve as foraged-for resources. The analytic approaches introduced here offer a broadly applicable framework to study interactive communication in other modalities, contexts, and species by decoupling endogenous and exogenous dynamics.

items.title: Pruning DNA Sequence
items.summary: Data pruning can substantially reduce training cost by removing examples that contribute little additional learning signal, but it has not been studied for DNA language-model pretraining. We introduce Sequence Pruning (SP), a dynamic pruning framework that removes genomic sequences as they become easy for the model to predict. SP uses per-sequence pretraining accuracy computed directly from the model's forward pass, requiring no separate scoring model or additional pass over the corpus. We evaluate SP across five pretraining settings spanning two corpora, three model families, and both MLM and CLM objectives, with downstream evaluation on five genomic benchmarks. SP reduces pretraining data processing by up to 96% while largely preserving downstream performance. At moderate savings, pruning improves performance by up to 1.2 MCC points over full-data pretraining; at the highest savings, pretraining uses only 4% of the baseline GPU hours with little performance loss. SP also outperforms the dynamic pruning methods InfoBatch and BPAS across most comparisons. Beyond accuracy, our framework supports alternative criteria such as perplexity and EL2N, although accuracy yields the strongest downstream performance at matched savings. These results show that genomic pretraining does not require repeatedly processing all available sequences and that dynamic sequence-level pruning can substantially improve its data and computational efficiency. Code is available at https://github.com/FaiasPromit/pruning-dna-sequence.

items.title: Quasispecies relocate rather than drift: hierarchical genotype networks track viral adaptation
items.summary: Viral populations are ensembles of mutationally related genotypes that explore sequence space locally. Their genotype networks are hierarchical: abundance decays with mutational distance from the most abundant genotype (the root) and degree distributions are heavy-tailed. How this architecture responds to selective challenges remains unclear. We combine simulations of sequence populations on NK fitness landscapes with longitudinal hepatitis B virus (HBV) deep-sequencing data from chronically infected patients under treatment. Quasispecies structure is rapidly rebuilt around the current root, while root replacement is occasional, when a fitter variant is found. Adaptation unfolds on two timescales: fast, local reorganisation and slow, stochastic relocation. HBV populations of patients not responding to therapy show stasis. Meanwhile, responders show either near-complete replacement by a new root, or transient excursions followed by return to the original root. These patterns resemble the stasis and relocation regimes found in simulations. Our results suggest that genotype network organization and dynamics under selective pressure present generic features of molecular adaptation, with a potentially informative clinical readout.

items.title: ImmSET: Sequence-Based Predictor of TCR-pMHC Specificity at Scale
items.summary: T cells are a critical component of the adaptive immune system, playing a role in infectious disease, autoimmunity, and cancer. T cell function is mediated by the T cell receptor (TCR) protein, a highly diverse receptor targeting specific peptides presented by the major histocompatibility complex (pMHCs). Predicting the specificity of TCRs for their cognate pMHCs is central to understanding adaptive immunity and enabling personalized therapies. However, accurate prediction of this protein-protein interaction remains challenging due to the extreme diversity of both TCRs and pMHCs. Here, we present ImmSET (Immune Synapse Encoding Transformer), a novel sequence-based architecture designed to model interactions among sets of variable-length biological sequences. We train this model across a range of dataset sizes and compositions and study the resulting models' generalization to pMHC targets. We describe a failure mode in prior sequence-based approaches that inflates previously reported performance on this task and show that ImmSET remains robust under stricter evaluation. In systematically testing the scaling behavior of ImmSET with training data, we show that performance scales consistently with data volume across multiple data types and compares favorably with the pre-trained protein language model ESM2 fine-tuned on the same datasets. Finally, we demonstrate that ImmSET can outperform AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3-based pipelines on TCR-pMHC specificity prediction when provided sufficient training data. This work establishes ImmSET as a scalable modeling paradigm for multi-sequence interaction problems, demonstrated in the TCR-pMHC setting but generalizable to other biological domains where high-throughput sequence-driven reasoning complements structure prediction and experimental mapping.

items.title: Turing Instability of a Closed Nutrient-Phytoplankton-Zooplankton-Detritus Model
items.summary: We study Turing instability in a closed Nutrient-Phytoplankton-Zooplankton-Detritus (NPZD) ecosystem model with nutrient recycling, formulated as a reaction-diffusion system without an explicit time-delay. The detritus compartment represents the biomass during the recycling process and acts to introduce a time delay in this process. Total biomass in the system is conserved, leading to a closed model. Although spatial diffusion typically promotes stability, our focus is on understanding how different diffusion rates for different species can destabilize steady states and give rise to spatial patterns. To address this, we first perform linear stability analysis to identify conditions under which Turing instability may occur. We then validate these theoretical predictions through numerical simulations. Our approach develops both intuition and rigorous analysis of how diffusion influences instabilities in the context of a conservative system, offering a comprehensive framework for understanding pattern formation in multi-species plankton ecosystems.

items.title: Synaptic Dendritic Neuron Model (scDNM) for Cell Type Classification in Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Data
items.summary: Cell type classification in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is challenging because of high dimensionality, sparsity, and transcriptionally similar cell types. We developed scDNM, an adaptation of the dendritic neuron model incorporating learnable synaptic thresholds, a supervised gene pool, staged training, and ensemble prediction. Six binary classification tasks were constructed from the Paul15, PBMC3k, and Nestorowa datasets. All models were evaluated using leakage-free nested cross-validation, with feature selection, scaling, and hyperparameter tuning performed independently of the outer test folds. scDNM ranked first in three of six tasks (including one tie) and achieved the best mean accuracy rank (2.00), followed by XGBoost (2.75), Random Forest (3.33), logistic regression (3.33), and SVM (3.58). In a six-class PBMC3k experiment, scDNM achieved 95.997% accuracy and 0.944 macro-F1, compared with 94.243% and 0.914 for SingleR. Garnett returned only Unknown labels and was treated as a zero-coverage technical outcome. Ablation analysis supported the contributions of dendrites and synaptic thresholds. However, XGBoost achieved higher mean binary-task accuracy (96.20% versus 95.32% for scDNM), and across-task rank differences were not statistically significant. These findings demonstrate that scDNM is competitive for scRNA-seq cell type classification, although broader independent validation is required.

items.title: BioBlobs: Unsupervised Discovery of Functional Substructures
items.summary: Protein function is often localized to cohesive substructures, such as catalytic triads, binding pockets, and structural motifs, that occupy only a small fraction of a protein's residues. Yet existing predictive pipelines typically aggregate residue-level embeddings and do not explicitly model or infer these functional substructures, leaving the central biological question unanswered: which substructure of a protein is responsible for its function? We introduce BioBlobs, an encoder-agnostic, end-to-end differentiable framework that compresses a protein into a small set of cohesive substructures (blobs) and predicts function from these blobs alone, so that each blob corresponds to a candidate functional region. Across diverse protein function prediction tasks and both sequence-only and structure-aware protein language models, BioBlobs is competitive with strong baselines while operating on only a small fraction of residues. Trained only on protein function labels, BioBlobs recovers expert-curated functional sites in InterPro and experimentally annotated catalytic sites in the Mechanism and Catalytic Site Atlas, demonstrating unsupervised functional substructure discovery and opening a path to large-scale functional site discovery in unannotated proteins. The discovered blobs adapt their spatial scale to the task, ranging from local catalytic sites to entire structural domains. Code is available at https://github.com/OliverLaboratory/BioBlobs.

items.title: Learning the interactions underlying multicellular migration using many-body stochastic inference
items.summary: Uncovering the interactions that give rise to emergent collective behavior in active and living matter remains a major challenge. Multicellular migration exemplifies this challenge: complex cell-cell interactions shape collective motion, but are difficult to measure directly. Here, we introduce a many-body stochastic inference framework that learns these interactions directly from experimental trajectories. We infer interaction models spanning different dynamical dependencies and complexities from short-time cell dynamics, and select among them based on their ability to predict emergent collective behaviors. Applied across three behaviorally distinct cell types, this approach yields minimal, predictive models of cell-cell interactions underlying multicellular migration. We find that non-cancerous epithelial cells coordinate multicellular migration through reciprocal repulsion and velocity alignment, while cancerous mesenchymal cells additionally exhibit previously unrecognized nonreciprocal interactions that couple to self-propulsion through two distinct mechanisms, which we term velocity inhibition in fibrosarcoma cells and velocity enhancement in breast cancer cells. Conceptually, these nonreciprocal interactions allow cells to tune the onset and speed of flocks, underscoring their role in collective migration and potentially enhancing cancer cell invasiveness at large cell densities. More broadly, our framework offers a general and principled route for extracting interaction laws of active and living systems directly from data.

items.title: Simple models outperform single-cell foundation models on downstream benchmarks
items.summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data exhibit strong and reproducible statistical structure. This has motivated the development of large-scale foundation models, such as TranscriptFormer, that use transformer-based architectures to learn a generative model for gene expression by embedding genes into a latent vector space. These embeddings have been used to obtain state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on downstream tasks such as cell-type classification, disease-state prediction, and cross-species learning. Here, we ask whether similar performance can be achieved without utilizing computationally intensive deep learning-based representations. Using simple, interpretable pipelines that rely on careful normalization and linear methods, we obtain SOTA or near SOTA performance across multiple benchmarks commonly used to evaluate single-cell foundation models, including outperforming foundation models on out-of-distribution tasks involving novel cell types and organisms absent from the training data. Our findings highlight the need for rigorous benchmarking and suggest that the biology of cell identity can be captured by simple linear representations of single cell gene expression data.

items.title: Health-System-Wide Mapping of Demographic Information in Routine Clinical Histopathology
items.summary: The extent to which demographic-associated information is detectable across organs and disease states in routine clinical histopathology remains unclear. Here, we analyzed 1.3 million hematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images from 257,322 patients across 25 organs, using pathology foundation-model representations and multiple-instance learning to systematically map information associated with sex, age group, and self-reported race. Across 69 organ-demographic combinations, demographic attributes were broadly recoverable, with pan-organ mean AUROCs of 0.828 for sex, 0.733 for age group, and 0.662 for self-reported race, and substantial variation across organs. Demographic-class balancing produced relatively small changes in performance, while evaluation within diagnosis-text clusters showed modest attenuation. Under training with diagnosis-based grouping, demographic-associated signals remained detectable across multiple organs, including sex in gastric tissue (AUROC 0.865), age group in breast (0.816), and self-reported race in skin (0.728). Literature-guided analysis of these settings generated candidate histomorphological and contextual explanations for further investigation. Together, these findings provide a systematic map of demographic-associated information in routine histopathology, informing investigations of its sources, assessments of potential shortcut learning, and the development of more interpretable computational pathology models.

items.title: Parameter Symmetries Determine Representational Geometry in Overparameterized Nonlinear Networks
items.summary: Representations are routinely used across machine learning, psychology, and neuroscience to draw inferences about the computations of biological and artificial systems. Such inferences presume that the geometry of these representations reflects the computation being performed. For artificial neural networks, however, the extent to which the function a network computes constrains this geometry remains unclear. One key obstacle is that these networks admit parameter symmetries: changes in parameterization that preserve function exactly while reshaping representational geometry. Here, we show that a broad class of parameter symmetries acts on representations through just three primitive feature transformations: addition, duplication, and scaling. This feature-level characterization yields a closed-form decomposition of representational geometry into essential and auxiliary components, revealing how representational degeneracy can exist without and grows with overparameterization even when function is held fixed. Finally, we establish conditions under which implementation-level selection rules resolve this degeneracy, yielding identifiable geometries in which features are weighted according to their contributions to the network's function. Together, our results delineate when representational geometry can support inferences about computation, and when it cannot.

items.title: Predicting fitness from genomic offset: a multivariate latent-trait framework
items.summary: Genomic offset methods quantify the genetic consequences of environmental change using genotype environment associations (GEA), but the conditions under which they predict fitness remain poorly understood. Here, we develop a theoretical framework linking genomic offset to relative fitness loss through multivariate latent adaptive traits under stabilizing selection. We show that squared genomic offset is linearly related to expected log relative fitness loss when averaged over genetic architectures, provided that direct environmental effects are absent. However, this relationship does not necessarily hold for a realized genetic architecture. We identify two complementary mechanisms that can explain high predictive accuracy of genomic offset statistics. First, when effective adaptive dimensionality is sufficiently large, the genetically mediated fitness response concentrates around its marginal expectation, reducing the dependence on the particular genetic architecture. Second, even with few adaptive traits, accurate predictions can arise from geometric alignment between the complete fitness loss matrix and the GEA metric. This second mechanism also encompasses direct environmental effects and their interactions with genetically mediated responses, which may preserve or weaken predictive accuracy depending on their alignment. We further derive bounds on predictive accuracy that characterize these effects. Our results clarify the assumptions and limitations underlying genomic offset predictions and suggest that genomic offset is best interpreted as a measure of genetically informed adaptive mismatch, rather than a direct predictor of realized fitness or any particular phenotypic trait.

items.title: Traits and tangles: An analysis of the Big Five paradigm by tangle-based clustering
items.summary: Using the recently developed mathematical theory of tangles, we re-assess the mathematical foundations for applications of the five factor model in personality tests by a new, mathematically rigorous, quantitative method. Our findings broadly confirm the validity of current tests, but also show that more detailed information can be extracted from existing data. We found that the big five traits appear at different levels of scrutiny. Some already emerge at a coarse resolution of our tools at which others cannot yet be discerned, while at a resolution where these _can_ be discerned, and distinguished, some of the former traits are no longer visible but have split into more refined traits or disintegrated altogether. We also identified traits other than the five targeted in those tests. These include more general traits combining two or more of the big five, as well as more specific traits refining some of them. All our analysis is structural and quantitative, and thus rigorous in explicitly defined mathematical terms. Since tangles, once computed, can be described concisely in terms of very few explicit statements referring only to the test questions used, our findings are also directly open to interpretation by experts in psychology. Tangle analysis can be applied similarly to other topics in psychology. Our paper is intended to serve as a first indication of what may be possible.

items.title: Path-dependent triage: Early judgments lead conversational AI chatbots to miss mental-health emergencies
items.summary: People increasingly bring mental-health concerns to consumer AI chatbots. In these conversations, clinically relevant information rarely arrives all at once. Instead, it unfolds over multiple turns, often in response to the questions the chatbot asks. Recognizing risk therefore depends on how a chatbot integrates newly disclosed information (inference) and on the questions it asks on each turn to elicit this information (context-seeking). Here we evaluated the conversational triage performance of 13 frontier AI chatbots tasked with engaging in 10-turn conversations with simulated users. Simulated users were grounded in one of 112 structured mental-health case files, each with an associated clinician-validated urgency level, from routine care to emergency. Chatbots failed to recognize one in five mental-health emergencies (20.3%), nearly four times the failure rate when all relevant clinical details were presented in a single message (5.6%). This gap was not explained by missing information: by the final turn, decisive facts had almost always been disclosed, and simply re-presenting those same facts as a single message reduced emergency under-triage to 12.1%. The problem lay instead in how the conversation unfolded, a phenomenon we refer to as path dependence. Early triage dispositions increasingly anchored later ones, such that emergencies missed early were rarely recovered as evidence accumulated. Context-seeking narrowed onto a small number of stereotyped questioning trajectories, with chatbots perseverating more than human clinicians given the same transcripts. Because the chatbot's running judgment shaped what it asked next, these two biases were plausibly coupled across turns. These dynamics are invisible to single-turn benchmarks but measurable in multi-turn evaluation, and point to concrete mitigations for safer conversational triage in consumer health AI.

items.title: The effect of limb kinematics on the speed of a legged robot on granular media
items.summary: Achieving effective locomotion on diverse terrestrial substrates can require subtle changes of limb kinematics. Biologically inspired legged robots (physical models of organisms) have shown impressive mobility on hard ground but suffer performance loss on unconsolidated granular materials like sand. Because comprehensive limb-ground interaction models are lacking, optimal gaits on complex yielding terrain have been determined empirically. To develop predictive models for legged devices and to provide hypotheses for biological locomotors, we systematically study the performance of SandBot, a small legged robot, on granular media as a function of gait parameters. High performance occurs only in a small region of parameter space. A previously introduced kinematic model of the robot combined with a new anisotropic granular penetration force law predicts the speed. Performance on granular media is maximized when gait parameters minimize body acceleration and limb interference, and utilize solidification features of granular media.

items.title: Platonic Representations in the Human Brain: Unsupervised Recovery of Universal Geometry
items.summary: The Strong Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that representational convergence in artificial neural networks can be harnessed constructively: embeddings can be translated across models through a universal latent space without paired data. We ask whether an analogous geometry can be recovered across human brains. Using fMRI data from the Natural Scenes Dataset, we propose a self-supervised encoder that learns subject-specific embeddings from brain data alone by exploiting repeated stimulus presentations. We show that these independently learned spaces can be translated across subjects using unsupervised orthogonal rotations, without paired cross-subject samples or intermediate model representations. Synchronizing pairwise rotations into a single shared latent space further improves cross-subject retrieval. These results provide evidence for a shared geometry in learned representations of human visual responses: subject-specific fMRI embeddings can be aligned across individuals within a common coordinate system.

items.title: Pangenome Peeling: Decomposing Weighted Adjacencies into Path-Forest Genomes
items.summary: One aspect of pangenome analysis that has received little attention is the recovery of the individual genomes that gave rise to a pangenome graph. While substantial effort has focused on constructing pangenomes from collections of genomes, the inverse problem remains largely unexplored: given a pangenome represented as a set of weighted adjacencies, can we reconstruct the constituent linear genomes that underlie it? Thus we introduce the pangenome peeling problem, which seeks to decompose a weighted adjacency graph into a collection of linear genomes whose combined adjacencies reproduce the observed edge weights. This problem is particularly relevant when considering ancestral pangenomes, where the graph structure may be known or inferred, but the underlying genomes are not. As a first step toward addressing this problem, we formally define pangenome peeling and derive a lower bound on the minimum number of genomes required to explain a given weighted adjacency graph. We then present two reconstruction methods: one based on the sequential addition of edges and a second based on extracting maximum-spanning-tree structures. Both methods produce genome collections that exactly explain the input adjacency data. To evaluate the recovered sets of genomes, we compare them to the set of input genomes using a maximum-weight matching framework based on the double-cut-and-join distance with indels. Here the maximum-spanning tree approach is superior, producing sets of constituent genomes close to the simulations while the sequential addition of edges approach yields constituent genomes increasingly divergent from the input as genomes sizes increase.

items.title: Atomic Trajectory Modeling with State Space Models for Biomolecular Dynamics
items.summary: Understanding the dynamic behavior of biomolecules is fundamental to elucidating biological function and facilitating drug discovery.While Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations provide a rigorous physical basis for studying these dynamics, they remain computationally expensive for long timescales.Recent deep generative models accelerate conformation generation but often either discard temporal correlations entirely or struggle to condition on the extended history required for faithful kinetics, a consequence of the effectively non-Markovian nature of partially observed subsystem coordinates.To bridge this gap, we introduce ATMOS, a novel generative framework based on State Space Models (SSM) designed to generate atom-level MD trajectories for biomolecular systems.ATMOS integrates a Pairformer-based state transition mechanism to capture temporal dependencies, with a diffusion-based module to decode trajectory frames autoregressively.We demonstrate that ATMOS achieves state-of-the-art performance in generating conformation trajectories for both protein monomers and protein-ligand systems.This work provides a unified and computationally efficient framework for biomolecular trajectory generation, taking a step toward dynamics foundation models.

items.title: Monroe: A Molecular Foundation Model for In-Context Probabilistic Inference
items.summary: Bioassay activity prediction is often data-limited because drug-discovery datasets rely on time-consuming and expensive wet-lab experiments for data generation and evaluation. This challenge has inspired recent research into molecular foundation models (MFMs), which aim to encode general-purpose chemical knowledge into molecular representations that generalize well in data-constrained scenarios. This paper presents Monroe, a new MFM with several innovations over the existing state of the art: increased scale allowing pre-training on over 81 million molecules from the PM6 quantum chemistry dataset; improved graph representation of stereochemistry; improved training losses including conformer denoising and embedding decorrelation; improved multi-task learning; and the use of a prior-data-fitted model (TabPFNv3) for downstream in-context prediction. Our evaluations use a principled pairwise comparison framework that measures statistically significant performance differences. Across established Polaris benchmarks, Monroe matches or exceeds existing MFMs, while on activity cliff benchmarks, designed to assess utility for molecular discovery, it achieves significant improvements over prior methods. Finally, ablation and transfer experiments show that PFN-based downstream predictors also substantially improve two leading existing models, MiniMol and CheMeleon, yielding new state-of-the-art variants we call MiniMol_PFN and CheMeleon_PFN, suggesting that our downstream adaptation strategy generalizes beyond Monroe. Source code is at github.com/blazejba/Monroe

items.title: A hair-thin implant opens the entire depth of the mouse brain to revisiting the same structures at subcellular resolution
items.summary: Ultrathin multimode-fibre endoscopes provide minimally invasive access to subcellular structures throughout the depth of the mouse brain. Here we introduce a chronically implantable interface with a diameter of 144 μm, about the thickness of a human hair, that extends this capability to longitudinal imaging, enabling repeated access to the same fine structures over extended periods. The system supports weeks-long tracking of individual dendritic spines, allowing quantitative comparison of their dynamics and survival across dendritic compartments. We further demonstrate longitudinal intracellular calcium imaging during spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity in the same cells across days, as well as repeated measurements of blood flow in the same vessels across multiple brain regions. This chronic endomicroscopic platform provides stable, minimally invasive optical access for longitudinal subcellular-resolution imaging of brain structure, activity and blood flow across depth.

items.title: Resolving non-neutrality across scales in a hyperdiverse tropical forest
items.summary: Different ecological processes operate at different spatial and temporal scales. Macroscopic regularities can therefore be captured by descriptions that ignore microscopic details, even when those details are mechanistically relevant to ecological processes. Here, we develop a framework inspired by statistical mechanics to track interspecific spatial correlations under spatial coarse-graining. To do so we combine random-matrix filtering with a spatially explicit neutral model. Applying this approach to eight censuses of the Barro Colorado Island tropical forest, we observe a continuous crossover from an interacting to an effectively neutral organization. Below a few tens of metres (20--35~m), the empirical correlation spectrum differs from neutral expectations, revealing scale-dependent species-specific structure. Part of this structure can be attributed to environmental heterogeneity. However, residual spatial associations provide candidate signatures of biotic interactions or other unmeasured ecological, non-neutral processes. With increasing spatial coarse-graining, empirical and neutral correlation spectra progressively converge, and above the crossover scale the neutral model provides an accurate description of the measured collective organization. Neutrality thus emerges as an effective description of the collective organization of the forest above a characteristic scale, without implying that species are equivalent at the individual level. Our framework provides an operational way to locate that scale.

items.title: Giant strongly biconnected components of directed networks: a generating function approach
items.summary: Strongly connected components (SCCs) characterize modular structure in directed networks but are fragile to single node failures. We study strongly biconnected components (SBCs), which are the set of nodes in which every node pair remains mutually reachable after the removal of any single node, as a more robust notion of connectivity. Using a generating function formalism, we derive the size of the giant SBC and analyze its percolation behavior under random node and link removal. We show that the giant SBC emerges at the same threshold as the giant SCC but grows more slowly, consistent with previous findings for undirected networks. We also applied our theoretical framework to real-world biological networks including gene regulatory networks and neural connectome. Our framework provides insight into the interplay between connectivity, redundancy, and robustness in complex directed systems.

items.title: Embedding stochastic dynamics in latent manifolds of recurrent neural networks
items.summary: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) provide a theoretical framework for understanding computation in biological neural circuits through their ability to support rich time-dependent behaviour. Whilst high-dimensional by construction, they can be used to encode low-dimensional dynamical systems, for example by restricting to low-rank connectivity, hence mirroring the emergence of latent neural manifolds found in empirical neural data. Here, we exploit a relationship between RNNs and a class of universal approximators to train networks that can represent arbitrary, nonlinear stochastic differential equations (SDEs), with given drift and diffusion coefficients, within a low-dimensional latent subspace. We show that RNNs can faithfully embed the drift and diffusion of a given SDE, including nonlinear and nonequilibrium dynamics such as chaotic attractors. We apply this approach by constructing RNN realisations of stochastic systems that transiently explore various attractors through both input-driven switching and autonomous transitions driven by nonequilibrium currents, which we interpret as models of associative and sequential (episodic) memory. To elucidate how these dynamics are encoded in the network, we introduce decompositions of the RNN based on its asymmetric connectivity and its time-irreversibility. Our results show that neural populations can implement a broad class of stochastic dynamics within low-dimensional manifolds, unifying ideas from the dynamics of neural computation, the theory of neural manifolds, associative memory, and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics.

items.title: Spatially explicit population modeling with habitat-preferential movement of Glis glis (edible dormouse)
items.summary: We develop a spatially explicit dynamical model for the dispersal of the edible dormouse, Glis glis, in a heterogeneous landscape. Population growth occurs within lattice cells, while movement between neighboring cells is governed by logistic functions representing density-dependent emigration and habitat preference. The model includes growth rate, carrying capacity, Allee threshold, home-range scale, and land-cover-based habitat suitability. Simulations over 100 years show that greater sensitivity to habitat preference tends to produce localized distributions with higher mean population density, whereas greater sensitivity to density dependence tends to yield larger occupied areas with lower mean population density. The model links local movement rules to emergent population-level patterns and offers a transparent, process-based framework for exploring potential invasive-species dispersal under field conditions where occurrence data are limited.

items.title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNs for Flexible Working Memory
items.summary: Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.

items.title: A Cytology Dataset for Early Detection of Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
items.summary: Oral squamous cell carcinoma OSCC is a major global health burden, particularly in several regions across Asia, Africa, and South America, where it accounts for a significant proportion of cancer cases. Early detection dramatically improves outcomes, with stage I cancers achieving up to 90 percent survival. However, traditional diagnosis based on histopathology has limited accessibility in low-resource settings because it is invasive, resource-intensive, and reliant on expert pathologists. On the other hand, oral cytology of brush biopsy offers a minimally invasive and lower cost alternative, provided that the remaining challenges, inter observer variability and unavailability of expert pathologists can be addressed using artificial intelligence. Development and validation of robust AI solutions requires access to large, labeled, and multi-source datasets to train high capacity models that generalize across domain shifts. We introduce the first large and multicenter oral cytology dataset, comprising annotated slides stained with Papanicolaou(PAP) and May-Grunwald-Giemsa(MGG) protocols, collected from ten tertiary medical centers in India. The dataset is labeled and annotated by expert pathologists for cellular anomaly classification and detection, is designed to advance AI driven diagnostic methods. By filling the gap in publicly available oral cytology datasets, this resource aims to enhance automated detection, reduce diagnostic errors, and improve early OSCC diagnosis in resource-constrained settings, ultimately contributing to reduced mortality and better patient outcomes worldwide.

items.title: Decoding spatial and semantic information from large-scale visual cortical activity for natural-movie reconstruction
items.summary: Reconstructing natural visual experience from cortical population activity is a central challenge in neural decoding, particularly for calcium imaging, where signals are noisy, temporally filtered, and paired neural-video data are limited. Here we present Ca2REAL (Calcium Activity to Reconstruct Events, Appearance, and Layout), a neural-to-video framework that conditions a pretrained video diffusion model through separate layout and semantic controls derived from calcium activity. Using measured responses from 7,863 V1 neurons in one mouse, Ca2REAL reconstructed held-out natural-movie clips with 81.4% all-pairs stimulus-identification accuracy, with its clearest gains over deterministic baselines in perceptual and semantic measures. We further evaluated the framework in a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons assembled from encoding-model-predicted responses across 11 independently recorded datasets. Perturbation and ablation analyses showed that reconstruction depends on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure, with layout and semantic pathways providing complementary spatial and identity information. Temporal analyses further showed improved preservation of semantic dynamics across reconstructed clips. These results show that large-scale cortical population activity constrains the spatial, semantic, and temporal structure of natural visual experience, providing a generative framework for high-fidelity neural reconstruction of dynamic visual scenes.

items.title: A multi-scale information geometry reveals the structure of mutual information in neural populations
items.summary: Understanding how neural population responses represent sensory information is a central problem in systems neuroscience. One approach is to define a representational geometry on stimulus space in which distances reflect how reliably stimuli can be distinguished from neural activity. However, different constructions of these distances can lead to qualitatively different conclusions about the neural code. Here, we show that a unique Riemannian representational geometry emerges from first principles governing how distances contract as stimulus resolution is lost through coarse-graining. This results in a multi-scale extension of the Fisher information metric, capturing encoding structure from fine stimulus details to coarse global distinctions. The resulting geometry is exactly related to the mutual information encoded by the population: well-encoded stimulus directions (those contributing more to mutual information) are expanded, whereas poorly encoded directions are contracted. The metric tensor can be estimated using diffusion models, making the framework practical for large neural populations and high-dimensional stimuli. Applied to visual cortical responses to natural images, the eigenvectors of the metric tensor identify stimulus variations that contribute most to the encoded stimulus information, yielding interpretable features that are robust to modelling choices. Together, these results provide a principled, information-theoretic framework for characterising neural population codes.

items.title: Uncertainty-aware neural emulation reveals climate-resilient maize traits at scale
items.summary: Climate change threatens maize yields worldwide, yet identifying which genetic traits sustain productivity under future conditions requires exploring an enormous space of genotype, soil, and climate combinations that process-based crop models are too costly to simulate at scale. Here we develop an integrated probabilistic emulation framework that transforms a mechanistic crop simulator (APSIM) into a fast, uncertainty-aware discovery engine. Built from two million simulations and coupled to a generative weather model that produces realistic climate sequences, the emulator reproduces thirteen maize growth outputs with high fidelity while returning calibrated confidence for every prediction, at a fraction of the original computational cost. Applying it across 100,000 trait configurations, six locations, and future climate projections extending to the year 2100, we identify 1,114 trait combinations that remain resilient under the 2100 future conditions and a stricter subset of 246 configurations that remain resilient across four future projection periods: 2040, 2060, 2080, and 2100. These resilient configurations occupy a distinct region of trait space, combining high radiation use efficiency with characteristic shifts in developmental and reproductive traits. Trait-importance analysis further identifies radiation use efficiency as the dominant driver of yield under future climate, while projected yields vary widely across locations and climate models, indicating strong spatial heterogeneity in the maize response to climate change.

items.title: Synchronized Optimal Transport Reconstructs Coupled Transcriptomic and Chromatin Dynamics
items.summary: Single-cell RNA and ATAC data collected across developmental stages provide time-course snapshots of transcriptional and regulatory states. Since sequencing is destructive, trajectories between these snapshots must be inferred from independently sampled cell populations. Existing approaches typically infer continuous dynamics in a single modality or integrate RNA and ATAC in a shared representation. Here we present Cross-Omics Aligned Trajectory Inference (COATI), which extends unbalanced synchronized dynamical optimal transport to time-dependent cross-modal maps for reconstructing coupled trajectories in distinct RNA and ATAC state spaces. We evaluated COATI on synthetic benchmarks and four developmental datasets using held-out-stage reconstruction and lineage analyses. COATI improved reconstruction of cell populations at held-out stages, including recovery of chromatin-state heterogeneity within cell types, and better preserved developmental lineage relationships. The unbalanced formulation allows the inference of population mass changes, which were shown to associate with DNA-replication programs at early stages and lineage-maturation programs later in development. The coupled trajectories enabled analysis of lineage-specific transcriptional and chromatin changes and their temporal relationships during development. Lineage responses inferred by COATI agreed with independent CRISPR perturbation results, and the inferred regulatory patterns were consistent with independent epigenetic data.

items.title: Multimodal Physiological Decoding Reveals Individualized Arousal Dynamics in Closed-Loop Neurofeedback
items.summary: Most arousal-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) use EEG to decode cognitive state. But arousal is an autonomic process. We examined if peripheral physiological signals give a better decode of task-related arousal. We used a public dataset from a difficult boundary-avoidance flight task. In this task, participants received EEG-based BCI neurofeedback, sham feedback, or no feedback. We trained a multimodal deep learning decoder on heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), respiration, electrodermal activity, and pupil diameter. We compared it with an EEG-only decoder and with the original filter-bank common spatial pattern (FBCSP) decoder. All analyses were offline. The peripheral decoder had a within-subject AUC of 93.0%. The EEG-only decoder had 85.2% and the FBCSP decoder had 79.8%. Only the peripheral decoder showed the Yerkes-Dodson inverted-U relation between decoded arousal and performance. The feedback conditions did not change the arousal trajectories. Thus, the BCI benefit possibly comes from regulation at critical moments in the task, not from a continuous shift. We calculated a time-varying optimal arousal trajectory from control trials. Per-trial deviations from this trajectory predicted performance (r = -0.28 to -0.24, p < 0.01). Baseline HRV and gamma power changed the arousal-performance curve of each subject. We used these values to divide subjects into arousal-sensitive and arousal-tolerant groups. Control bands specific to each group increased trial separation (Cohen's d from 1.21 to 1.32 and from 0.85 to 1.10). These results show that peripheral signals are better than EEG for continuous arousal decoding. They also give a specification for individualized closed-loop arousal regulation. A prospective study must test this specification, for example with personalized transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation.

items.title: Protein B-factor modeling with local magnitude
items.summary: Topological magnitude characterizes the effective size and spatial organization of metric spaces, offering a geometric approach with potential applications in molecular biology and materials science. Previous work has demonstrated its utility in modeling protein flexibility from structure, but global magnitude weighting requires dense linear systems whose computational cost increases with protein size. We introduce a local magnitude representation that retains residue-level structural information through nearest-neighbor environments. The construction is well posed and geometrically invariant, with central weighting distinguished from scalar neighborhood magnitude. Across 364 proteins, the mean within-protein fitting Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) increases from 0.725 for global magnitude to 0.728 for local magnitude. Blind-prediction experiments on 345 proteins combine each representation with identical auxiliary descriptors and evaluate random forests and gradient boosting under three validation protocols. Local features improve the primary PCC in all six model--protocol comparisons, with a maximum absolute increase of 0.008 in protein-level ten-fold gradient boosting. For a fixed feature bank, local factorization costs $O(Nk^3)$ compared with $O(N^3)$ for global factorization, where $N$ is the number of C$_α$ atoms and $k$ the neighborhood size. Timing measurements show a computational advantage of local magnitude on large structures. Within the tested single-seed configuration and distinct global and local scale banks, these results support local magnitude as a compact representation that preserves useful B-factor information while reducing feature-extraction costs for large proteins.

items.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Annealing for Protein Side-Chain Optimization: A Feasibility Study
items.summary: Hybrid quantum-classical annealing solvers are moving from research laboratories toward industrial use, but their advantage over classical optimization appears to be confined to a narrow class of problems. A recent systematic benchmark of the D-Wave hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers, across several classes of optimization problems, found it to be most competitive on binary quadratic programs, while noting that few industrial problems take this form. Therefore, identifying real-world industrial problems that can be modeled with this structure is a key challenge. We propose protein side-chain optimization, a core step of computational protein design, as one of these problems: it is natively a binary quadratic program, and its application context requires pools of low-energy solutions, which annealers naturally return. In this feasibility study, we test whether the competitiveness of the hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers extends to this problem. On 40 instances derived from 20 experimentally determined protein structures with up to about 200 amino acids and 2000 binary variables, we compare the results achieved with a hybrid solver, run for 5 seconds, against those of the commercial solver Gurobi, run for 10 seconds, 1000 seconds, and 4 hours. The hybrid solver reaches the certified optimum whenever one is available, matches Gurobi's performance on smaller instances, and outperforms it on larger instances, finding lower-energy solutions. These results show that the competitiveness of the hybrid solver on binary quadratic programs, so far observed only on a synthetic benchmark, extends to a real-world problem. This motivates comparisons with classical heuristics specific to protein side-chain optimization.

items.title: Agentic AI uncovers conserved cross-tissue protein co-abundance programs inaccessible to single-dataset analysis
items.summary: Protein co-abundance clusters preserved across tissues can nominate shared disease mechanisms and therapeutic targets, particularly where proteins implicated in organ-confined diseases converge in other tissues. Yet cross-tissue proteomic studies have examined pre-selected tissue pairs, leaving most combinations, and non-obvious relationships among them, unexplored. Exhaustive comparison requires consistently assessing thousands of candidate clusters from hundreds of tissue-pair networks across heterogeneous evidence, a scale beyond manual curation. We present an LLM-agent framework for large-scale, evidence-grounded comparison of tissue-specific protein co-abundance networks. From sample-level proteomic data, it constructs tissue networks, derives conserved clusters for each tissue pair, integrates evidence from expression atlases, interaction and complex databases, pathways, disease associations and the literature, and proposes mechanistic hypotheses in which every conclusion cites its evidence. Applied to all 231 pairs among 22 human tissues and sample groups, it identified 1,825 conserved clusters in 216 tissue pairs. Co-abundance relationships were shared beyond chance in 76% of pairs, including unrelated organs, and shared clusters were only weakly associated with abundance similarity. Clusters were enriched 3.7- to 6.9-fold for known interactions and complex memberships, and 379 of 793 testable clusters replicated in independent CPTAC proteomes. Some clusters pointed to relationships absent from current databases: one shared by liver and bone marrow linked three genes causing inherited white matter disorders, suggesting a common mechanism via the integrated stress response. Conserved co-abundance clusters thus offer a hypothesis-generating resource for studying disease proteins beyond the affected organ. Code: https://github.com/jacob20030316-crypto/Protein_Co_Abundance_Agent

items.title: A tractable transition function for the Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection via gamma duality
items.summary: The transition function of the Wright-Fisher diffusion with selection is a fundamental object for non-neutral evolutionary modelling and likelihood-based inference, but, unlike in the neutral case, existing representations are impractical or inefficient. Spectral approaches rely on truncation levels that grow with selection strength and the number of alleles, thus leading to rapidly increasing computational costs, while existing duality-based expansions lead to multi-type dual processes whose transition probabilities involve intractable normalising constants. In this paper we obtain a new transition-function representation for the multi-allelic Wright-Fisher diffusion with parent-independent mutation and genic selection that makes transition-law evaluation and simulation practically feasible in regimes where existing methods are costly or unavailable. The key tool is a new gamma duality, obtained by augmenting classical polynomial duality by an exponential tilting and yields a multivariate birth-death dual with fully explicit infinitesimal rates and an entrance-boundary construction. This is used to express the Wright-Fisher transition law as an explicit mixture of standard Dirichlet components, with mixing weights obtained from the dual started from its entrance boundary. We characterise the dual stationary distribution and its small-time behaviour, and develop practical and efficient sampling procedures for both transition and stationary laws, including a fast approximate stationary sampler with explicit error control. Numerical experiments illustrate substantial runtime gains over specialised methods in regimes where they apply, while our approach remains applicable for arbitrary numbers of alleles and selection coefficients.

items.title: C3P: Contrastive promoter-protein pretraining yields representations capturing bacterial gene regulation
items.summary: Despite the increasing scale of genome language models (gLMs), their ability to decode the function of regulatory sequences remains unclear. gLM pretraining relies on sequence reconstruction, which may struggle due to the noisy, rapidly evolving nature of regulatory DNA. Self-supervised contrastive approaches provide a promising alternative. Inspired by language-image architectures like CLIP, we introduce contrastive promoter-protein pretraining (C3P). By learning to align promoters to their corresponding proteins, we leverage the rich representations of proteins learned by protein language models as supervisory signal for the learning of promoter representations. After training on 88 million bacterial promoter-protein pairs, we evaluate the predictive power of C3P-learned promoter representations for inference of curated regulatory annotations, finding multi-fold improvement over leading gLMs. We also introduce zero-shot co-regulated gene retrieval, the ability to find co-regulated genes in a genome using no experimental data. We find that compared to a randomly initialized baseline, C3P training consistently provides significant zero-shot performance gains, unlike gLMs. Scaling analysis reveals the potential for further improvement as well as the efficiency of C3P, which achieved strong performance at a fraction of the training cost of leading gLMs. In addition to demonstrating that C3P training is effective for learning representations of bacterial regulatory sequences, our strong zero-shot co-regulated gene retrieval performance suggests the possibility of decoding gene regulation for millions of bacteria from their genomes alone.

items.title: Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information
items.summary: Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $α$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers.

items.title: Spiking neuromodulation: a linear control perspective
items.summary: Neuronal excitability is a nonlinear phenomenon, and the complexity of spiking experimental traces sometimes looks defeating. The present paper takes the view point that excitability is a neuromodulated property, and aims to demonstrate that the neuromodulation of spiking is amenable to the classical linear analysis tools of control theory. We illustrate the value of linear feedback analysis as an alternative to bifurcation analysis in the simple yet classical example of spiking modulation by the A-type potassium current.

items.title: Personalized health coaching via coachable health age and counterfactual wearable trajectories
items.summary: Personalized health coaching requires moving beyond retrospective wearable summaries toward quantitative, actionable behavioral prescriptions. We introduce Coachable Health Age (CHA), an interpretable health-age metric built from modifiable physiological and behavioral signals passively captured by consumer wearables. Across the WEAR-ME (N=2,780), All of Us (N=22,748), and longitudinal Fitbit (N=1,464) cohorts, CHA aligns with established cardiometabolic health constructs and improves prognostic discrimination for incident cardiovascular and metabolic disease beyond age, sex, and body mass index. To enable prospective behavioral optimization, we developed Sensor World Model (SensorWM), an action-conditioned wearable world model pretrained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of longitudinal sensor data from approximately 100,000 participants. SensorWM accurately forecasts multi-week physiological responses to candidate lifestyle changes ($R^2=0.664$), outperforming generic time-series foundation models while preserving downstream clinical signal for diabetes, hypertension, and other health outcomes. Finally, we integrate CHA and SensorWM into an agentic counterfactual coaching system to synthesize personalized 12-week coaching plans. In blinded paired reviews, certified lifestyle coaches preferred counterfactual-grounded plans over plans grounded in wearable history alone for overall quality (71.4%, P < 0.001) and anticipated adherence (71.0%, P < 0.001), and board-certified clinicians judged 99.2% of counterfactual-grounded plans to meet clinical safety criteria (vs. 97.6% of comparison plans). Automated evaluations across the full cohort (N=2,780) also favored counterfactual-grounded plans. By closing the loop between longitudinal tracking, trajectory prediction, and counterfactual coaching, our framework provides a scalable path to systematically improve cardiometabolic health.

items.title: Kinetic models of a K channel with 2 stage voltage sensor activation and an opening step
items.summary: The activation of a K channel with 2 voltage sensors and a separate opening step may be described by a 4 state kinetic equation. If $k_{o}$ and $k_{c}$ are the opening and closing rates, and $α$ and $β$ are the voltage sensor rates such that $k_{o}$ $\ggα,k_{c}\ggβ$ and $k_{o}$ $\gg k_{c}$, the kinetic equation may be reduced to a 3 state model where the effective backward rate from the activated-open state is $2βk_{c}/(k_{o}+k_{c})$. However, if a K channel voltage sensor activates in 2 stages, and there is a separate opening step, the occupation probabilities of the states of the channel satisfy a 10 state kinetic equation. When the time constants of the characteristic equation for each voltage sensor differ by an order of magnitude, and $k_{o}$ $\gg k_{c}$, the open state probability is proportional to $n^{2}$, where $n$ satisfies a rate equation, and the derived rates have a similar voltage dependence to the rates $α_{n}$ and $β_{n}$ from voltage clamp data.

items.title: Interpretable many-body interaction laws for collective motion from few trajectories
items.summary: Models of collective motion usually reduce social interactions to pairwise forces, despite empirical evidence for many-body effects. We introduce the directional atomic cluster expansion (dACE), which adapts the atomic cluster expansion (ACE) of interatomic potentials to self-propelled agents. dACE provides a systematically improvable, exactly equivariant expansion of an agent's acceleration that splits uniquely into 1-, 2-, 3-body and higher contributions, along with a self term for the agent's own past motion that is fitted so that it does not absorb the interactions. On simulated collectives in two and three dimensions with known rules, dACE recovers the interaction law body order by body order from little data, while the neural model SocialNet, the current closest competitor, needs more data, has much larger errors on many-body or chiral rules and is restricted to 2D. On real data sets of tracked zebrafish and golden shiners, the laws learned by dACE agree better between disjoint halves of the data than SocialNet's. The learned laws are interpretable, and in the shiners the 3-body term opposes the pairwise response as neighbourhoods get dense. Finally, we show that next-step prediction accuracy mostly measures self-propulsion and noise rather than the interactions, and suggest more robust combinations of error measures for interaction learning.

items.title: Geometric Relevance Is Not Sufficient: Evaluating Focused Post-Training Supervision in Diffusion Docking
items.summary: Diffusion-based molecular docking requires learning a corrective score field across a broad corruption distribution, yet individual pose errors can differ substantially in their structural consequences. This creates a post-training conflict between preserving broad score-field coverage and concentrating supervision on corrections that appear more relevant to docking geometry. Using DiffDock, a fixed-budget study compares broad continuation with torsional supervision focused on Cartesian consequence or conditional target consistency, and with a broad/focused mixture. Evaluation separates fixed score fidelity, generated-pose quality, best-of-10 sampling capacity, and confidence-selected Top-1 docking performance. At <5 Angstrom, broad continuation had the highest mean Top-1 success among trained policies, and focused or mixed supervision showed no consistent advantage under the tested budget. The starting model had better fixed score fidelity, whereas the evaluated broad-continuation model had higher mean Top-1 success with the same aggregate best-of-10 recovery. Focusing supervision on structurally consequential or more consistently specified corrections did not consistently improve returned-pose success over broad continuation.

items.title: Building Barricades: Red-Teaming Agentic Biosynthesis Planning
items.summary: The rapid democratization of biotechnology, enhanced by large language models (LLMs) and agentic software, is eroding longstanding barriers that have limited biosynthesis planning to experts. We present BioBulbul, an agentic system that couples LLMs with open-source biodesign tools for retrobiosynthesis, enzyme selection, gene cluster design, and DNA assembly planning. Using simple natural language prompts, BioBulbul autonomously generates plausible biosynthesis pathways and corresponding gene cluster sequences for several known small molecule toxins, demonstrating that non-experts could feasibly access them using an agentic system. Our red-teaming experiments confirm the technical viability of LLM-driven toxin biosynthesis while highlighting three principal barriers: scarcity of open-source biodesign tools, limited structured enzymatic reaction data, and the complexity of many small molecule toxin pathways. We argue that these barriers are likely to diminish within a decade, expanding the biological threat landscape. To mitigate emerging risks, we recommend expanding DNA synthesis screening to include chokepoint enzymes, extending chemical supplier controls to precursor compounds, establishing continuous AI-assisted threat surveillance pipelines, and developing robust LLM guardrails. Coordinated investment across government, industry, and AI developers is essential to safeguard against the misuse of agentic biosynthesis planning.

items.title: Pattern selection and biomass shifts in a vegetation model with nonlocal competition and Allee activation
items.summary: We study a single-species vegetation model in which a strong Allee effect acts locally and competition acts through a nonlocal kernel, and we describe the kernel with the one-parameter family of q-Gaussians, which goes from compact support to power-law tails. The local activation introduced by the Allee effect allows a finite-wavelength instability even when the Fourier transform of the kernel is positive, so Gaussian and heavy-tailed kernels can produce patterns. We derive in closed form the coefficients of the hexagonal amplitude equations and verify them against independent numerical steady states. The quadratic coefficient $Q$ results from the balance between the curvature of the local growth and the competitive inhibition at the pattern scale, and at onset its sign depends only on the fraction of the local activation that diffusion removes at the critical wavenumber. The same coefficient controls the morphology, since spots, labyrinths and gaps appear with pairwise competition only as $Q$ changes sign, and the amplitude equations predict the choice between hexagons and stripes in every simulated state in which the cubic truncation holds. It also controls the total biomass, which increases for spots and decreases for gaps.

items.title: Do sEMG Foundation Models Improve Cross-Subject Generalisation?
items.summary: sEMG Foundation Models aim to learn general purpose representations over diverse subjects and recording conditions that boost performance on a variety of downstream tasks. However, existing evaluations make it difficult to discern whether pretraining alone is sufficient to combat the cross-subject overfitting which makes machine learning on sEMG so challenging. We conduct a systematic evaluation of three sEMG foundation models across three gesture classification datasets under both intra-session and inter-subject splits, using three fine-tuning strategies designed to isolate the contribution of pretraining.
