items.summary: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.

items.title: Zeroes and Extrema of Functions via Random Measures
items.summary: We present methods that provide all zeroes and extrema of a function that do not require differentiation. Using point process theory, we are able to describe the locations of zeroes or maxima, their number, as well as their distribution over a given window of observation. The algorithms in order to accomplish the theoretical development are also provided, and they are exemplified using many illustrative examples, for real and complex functions.

items.title: Sampling the Funnel: A Comprehensive Survey of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical Bayesian Inference
items.summary: Hierarchical models are central to applied Bayesian statistics, yet the variance structures they depend on can produce posterior geometries that remain difficult to explore even with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), a designation now covering a large and increasingly heterogeneous family of algorithms. This survey uses Generalized HMC as an organizing framework to describe the many variants of HMC, their methodological and computational properties, and their empirical consequences. Varying the trajectory length, the degree of momentum refreshment, and the presence of a Metropolis correction recovers several familiar Hamiltonian and Langevin samplers as special cases. Three further, largely independent directions account for much of the remaining literature: modifying the metric, as in Riemannian HMC; modifying the Hamiltonian used by the acceptance test, as in modified or shadow HMC; and modifying the numerical integrator, as in multi-stage splitting schemes. We review these variants alongside the procedures used to tune and diagnose them, with particular attention to the effective sample size, whose standard estimators assume a reversibility that generalized and modified samplers lack, and ignore the importance weights that modified Hamiltonians introduce. We close with the open problems these methods face for hierarchical models, taking joint longitudinal and time-to-event models as the motivating example.

items.title: Robust Tests for Heteroskedasticity in Nonparametric Regression under Covariate-Dependent Higher-Order Moments
items.summary: We propose Cramér--von Mises- and Kolmogorov--Smirnov-type tests of constant conditional variance in nonparametric regression. The test statistics are constructed from a third-order $U$-process and remain valid when higher-order features of the conditional error distribution vary with the covariates. We derive their limiting distributions under the null hypothesis and study their asymptotic behavior under fixed alternatives and Pitman-type local alternatives. A multiplier bootstrap procedure calibrates the critical values, and Monte Carlo experiments show that the proposed tests have rejection frequencies close to the nominal level in the simulation designs. An application to the National Child Development Study provides evidence of heteroskedasticity in pooled weekly earnings. In the male hourly-earnings sample, rejecting a stronger error-distribution restriction does not entail rejecting homoskedasticity.

items.title: Data augmentation for the generalizability and transportability of fairness in a clinical heart failure algorithm
items.summary: Synthetic data augmentation has been proposed as a way to artificially supplement clinical datasets to address fairness concerns in downstream classification algorithms. This approach is closely related to upweighting or upsampling methods employed for the problem of class imbalance, which have shown mixed empirical results in practice. Synthetic data augmentation also runs the risk of overfitting to the noise present in subgroups with relatively small sample sizes, raising both generalizability and transportability concerns. We present an empirical evaluation of synthetic data augmentation for fairness in tabular data using simulation studies as well as a real-world application of in-hospital mortality classification for heart failure patients in two distinct data samples. We implement upsampling and upweighting methods as benchmarks for the implicit fairness objective of synthetic data augmentation. Our results suggest that the fairness impacts of data augmentation are sensitive to the design of the downstream algorithm as well as the deployment context and its similarity to the training data. It is crucial that studies making generalizability and transportability claims should provide empirical support for these assertions.

items.title: Causal invariance and identifiability for interventions in multi-state models
items.summary: We propose an identification theory for stochastic interventions on the transition dynamics in continuous-time multi-state models. Interventions are formalized as local modifications of a likelihood satisfying a causal invariance property. We show that identification from observed data is achieved when no unmeasured process simultaneously affects an intervened local characteristic and a competing or subsequent non-intervened local characteristic, covariate local characteristic, or censoring intensity. Our framework allows for intervening on both the timing and type of events, accommodates measured and latent covariates as time-varying marked point processes, and extends to right-censored data. We exemplify by considering identifiability in two concrete applications: one studying the effect of changing the timing of intrauterine insemination on the probability of pregnancy, and one studying the effect of changing the type of dysphagia relieving surgery on the risk of death in esophageal cancer patients.

items.title: The predictive discrepancy: an objective Bayes criterion for constructing calibrating priors
items.summary: We construct objective priors for regular univariate parametric models designed to produce low coverage probability bias of Bayesian predictive distributions, giving rise to calibrated prediction in repeated use. This is achieved by defining the predictive discrepancy and deriving a class of minimum predictive discrepancy priors. In the multiparameter case these priors will often be data-dependent. The predictive efficacy of alternative global priors can be assessed by comparison with these priors. The effectiveness of the theory is illustrated by a number of examples.

items.title: FADO: Learning Causal Explanations with Prior-Fitted Networks
items.summary: In regression and classification tasks with tabular datasets, most of the literature on explanation in ML (e.g. SHAP, permutation importance) has focused on predictive attribution: does feature $X_i$ help predict outcome $Y$? At its heart, predictive attribution captures correlation, not causation. We instead ask a causal question: would manipulating feature $X_i$ change outcome $Y$? We define a natural quantity to answer this question, the feature intervention effect: $Δ_i = E[Y\mid do(X_i=+1)]-E[Y\mid do(X_i=-1)]$. In general, estimating this quantity from observational data alone would entail strong causal assumptions. We propose FADO (Feature-wise Amortized Do-Operators), an amortized inference method using prior-fitted networks trained on synthetic tabular datasets generated by structural causal models. During training, the synthetic data-generating process is known, so we can compute ground-truth intervention effects $Δ_i$, and train a model to predict them at test time from a purely observational tabular dataset. As we demonstrate through extensive experiments, our new causal explainability method is easy to train and provides better explanations under a range of settings for which standard predictive attribution fails, including proxy variables, confounders, colliders, and placebos. We evaluate it on real, synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets, with and without hidden confounders, and compare it to existing predictive attribution methods and state-of-the-art causal inference methods.

items.title: An Asymptotic Theory of Chain-of-Thought in In-Context Learning
items.summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become a widely used mechanism for eliciting multi-step reasoning in large language models by generating intermediate reasoning steps at inference time. Yet the scaling behavior of generalization with CoT depth remains poorly understood. To address this question, we study a theoretically solvable model of CoT for in-context weight prediction in linear regression, where test-time reasoning is represented as an iterative refinement of the weight-parameter estimate. Using tools from random matrix theory under high-dimensional asymptotics, we derive an exact formula for the generalization error as a function of reasoning depth, pretraining data amount, and context length. Our analysis reveals a sharp phase transition separating exponential and polynomial improvement, saturation, and overthinking, and characterizes how the optimal reasoning depth scales. We further show that deeper reasoning is most effective with sufficiently rich pretraining and in-context information, whereas limited pretraining or context makes longer reasoning prone to error amplification or saturation. We also validate these predictions through experiments on fully learned linear attention and softmax attention models. Our results provide a unified theoretical account of how test-time CoT depth affects generalization.

items.title: Can Model Answer Probabilities Represent Survey Populations? Conditional Prediction and Joint Validity in Jev Survey Simulation
items.summary: Survey simulations require realistic combinations of answers, but predictive accuracy alone does not establish that a model can generate them. We evaluate the option probabilities returned by Jev, a TypeSafe decision model, using linked responses to 20 binary items from five archived survey waves. We compare population-only prediction, prediction given recorded answers, and sequential completion that uses generated answers to predict later responses. Joint comparisons hold the starting population information fixed, and two three-question cases are completed in both question orders. We evaluate predictive scores, answer frequencies, and associations against the survey records. Recorded answers can improve predictive scores while associations remain distorted. Large conditional errors also occur. For example, among men who described themselves as having traditional values, the model predicted that 16% would see men and women as similar in workplace abilities, compared with 56% in the survey. Sequential completion has mixed effects on joint validity, and reversing question order produces different joint distributions in both tested cases. Order checks and classical marginal bounds clarify what can be assessed before linked validation answers are available. The findings support validating the joint events a simulation uses and separating empirical constraints from model assumptions. The evidence concerns selected binary tasks and one model version.

items.title: Measuring Kaplan--Meier Overestimation Under Competing Risks: Event Ordering, Quantification, and Exact Inference
items.summary: Competing risks arise when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types. Competing events are frequently treated as censoring and analysed using Kaplan--Meier (KM) methods, which overestimate real-world event risks. While the existence of KM overestimation is well known, its determinants, magnitude, and inferential properties remain poorly characterised. We develop a nonparametric framework that treats competing risks overestimation as a statistical quantity in its own right. We show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise KM overestimation and develop an event ordering theory describing how temporal event allocation influences overestimation. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) that quantifies total KM overestimation directly from routine survival analysis output. We establish exact error equivalence results for both cause-specific and total overestimation. In particular, Product Limit Error Equivalence shows that inference for TOD reduces exactly to ordinary overall survival estimation. Simulation experiments validate the theoretical results and show that independent censoring primarily affects precision rather than overestimation magnitude. Across six benchmark competing risks datasets, cause-specific overestimation is characterised by both total overestimation and temporal event allocation. These results provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance and determining when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to naïve KM risks. The proposed framework transforms competing risks overestimation from a qualitative warning into a measurable quantity that can be routinely quantified, interpreted, and incorporated into reporting practice.

items.title: Backtracking Direct, Indirect and Total Effects
items.summary: Natural direct and indirect effects are defined through cross-world interventional counterfactuals. We propose an alternative construction based on backtracking counterfactuals. Rather than intervening on the treatment or mediator and change the structural equations, we use a backtracking conditional distribution to construct an alternative exogenous state satisfying a desired treatment-mediator constraint and then evaluate the unchanged structural equations on that state. This yields the backtracking direct and indirect effects, and also the backtracking total effect. Likewise, we adapt the population intervention effects.

items.title: Debiased Counterfactual Generation via Flow Matching from Observations
items.summary: Estimating the full counterfactual distribution under an intervention is central to treatment risk assessment and counterfactual generation tasks. Existing approaches model the counterfactual distribution as a standalone generative target, without exploiting its relationship to the observational data. In this work, we show that under standard assumptions, observational distributions and marginal counterfactual distributions over outcomes are tightly linked: they have identical support and tail behavior, remain statistically close under weak confounding, and share any outcome features which are invariant to confounders. These properties motivate learning counterfactual distributions not from scratch, but via a deconfounding flow from the observational distribution. We formulate this problem via flow-matching and derive a semiparametrically efficient estimator based on a novel efficient influence function correction. We subsequently extend our estimator to target minimal-energy flows in high-dimensions, which we show can be especially simple targets between observational and counterfactual distributions. In experiments, deconfounding flows outperform existing debiased counterfactual distribution estimators, while also mitigating known failure modes of flow-based methods.

items.title: Convergence and global optimality of Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao descent for Gaussian mixtures
items.summary: We study explicit Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao descent for fitting Gaussian location mixtures by nonparametric maximum likelihood. The full sequence converges weakly and has finite length in the bounded-Lipschitz metric throughout the original step-size range. These conclusions hold for any fixed data set in any dimension and any initial probability measure. By an earlier conditional optimality theorem, the limit maximizes the likelihood under full-support initialization. Fix any particle step size in $(0,1]$. Initialize the particles by resampling the observations. For an open set of triples of points in the plane, the probability of convergence to a strictly suboptimal fixed point tends to one exponentially as the particle count grows. Without reweighting, a centered Gaussian initialization can give a strictly suboptimal limit. Every finite iterate has a smooth, strictly positive density. The limit assigns positive mass to a nonglobal local maximum of the associated Gaussian sum. We also give the exact pure-transport limit for a one-dimensional initialization with full support and an atom. An exact finite-dimensional representation preserves the truncated likelihood moments and the retained region's contribution to the current dissipation. This lets us transfer an analytic gradient inequality to the measure trajectory.

items.title: Inference After Model Refutation: Uniform Post-Relaxation Inference for Partially Identified Models
items.summary: When data reject an econometric model, the researcher must decide which identifying assumptions to give up. If several equally preferred repairs restore compatibility, the repair itself is unknown, and inference under any one of them can exclude structural values supported by the others, even when that inference is exact. I propose Post-Relaxation Projection (PR), which carries one simultaneous confidence event through every repair that may be minimal. With repair-by-repair primitive bounds, PR equals the union of all post-relaxation targets compatible with the band, so no smaller band-based set has the same guarantee. I derive limits on learning the repair, the exact perturbation radius of the minimal-repair correspondence, oracle-equivalent adaptation, and a reduced-form version valid at zero first stages. In cross-country data on institutions and income, the data do not settle which historical instrument should be dropped, yet every admissible minimum repair implies a positive effect of institutions.

items.title: Drift Parameter Estimation for an Ergodic Extension of the Double Heston Model
items.summary: The double Heston model is a widely used stochastic volatility model in financial mathematics, particularly for option pricing, risk management, and volatility surface calibration. This paper investigates the joint estimation of the drift parameters for an ergodic extension of the double Heston model. We first establish stochastic properties of the underlying process, including the existence of a stationary distribution and ergodicity. We then study maximum likelihood and conditional least squares estimators based on continuous-time observations. For both estimation procedures, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality under suitable ergodicity conditions.

items.title: Bet Imaginatively, not Historically in Independent-Data Sequential Testing
items.summary: Sequential testing avoids some of the many controversies and drawbacks related to traditional batch testing with p-values. In particular, the testing by betting paradigm has developed rapidly in recent years; it frames the level of evidence against the null as the wealth of a player in a betting game. Naturally, how much a player should bet is a key consideration, and should reflect their confidence in what they know about the next observed data point. Much current work uses standard betting strategies developed for adversarial problems. In the stochastic setting, where the observed data is independent and stationary, these approaches may be suboptimal. We propose a simple betting strategy, follow the leave-one-out e-power (FLOE), that exploits the i.i.d. nature of a data stream to estimate the e-power of our current test on the underlying distribution. We average not over the historical evidence collected so far, as generic online learning-based methods do, but instead over the equally-likely possible data sequences we might have seen based on shuffling the data. With an additional principled regularization technique, this simple drop-in method yields substantial improvements in testing performance on a variety of kernel two-sample and independence testing problems.

items.title: Sharp Gaussian approximation for Polyak--Ruppert averaged linear stochastic approximation
items.summary: We study how quickly the normalized Polyak--Ruppert average approaches its Gaussian limit in linear stochastic approximation with bounded i.i.d.\ coefficients. For step sizes decaying as $k^{-γ}$, with $1/2\leγ<1$, we prove an upper bound of order $n^{γ-1}$ on the approximation error over convex sets in fixed dimension. A matching lower bound holds for every fixed model. The fastest rate in this range is $n^{-1/2}$, attained at $γ=1/2$. We also obtain an $O(n^{-1/2})$ bound on the error of the recursive multiplier bootstrap procedure.

items.title: Training Dynamics of Softmax Self-Attention: Fast Global Convergence via Preconditioning
items.summary: We study the training dynamics of gradient descent in a multilayer softmax self-attention network trained to perform linear regression and show that in the infinite-data limit this regression problem is equivalent to a matrix factorization problem. This connection motivates the design of Hera, a new first-order optimization algorithm for training self-attention networks. Key features of Hera include a reparameterization of the model arising from the matrix factorization geometry and a rescaling of the parameters which ensures that the empirical loss gradients remain close to the auxiliary matrix factorization gradients throughout training. Hera updates in the reparameterized model are equivalent to a certain preconditioned update in the original parameterization. We also propose a variant of Hera called Hera-PSD; our main theoretical result is that under small Gaussian initialization the excess risk of the model trained by Hera-PSD decreases exponentially fast in the number of gradient descent iterations, up to an additional error term that decreases as $1/n$, up to logarithmic factors, in the size of the training set. A particularly appealing aspect of our excess risk bound is that it does not degrade as the number of self-attention layers increases. In a stylized time-series prediction experiment in a nonlinear dynamical system, we find that a model trained by Hera achieves $98.1\%$ lower mean-squared test error than a model trained by AdamW and $97.7\%$ lower than a model trained by Muon at the same iteration budget.

items.title: A Modified Glicko Model for Rating Soccer Clubs and National Teams Worldwide
items.summary: Comparing soccer teams that rarely or never meet is a fundamental challenge in sports analytics: clubs play mostly within their national leagues, and national teams within their confederations. We propose a rating framework that places clubs and national teams worldwide on a common probabilistic scale. Building on a recent extension of Glicko with order effects and strength-dependent draw probabilities, we adapt the model to soccer with goal-scoring adjustments, a decomposition of home advantage, extra time, league-aware rating initialization and rules of promotion and relegation that do not inflate the levels of leagues; national teams start from the levels of their confederations. The models are evaluated on about 1.2 million club matches of 252 leagues from 166 countries (2000-2026) and 12.6 thousand national team matches (1998-2026). On held-out seasons, the modified Glicko model is clearly more accurate than Elo and as accurate as score-matrix models built on the goal expectations of a gradient boosting model, including the Dixon-Coles and Markov chain models, while it is substantially more accurate in international club matches. Averaging the predictions of the rating model and the Markov chain model is more accurate than either model alone. For national teams, the model is significantly more accurate than all baselines, especially in the final tournaments, where teams of different confederations meet. The resulting ratings are interpretable and can be used for player evaluation, transfer analysis and match forecasting. The match data, the ratings and the code are publicly available at https://github.com/andreyshelopugin/SportsRatings

items.title: An Integrated Framework for Rule-Based Data Editing
items.summary: Statistical data editing in official statistics must restore consistency while limiting changes to observed data. Exact minimum-change correction can be computationally demanding. This paper develops a general framework for structured data whose dependencies admit a normalized acyclic routing representation. It connects routing metadata and explicitly specified semantic edits to logical admissibility, violation diagnosis, and correction. Under stated record semantics, the generated Horn theory characterizes admissibility without materializing its deductive closure. Canonical indices preserve the origin of each requirement and identify the variables that can affect a violation. With complete diagnostics and strictly positive weights, a nonnegative violation Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on admissible records within the specified domain. This characterization is independent of the correction procedure and provides both an objective for correction and a certificate: a verified zero-energy output is admissible and globally minimizes violation energy within its permitted candidate domain. Minimum modification cost is formulated separately, with sufficient conditions for an equivalent penalized objective and optimality certificates based on attained lower bounds. A household survey application illustrates the construction, the verification of admissible corrections, and minimum-cost certification for a subset of outputs. The framework supports traceable validation and correction in official statistics, while statistical accuracy of replacement values requires separate assessment.

items.title: Regularized trimmed Factorial and Reduced K-means for contaminated high-dimensional data: separating geometry, search and selection
items.summary: Factorial and Reduced K-means estimate a partition and a low-dimensional clustering subspace jointly, which makes them attractive when the variables that separate groups are not those that dominate total variance. On contaminated high-dimensional data they face three linked problems: trimming can make the scatter matrices singular, the criterion has many local optima, and the rank, number of groups and trimming proportion are unknown and interact. We propose REG-HD-TFKM and REG-HD-TRKM, regularized trimmed versions of the two methods, together with a selection procedure that handles these problems as separate decisions. A ridge-stabilized spectral step keeps every fit well defined; heterogeneous multistart search explores alternative solutions; method-specific agreement and reproducibility scores choose among them; and trimming is applied only when a radial diagnostic or the path over trimming levels supports it. A simulation study with 41 design cells shows why the separation matters. Two representations of euro-area bank balance sheets show that similar partitions can rest on nearly orthogonal subspaces, and that the same selected structure can describe different retained samples.

items.title: The C-index Multiverse
items.summary: Quantifying out-of-sample discrimination performance for time-to-event outcomes is a fundamental step for model evaluation and selection in the context of predictive modelling. The concordance index, or C-index, is a widely used metric for this purpose, particularly with the growing development of machine learning methods. Beyond differences between proposed C-index estimators (e.g. Harrell's, Uno's and Antolini's), we demonstrate the existence of a C-index multiverse among available R and python software, where seemingly equal implementations can yield different results. This can undermine reproducibility and complicate fair comparisons across models and studies. Key variation sources include tie handling and adjustment to censoring. Additionally, the absence of a standardised approach to summarise risk from survival distributions, result in another source of variation dependent on input types. We demonstrate the consequences of the C-index multiverse when quantifying predictive performance for several survival models (from Cox proportional hazards to recent deep learning approaches) on publicly available breast cancer data, and semi-synthetic examples. Our work emphasises the need for better reporting to improve transparency and reproducibility. This article aims to be a useful guideline, helping analysts when navigating the multiverse, providing unified documentation and highlighting potential pitfalls of existing software. All code is publicly available at: www.github.com/BBolosSierra/CindexMultiverse.

items.title: Non-normal Limits and Joint Calibration of Cross-fitted Heterogeneity Tests
items.summary: Cross-fitting is used to test whether a ranking learned in a randomized experiment separates units that benefit from treatment from those that do not: each fold is ranked by a model fitted to the other folds, and the standardized difference in estimated effects between units ranked high and low is compared with a normal distribution. Under the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity the ranking is determined by noise, and because each fold helps to rank the others the fold estimates are dependent. We show that this dependence changes the shape of the null distribution, not just its variance. For least squares on one covariate the limit is bimodal for two folds and skewed for many, no variance correction restores the level, and the model is a counterexample to a published central limit theorem. With many covariates the limit approaches normality, but its variance stays inflated. Removing the non-normal component of the statistic removes its power, so we keep the statistic and change its reference distribution: joint calibration simulates together the moments that choose the rankings and those that evaluate them and applies the same selection to the draws; it has asymptotically exact level and requires no refitting. Applications to clinical and marketing trials, together with random treatment reassignments on their covariates, demonstrate that the standard test substantially inflates Type I error and can produce spurious rejections that joint calibration avoids.

items.title: Semiparametric Copula Estimation for Spatially Correlated Multivariate Mixed Outcomes: Analyzing Visual Sightings of Fin Whales from a Line Transect Survey
items.summary: For marine biologists, ascertaining the dependence structures between marine species and marine environments, such as sea surface temperature and ocean depth, is imperative for defining ecosystem functioning and providing insights into the dynamics of marine ecosystems. However, obtained data include not only continuous but also discrete data, such as binaries and counts (referred to as mixed outcomes), as well as spatial correlations, both of which make conventional multivariate analysis tools impractical. To solve this issue, we propose semiparametric Bayesian inference and develop an efficient algorithm for computing the posterior of the dependence structure based on the rank likelihood under a latent multivariate spatial Gaussian process using the Markov chain Monte Carlo method. To alleviate the computational intractability caused by the Gaussian process, we also provide a scalable implementation that leverages the nearest-neighbor Gaussian process. Extensive numerical experiments reveal that the proposed method reliably infers the dependence structures of spatially correlated mixed outcomes. Finally, we apply the proposed method to a dataset collected during an international synoptic krill survey in the Scotia Sea of the Antarctic Peninsula to infer the dependence structure between fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus), krill biomass, and relevant oceanographic data.

items.title: Sharp Covering-Number Bounds for Feedforward ReLU Networks via Parameter Symmetries
items.summary: In neural networks, distinct parameter configurations often realize the same input--output mapping, indicating that nominal parameter counts can overstate functional complexity. In this paper, we characterize the parameter-space symmetries of ReLU and Leaky ReLU networks across fully connected, convolutional, and residual architectures. We prove that every quasianalytic parameter map preserving the network function is a composition of positive channel scaling and channel permutation. By quotienting out both symmetries, we derive uniform covering-number upper bounds in which positive scaling reduces the complexity exponent from the total parameter count $S$ to $S-H$ (with $H$ denoting the number of scalable channels) and permutation symmetry divides the bound by the factorial count $G$ of channel permutations. We establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponent $S-H$ is sharp in general and that the divisor $G$ is attained for one-hidden-layer and generically identifiable networks. We further extend these results to general continuous piecewise-linear activated networks. Finally, we apply our covering-number bounds to derive statistical risk guarantees for empirical risk minimization and capacity control beyond i.i.d.\ settings, and show how the underlying symmetries help explain weight rebalancing in function approximation and flat directions in empirical risk optimization.

items.title: Large sample scaling analysis of the Zig-Zag algorithm for Bayesian inference
items.summary: Piecewise deterministic Markov processes provide scalable methods for sampling from the posterior distributions in big data settings by admitting principled sub-sampling strategies that do not bias the output. An important example is the Zig-Zag process of [Ann. Stats. 47 (2019) 1288 - 1320] where clever sub-sampling has been shown to produce an essentially independent sample at a cost that does not scale with the size of the data. However, sub-sampling also leads to slower convergence and poor mixing of the process, a behaviour which questions the promised scalability of the algorithm. We provide a large sample scaling analysis of the Zig-Zag process and its sub-sampling versions in settings of parametric Bayesian inference. In the transient phase of the algorithm, we show that the Zig-Zag trajectories are well approximated by the solution to a system of ODEs. These ODEs possess a drift in the direction of decreasing KL-divergence between the assumed model and the true distribution and are explicitly characterized in the paper. In the stationary phase, we give weak convergence results for different versions of the Zig-Zag process. Based on our results, we estimate that for large data sets of size n, using suitable control variates with sub-sampling in Zig-Zag, the algorithm costs O(1) to obtain an essentially independent sample; a computational speed-up of O(n) over the canonical version of Zig-Zag and other traditional MCMC methods

items.title: A hybrid machine learning-analog framework for downscaling unprecedented climate extremes
items.summary: Extreme weather events are critical for climate impact assessments. While physical models can simulate unprecedented extremes, for example, through ensemble boosting, this approach is computationally demanding, often restricting output to coarse spatial resolutions. Probabilistic generative downscaling offers a solution by enabling efficient sampling from the entire climate distribution, including its extreme tails. Here, we first demonstrate that machine learning generated regional climate model heatwaves over Paris are physically realistic. We then leverage an emulated machine learning dataset to perform analog-based downscaling of coarse global climate model ensemble boosting events. Our hybrid framework effectively bridges high-resolution regional detail with rare-event sampling, providing an efficient tool for extreme event downscaling and capturing multi-model uncertainty.

items.title: Structure-based Transfer Learning
items.summary: Transfer learning improves estimation in a target study using information from related sources. Classical transfer learning is typically data-based, requiring access to the source data or to a model fitted on them. Neither is available in many modern studies, as both are often proprietary or unreported. What can be transferred instead is structure: summarized information derived from a source, such as the supports of predictors, which is available and interpretable without access to the source data or model. The prevalence of the Large Language Model (LLM) provides a rich source of such structure information. However, data-based transfer learning can not well utilize it as accessing the data and model of the LLM is often infeasible. In this paper, we propose a novel transfer learning framework based on structure. In particular, we focus on linear model and aim to use supports generated by multiple agents, such as LLM, to improve estimation in the target study. Our procedure maps each support into the target parameter space, aggregates the results with data-driven weights, and applies a sparse correction against inaccurate supports. We establish interpretable conditions for retaining the target-only Lasso rate and for a faster convergence rate, together with minimax optimality under joint coverage. Simulations and a DNA-methylation application illustrate gains and robustness.

items.title: Can We Ignore Data Dependence in Inference Implementation? A Positive Answer for Regression Discontinuity Designs
items.summary: In empirical economics, regression discontinuity design (RDD) inference is commonly based on asymptotic normality under an independence assumption, but the running variables or disturbances may exhibit unknown and complex dependence. We first rigorously identify a fundamental dilemma for this conventional practice. To address it, we propose a validity recovery procedure that redefines the roles of bias and stochastic calibration, thereby decoupling data dependence from stochastic calibration. Taking the independence-assumption-based confidence interval as our inferential anchor, our procedure restores its validity while preserving its asymptotic leading constant, even when the data are dependent. For fixed-design RDD based on local linear regression, our intervals achieve asymptotically exact nominal coverage and, compared with the anchor, exploit higher-order smoothness without enlarging the asymptotic variance constant, attaining the minimax-optimal shrinking rates up to a mild factor, such as $\sqrt{\log T})$. The procedure requires neither specific dependence frameworks (e.g., mixing or physical dependence) nor dependence-modeling techniques (e.g., long-run variance estimation). For random-design RDD, under more specific dependence assumptions, we derive the rate-explicit coverage error at each nominal level and characterize the trade-off between this rate and interval length. Moreover, modeling dependence becomes an optional enhancement that can further enable validity recovery and improve finite-sample coverage, while averaging over repeated calibrations stabilizes the randomized center and protects against undercoverage in finite samples without increasing interval length. In short, under mild dependence and moment conditions, our procedure makes data independence an implementation default rather than a validity requirement. Simulations support the theoretical results.

items.title: Communication-Efficient Federated Multi-View Clustering via View-Aware Quantization
items.summary: Federated multi-view clustering (FedMVC) has recently attracted increasing attention for its ability to exploit complementary clustering structures across multiple clients while preserving data privacy. However, existing FedMVC methods often suffer from high communication overhead due to the repeated transmission of high-dimensional representations, which limits their scalability in practical federated systems. Moreover, different views may contribute unequally to the clustering performance, calling for adaptive communication strategies. In this paper, we propose a view-aware quantization algorithm for communication-efficient FedMVC. By dynamically assigning quantization bits based on iteratively updated view importance scores, the proposed algorithm effectively balances clustering performance and communication efficiency under a global bit budget constraint. To validate its generality, we integrate our approach into four state-of-the-art FedMVC methods. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that view-aware quantization achieves up to 6.59x communication reduction while maintaining and in some cases surpassing baseline clustering performance, confirming the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed approach.

items.title: Super Learner: A Practical Tutorial
items.summary: The selection of an optimal predictive model is a pervasive challenge in biostatistics and epidemiology. Relying on a single a priori algorithm risks overfitting and reduced generalizability when applied to new settings. Super Learner is a flexible ensemble machine-learning method that mitigates these risks by combining multiple candidate algorithms into a single prediction model. Using cross-validation, it defines a weighted combination of learners that minimizes a specified loss function, ensuring performance asymptotically equal to or better than the best candidate algorithm. This tutorial provides a comprehensive, practical guide to implementing Super Learner in R for applied researchers. Using a simulated epidemiological dataset with a binary outcome, we demonstrate the step-by-step construction of the ensemble. We cover the foundational statistical concepts, basic implementation, evaluation through cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, feature screening, and performance optimization for metrics such as the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC). Additionally, we detail advanced usage, including computational parallelization and the integration of custom algorithms and screening procedures. The guide also includes a consolidated section on best practices for specifying SL, covering loss function selection, effective sample size determination, CV scheme definition, library curation, and discrete vs. ensemble SL decisions, plus a practical reference to the caret package for model preprocessing and comparison. This guide equips epidemiologists and clinical researchers with the tools to confidently incorporate robust machine learning techniques into their predictive modeling workflows.

items.title: Winter wheat improves soil carbon sequestration with reduced gains in warmer climates
items.summary: Sustainable agricultural intensification requires a precise understanding of how land use decisions influence soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration under varying environmental conditions. We apply causal machine learning to evaluate the heterogeneous impact of winter wheat-based rotations on SOC at the field-level across Lithuania. Using a nationwide dataset collected over five years (2018-2022), including crop types, management practices, soil properties, and environmental conditions, we estimate how the effects of winter wheat-based rotation vary across space and climate. Our results indicate that winter wheat generally enhances SOC levels, but its effectiveness is modulated by climate. Cooler regions experience higher SOC gains, whereas warmer regions show diminished or even negative effects. Future climate projections suggest that the potential for winter wheat carbon sequestration may decline under high-emission scenarios. These findings highlight the importance of localized agricultural strategies that account for climate variability to maximize SOC sequestration and ensure long-term soil sustainability.

items.title: Balancing Weights for Causal Mediation Analysis
items.summary: Causal mediation analysis decomposes the average treatment effect into components that operate through intermediate variables and a component that does not. This paper studies weighting estimation of generalized mediation functionals, whose contrasts include natural direct and indirect effects, for any fixed finite number of causally ordered mediators. Inverse propensity score weights are vulnerable to (a) weight instability, because they are products of estimated probability ratios, and (b) finite-sample covariate and mediator imbalance, which can bias the estimator. We instead propose sequential balancing weights, which address (a) by minimizing weight dispersion and (b) by imposing exact balance. Stage one balances covariates between a treatment group and the full sample. Each later stage adds the next mediator and balances a treatment group against the preceding weighted group. A finite-sample bias decomposition of the augmented weighting estimator determines these variables and targets. When exact balance cannot be attained in a small sample, the procedure relaxes the balancing conditions by tolerances selected without using the outcome. Under the stated assumptions, the estimated weights converge at every stage to their population inverse-probability counterparts, with errors from preceding stages entering additively. We also establish asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency of the augmented weighting estimator, together with conditions for consistent variance estimation. In the main simulation design with two ordered mediators, the proposed weights outperform the compared methods in bias, root mean squared error, and coverage. In a small media-framing experiment with two ordered mediators, the proposed weights reduce the imbalance left by propensity-score weighting.

items.title: FréchetFlow: Flow Matching for Non-Euclidean Data
items.summary: Scientific observations such as probability distributions, trees and covariance matrices call for generative models that respect their non-Euclidean geometry. While flow matching has been extended to manifolds by utilizing geodesics and velocities, such manifold structures are not available in a general metric space. We introduce FréchetFlow, a generative modeling framework for metric space-valued data that requires neither linear operations nor a smooth manifold structure. A key feature of the proposed approach is that we utilize well-established Euclidean flows to learn the joint distribution of distances to a set of landmarks, whereupon new objects are reconstructed from generated landmark representations. The reconstruction step utilizes weighted Fréchet means of reference objects, drawing on Fréchet regression. We establish Wasserstein error bounds that connect accuracy of the generated object distributions to the placement of landmarks, flow approximation and reconstruction error and prove consistency under finite second moments. This leads to convergence rates that depend on the metric complexity of the target objects, tail moments and fitting accuracy. Experiments show competitive accuracy with established flow matching methods in Euclidean simulations and lower Wasserstein errors than specifically tailored methods for several scientific datasets. Across simulation settings, we find that generation error decreases as sample size increases.

items.title: Structural Analysis of Object-Valued Time Series
items.summary: We develop inference for structural patterns in the temporal association of object-valued time series. Our framework is built on pairwise lag profiles, which record the expected value of a chosen pairwise function at each lag and serve as a unified inferential target. We consider three representative structural features: whether a profile reaches stability beyond a finite lag, remains constant over time, and displays geometric regularity at short lags. To assess these properties, we design statistical tests calibrated by a common block multiplier bootstrap that accommodates serial dependence and the overlap inherent in lagged pairs. Gaussian approximation results establish bootstrap validity for asymptotic size control, while suitable signal conditions guarantee consistency against the corresponding alternatives. Finite-sample performance is examined through simulations in both Euclidean and density-valued settings. Applications to electricity load curves and stock-return distributions illustrate how the proposed procedures characterize association across lags.

items.title: Conditional Neural SDEs for Financial Time-Series Generation
items.summary: Conditional generation of time-series paths is a central problem in probabilistic modeling, where the goal is to simulate future trajectories that are both realistic and responsive to external context. It has direct applications in finance and economics. Neural stochastic differential equations provide a natural framework for this task by combining continuous-time stochastic dynamics with learnable drift and diffusion functions. However, directly modeling the target state can be unstable in conditional settings, especially when the target and conditioning variables have strong level dependence, limited training data, or different dimensions. We propose a residual-anchor Neural SDE architecture that decomposes the target into a learned conditional anchor and a stochastic residual. The anchor captures the context-dependent baseline, while the Neural SDE (Stochastic Differential Equation) models the residual dynamics around this baseline. This separation reduces the burden on the stochastic dynamics and generalizes spread-based representations to more general conditioning settings. We evaluate the approach on real-world financial time series, including conditional interest-rate scenarios and a comparison with a time-series foundation model. The results show that the proposed model can generate plausible conditional paths, maintain competitive point accuracy, and provide calibrated uncertainty estimates.

items.title: Knowledge Transfer for Conditional Flow Matching: Frozen Estimation and Adaptation
items.summary: Conditional generative modeling with limited target data can benefit from representations learned in a related source population. We develop a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching that accommodates distinct source and target response distributions and dimensions. Two procedures exploit a representation learned from source data: TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head with the representation fixed, whereas TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a representation adaptation under a functional anchoring penalty. For explicit neural network classes, we establish bounds on conditional squared Wasserstein risk that account for source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration. When the source representation admits a smooth correction, adaptation replaces the frozen mismatch contribution by the cost of learning the correction and a controllable regularization bias. An information lower bound identifies regimes in which adaptation attains a strictly faster conditional squared Wasserstein risk rate than any generator restricted to the frozen context information. We also develop independent validation procedure for selecting among fitted conditional generators. We show that the selection procedure satisfies an oracle inequality, and the switching rule guarantees, with high probability, no increase in conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator. Simulations and real data applications illustrate the gains from our proposed methods and the effectiveness of target validation in guarding against negative transfer.

items.title: Location--Scale Calibration for Generalized Posteriors
items.summary: General Bayesian updating replaces the likelihood with a loss scaled by a learning rate, but posterior uncertainty can depend sharply on that scale. We propose a simple post-processing that aligns generalized posterior draws with the asymptotic sampling distribution of a penalized estimator, yielding uncertainty quantification that is asymptotically invariant to the learning rate. We prove a total-variation normal approximation at an effective scale determined by a score central limit theorem, allowing sample-size-dependent prior factors, non-i.i.d. observations, and locally smooth convex penalties under model misspecification. Within this framework, we justify the open-faced sandwich adjustment (Shaby, 2014) and extend it from covariance rescaling to a location--scale calibration whose draws converge in total variation to the target for any learning rate. In our empirical illustration, calibrated draws maintain stable coverage, interval width, and bias over orders of magnitude in the learning rate and closely track frequentist benchmarks, whereas uncalibrated posteriors vary markedly.

items.title: Comparing survival prediction models with sharp bounds on Brier-risk differences before local outcomes are available
items.summary: Hospitals may need to compare an existing survival prediction model with a candidate before outcomes in their own patients become available. We develop a procedure to support this comparison under explicit assumptions about between-cohort differences and to identify when judgment should be deferred. For two fixed predictors, we derive and prove closed-form sharp bounds on their difference in fixed-horizon Brier risk under bounded, profile-specific conditional survival log-odds shifts. Evaluating both predictors against the same unknown target outcomes yields intervals no wider than subtraction of separately bounded risks. Censoring-adjusted estimation and simultaneous bootstrap confidence envelopes distinguish candidate support, reference support, and deferred judgment. In simulations with a superior reference predictor, separate identified intervals were on average 2.5-2.6 times as wide as direct intervals. At a sensitivity bound of 0.2, correct reference support occurred in 24.8-83.5% of replications with direct identification versus 6.5-19.6% with separate-risk subtraction; incorrect candidate support with direct identification was at most 0.1%. Coverage was 0.88-0.95 with 30% or 50% censoring but fell to 0.79-0.86 under 70% censoring. Three public-data applications examined transfer between hospitals, across time, and between successive clinical studies. Across fixed configurations, separate identified intervals were 1.77-16.4 times as wide as direct intervals. In 100 repeated splits per application, only direct identification supported the candidate at a sensitivity bound of 0.2 in 29%, 11%, and 8% of splits, respectively. The procedure provides additional evidence for provisional model comparison while allowing judgment to be deferred; it complements external validation, with caution required when censoring compromises confidence-envelope coverage.

items.title: Hierarchical Bayes meets hierarchical forecasting: A flexible framework for level-focused forecasts
items.summary: Decision-making in hierarchical systems requires probabilistic forecasts at all cross-sectional levels. Current hierarchical forecasting methods typically generate independent forecasts at each level and reconcile them post hoc to ensure coherence between upper and lower levels. Such post hoc corrections do not incorporate hierarchical structure or decision goals into the underlying parameter estimation. We propose a fully Bayesian hierarchical forecasting framework that shares information more effectively between and across levels than reconciliation alone. Our approach has the flexibility to softly penalise incoherence, subject to model specification, and to focus the global model and coherence update on hierarchical levels most relevant to decision outcomes. This yields parameter estimates that are focused towards the forecasting goals and capture the requirement for coherency, removing the need to estimate covariance matrices for multi-step forecasting horizons. We demonstrate improvements in predictive accuracy metrics on both simulated data and Australian domestic tourism forecasting.

items.title: Neural Networks With Dense Computational Graphs Are Not Universal Approximators
items.summary: We investigate the approximation capabilities of dense neural networks. While universal approximation theorems establish that sufficiently large architectures can approximate arbitrary continuous functions when there are no restrictions on the weights, we show that dense neural networks do not possess this universality. Our argument is based on a model compression approach, combining the weak regularity lemma with an interpretation of feedforward networks as message passing graph neural networks. We consider ReLU neural networks subject to natural constraints on weights and input and output dimensions, which model a notion of dense connectivity. Within this setting, we demonstrate the existence of Lipschitz continuous functions that cannot be approximated by such networks. This highlights intrinsic limitations of neural networks with dense layers and motivates the use of sparse connectivity as a necessary ingredient for achieving true universality.

items.title: Improving Efficiency and Power in Small Rare-Disease Trials Through Prespecified, Data-Adaptive Covariate Adjustment
items.summary: Covariate adjustment can potentially improve efficiency in randomized clinical trials, but in rare diseases, limited prior knowledge makes it difficult to specify an adjustment at the design stage. Targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) with the Super Learner (TMLE+SL) can outperform fixed adjustment methods, such as the G-computation estimator, by leveraging machine learning to learn both the covariates and the functional form of the adjustment from the trial data. Estimating the known treatment mechanism can improve efficiency further. In simulations reflecting real rare-disease trials, TMLE+SL yielded valid inference and achieved greater efficiency and power than conventional analyses. Finally, we also provide practical guidance on specifying TMLE+SL in rare-disease trials.

items.title: Common-DAG Support from Targeted Covariance Changes under Confounding
items.summary: Targeted covariance changes couple structural rows through a common directed acyclic graph. We study the graph support determined by these experiments when structural errors may be correlated. A positive-gap four-node family has a shortcut identified by common acyclicity. A response indegree of at most two additionally gives unique complete support and two compatible coefficient matrices. The same experiments admit a stable feedback model with the shortcut absent. The result extends to connected graphs with repeated branching and merging. Finite response-column alternatives yield exact bounded-parent compatibility decisions through Horn propagation and partial-target completion. Certified ancestry then supplies an observed-ancestor covariance restriction. Gaussian regression and Fieller inversion reduce inference to a scalar confidence set, and quadratic elimination retains the shared nuisance coefficients with finite-sample edge-error control. In 2048 Gaussian conditions, the scalar procedure reports 127/128 positive edges at gap 1/4 and 524288 observations per cell. Its decisions agree with the joint outer-polynomial reference on the same inputs in all 2022 qualified conditions, with zero reports in 512 null conditions. Exact 16-, 32- and 64-node evaluations verify support and target-coverage conclusions. A root-target characterization connects the identifying information to intervention design.

items.title: Hierarchical Projection for Adaptive Knowledge Transfer
items.summary: Transfer learning aims to improve estimation in a target population with limited data by borrowing information from related external datasets, referred to as sources. However, heterogeneity in target-source relevance and predictor-outcome relationships can lead to negative transfer, where model performance is worse than using target data alone, particularly in high-dimensional settings with partially overlapping features. We propose Projection Transfer Learning (ProjectionTL), a Bayesian framework that integrates hierarchical modeling with adaptive posterior projection to enable selective knowledge transfer at both the source and feature levels. In the first stage, a source-guided hierarchical prior adaptively combines information from multiple sources using data-driven weights that capture their global alignment with the target. In the second stage, a weighted posterior-projection procedure induces sparsity by preferentially retaining features supported by stronger agreement between source and target signals. This two-stage framework distinguishes global source relevance from coordinate-specific transferability, allowing informative components to be retained while reducing the influence of heterogeneous or non-transferable signals. We establish theoretical guarantees for posterior contraction and model selection consistency under high-dimensional regularity conditions, without requiring all sources to be informative. Simulation studies and applications to Alzheimer's disease neuroimaging data demonstrate improved estimation accuracy, variable selection, and predictive performance compared with others, including settings with heterogeneous sources and block-wise missing modalities.

items.title: MediPFN: Amortized In-Context Nuisance Learning and Inference for Causal Mediation Analysis
items.summary: Causal mediation analysis decomposes a treatment effect into indirect pathways through mediators and direct pathways through other processes. Tabular foundation models perform classification and regression through in-context learning, providing estimates of conditional means and propensity scores used in causal mediation analysis. Constructing confidence intervals from these estimates requires accounting for uncertainty introduced by fitting and combining several nuisance functions. We introduce MediPFN, an amortized inference framework that adapts a pretrained tabular foundation model to nuisance prediction and combines its predictions through a cross-fitted influence-function estimator. A separate head learns quantiles of the estimator's standardized error from simulated tables with known indirect effects. Supervised fine-tuning, symmetrization, and independent calibration then produce a confidence interval. We establish coverage bounds for the resulting intervals under standard assumptions. Across experiments, MediPFN attains coverage closer to the nominal level than several comparators. It also reduces the computational cost of uncertainty quantification, running 59.1 times faster than bootstrap in matched comparisons.

items.title: Low Rank Matrix Completion via Robust Alternating Minimization in Nearly Linear Time
items.summary: Given a matrix $M\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, the low rank matrix completion problem asks us to find a rank-$k$ approximation of $M$ as $UV^\top$ for $U\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times k}$ and $V\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times k}$ by only observing a few entries specified by a set of entries $Ω\subseteq [m]\times [n]$. In particular, we examine an approach that is widely used in practice -- the alternating minimization framework. Jain, Netrapalli, and Sanghavi [JNS13] showed that if $M$ has incoherent rows and columns, then alternating minimization provably recovers the matrix $M$ by observing a nearly linear in $n$ number of entries. While the sample complexity has been subsequently improved [GLZ17], alternating minimization steps are required to be computed exactly. This hinders the development of more efficient algorithms and fails to depict the practical implementation of alternating minimization, where the updates are usually performed approximately in favor of efficiency. In this paper, we take a major step towards a more efficient and error-robust alternating minimization framework. To this end, we develop an analytical framework for alternating minimization that can tolerate a moderate amount of errors caused by approximate updates. Moreover, our algorithm runs in time $\widetilde O(|Ω| k)$, which is nearly linear in the time to verify the solution while preserving the sample complexity. This improves upon all prior known alternating minimization approaches which require $\widetilde O(|Ω| k^2)$ time.

items.title: Local Fréchet regression with polyspherical predictors: Uniform convergence rates and factor selection
items.summary: We study local Fréchet regression for responses taking values in a metric space and predictors on a product of spheres of possibly different dimensions. We propose local constant and local linear estimators with factor-specific bandwidths and establish uniform convergence rates. We select sphere factors by comparing cross-fitted prediction risks for the full and leave-one-factor-out models. The procedure consistently recovers the active factor set, and the selected local constant and local linear estimators attain the same uniform convergence rates as if the active factor set were known. For univariate Wasserstein responses supported on a common compact interval, the uniform rate holds without an entropy condition on the response space. Simulations with scalar and spherical responses and analyses of vessel speeds and drifter speed distributions illustrate the methods.

items.title: A Practical Guide to Instrumental Variables Methods with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
items.summary: Instrumental variables (IV) methods are central to applied microeconomics. While classical approaches assume linear models with constant effects, recent literature has shifted toward the local average treatment effect (LATE) framework to accommodate heterogeneous treatment effects. This paper provides a practical guide to aligning empirical practice with recent theory. We first examine how different specifications with covariates lead to distinct weighted averages of covariate-specific LATEs. We then discuss how parametric misspecification can undermine the causal interpretation of these estimands and suggest flexible specifications as essential robustness checks. Finally, we review formal tests for LATE assumptions and methods robust to monotonicity violations. We provide a guide to software implementations to help researchers apply the methods in practice.

items.title: A Family-Level Graphical Gatekeeping Procedure with Iterative Retesting
items.summary: Confirmatory clinical trials often involve multiple objectives grouped into families according to scientific priorities. At the intersection of graphical multiple testing and gatekeeping methods, we develop a Bonferroni-based family-level graphical procedure with partial-rejection-based transfers and iterative re-testing. Families are tested sequentially within each stage, using fixed component tests and a prespecified transition matrix. The updating rule combines current-stage forward contributions based on current family levels with previous-stage backward contributions based on initial allocations. We establish strong global familywise error rate control at a prespecified level under arbitrary dependence. The construction permits backward feedback while retaining fixed component tests and transition coefficients, distinguishing its implementation from forward-only family-level procedures and the specified superchain algorithm. Simulations demonstrate gains over the corresponding No-retest procedure, while identifying an efficiency cost relative to a hypothesis-level graphical comparator with matched initial allocations and edge weights. Clinical illustrations show how the procedure implements family-level priorities and feedback, and an extension accommodates a two-layer structure with multiple families per layer.

items.title: Prediction Sets and Conformal Inference with Interval Outcomes
items.summary: Given data on a random variable $Y$, a prediction set with miscoverage level $α\in (0,1)$ is a set that contains a new draw of $Y$ with probability at least $1-α$. Among all prediction sets satisfying this coverage property, the oracle prediction set is the one with minimal volume. The oracle prediction set offers a complementary view of the distribution of $Y$, beyond point estimators such as the mean and quantiles, and has attracted considerable interest recently. This paper develops methods for estimating such prediction sets conditional on observed covariates when $Y$ censored or interval-valued. We characterise the oracle prediction set under partial identification induced by interval censoring and propose consistent estimators for both oracle prediction intervals and more general oracle prediction sets consisting of multiple disjoint intervals. In addition, we apply conformal inference to construct finite-sample valid prediction sets for interval outcomes that remain consistent as the sample size grows, using a conformity score tailored to interval data. The proposed procedure accounts for irreducible prediction uncertainty due to the stochastic nature of outcomes, modelling uncertainty arising from partial identification, and sampling uncertainty that vanishes as sample size increases. We conduct Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical applications using UK job postings data and the US Current Population Survey. The results demonstrate the robustness and efficiency of the proposed methods.

items.title: Conformal Risk Control under Non-Monotone Losses: Theory and Finite-Sample Guarantees
items.summary: Conformal risk control (CRC) provides distribution-free guarantees for controlling the expected loss at a user-specified level. Existing theory typically assumes that the loss decreases monotonically with a tuning parameter that governs the size of the prediction set. However, this assumption is often violated in practice, where losses may behave non-monotonically due to competing objectives such as coverage and efficiency. In this paper, we study CRC under non-monotone loss functions when the tuning parameter is selected from a finite grid, a setting commonly arising in thresholding and discretized decision rules. Revisiting a known counterexample, we show that the validity of CRC without monotonicity depends critically on the relationship between the calibration sample size and the grid resolution. In particular, reliable risk control can still be achieved when the calibration sample is sufficiently large relative to the grid size. We establish a finite-sample guarantee for bounded losses over a grid of size $m$, showing that the excess risk above the target level $α$ scales on the order of $\sqrt{\log(m)/n}$, where $n$ is the calibration sample size. A matching lower bound demonstrates that this rate is sharp for the CRC selection rule under the same population-safe endpoint condition. We also derive refined guarantees under additional structural conditions, including Lipschitz continuity and monotonicity, and extend the analysis to settings with distribution shift via importance weighting. Numerical experiments on synthetic multilabel classification and real object detection data illustrate the practical implications of non-monotonicity. Methods that explicitly account for finite-sample uncertainty achieve more stable risk control than approaches based on monotonicity transformations, while maintaining competitive prediction set sizes.

items.title: Understanding the Asymptotic Transience of Q-Learning via Distributional Expansion
items.summary: Q-learning has been empirically observed to exhibit substantial transient error. This transient remains uncaptured by the leading Gaussian limit because the central-limit normalization removes the smaller-scale displacement generated by the initial nonlinear evolution. On the other hand, worst-case finite-sample guarantees, while accounting for transient effects, can obscure the mechanisms responsible for the error on a particular problem instance. We develop a finer asymptotic analysis that gives an asymptotically exact characterization of this transient for a fixed instance. Specifically, for synchronous Q-learning in finite discounted Markov decision processes, we separate the last-iterate error into an optimal-policy temporal-difference (TD) component and a nonnegative displacement caused by maximization. The centered TD component has Gaussian fluctuations at scale $n^{-1/2}$, whereas the maximization transient is of order $n^{-1}$ and converges almost surely, after rescaling by $n$, to a random limit. This limit represents the propagated effect of maximization errors generated before the greedy policy stabilizes. We combine this characterization with an Edgeworth expansion of the TD component to identify the corrections to its Gaussian approximation, separating the effects of initialization, non-Gaussian TD fluctuations, and maximization. The results reveal how transient errors arise for individual Q-learning instances and how their effects persist below the central-limit scale.

items.title: Bias-Aware Adjoint Calibration and Optimal Control of Stochastic Multiscale Bioprocess Digital Twins
items.summary: We develop a bias-aware digital-twin calibration and control framework for multiscale bioprocess models within a biological systems-of-systems (Bio-SoS) paradigm. The digital twin is represented by a stochastic differential equation (SDE) model and calibrated from sparse observations using quasi-likelihood estimation and adjoint sensitivity analysis. SDE generator-based moment expansions characterize truncation-induced parameter bias, while forward-backward adjoints quantify how calibration uncertainty propagates to value functions and policy performance. The resulting parameter-error distribution supports both policy-directed data acquisition and uncertainty-aware policy optimization through a second-order Gaussian-averaged objective. We characterize the asymptotic behavior of the resulting exploration criterion and derive a physical-system performance under the optimized policy. To implement these ideas, we develop an Actor-Simulator algorithm that jointly updates model parameters, selects informative experiments, and optimizes control policies. Numerical studies demonstrate improved calibration accuracy, sample efficiency, and control performance relative to state-of-the-art baselines.

items.title: Generalized linear models under distribution uncertainty
items.summary: In this paper, we study generalized linear models under distribution uncertainty, where the random intercept has mean uncertainty and takes values in an unknown bounded interval. We develop a novel two-step method, named Firth-corrected Expectation-Maximization with Moving Block (FEMMB), to estimate the regression coefficients as well as the lower and upper bounds of the intercept. A Firth bias correction is incorporated into the EM algorithm to mitigate the incidental parameters problem, which is prominent in generalized linear models with many nuisance intercepts. Under mild regularity conditions, we establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimated regression coefficients, and the consistency of the estimated intercept bounds. Simulation studies and a real-data application to an imbalanced credit card dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

items.title: Nested Ensemble Learning with Topological Data Analysis for Graph Classification and Regression
items.summary: We propose a nested ensemble learning framework that utilizes Topological Data Analysis (TDA) to extract and integrate topological features from graph data, with the goal of improving performance on classification and regression tasks. Our approach computes persistence diagrams (PDs) using lower-star filtrations induced by three filter functions: closeness, betweenness, and degree2 centrality. To overcome the limitation of relying on a single filter, these PDs are integrated through a data-driven, three-level architecture. At Level-0, diverse base models are independently trained on the topological features extracted for each filter function. At Level-1, a meta-learner combines the predictions of these base models for each filter to form filter-specific ensembles. Finally, at Level-2, a meta-learner integrates the outputs of these filter-specific ensembles to produce the final prediction. We evaluate our method on both simulated and real-world graph datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms base models and standard stacking methods, achieving higher classification accuracy and lower regression error. It also surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches, ranking among the top three models across all benchmarks.

items.title: Model Criticism via Stochastic Optimization
items.summary: Many generative models are specified by how data are simulated. An observation is a deterministic transform $Y=G(θ,X)$ of a draw $X$ from an assumed noise law, indexed by a structural parameter $θ$. Such models cover discrete, continuous and functional data, as well as i.i.d. replicates of stochastic processes, but their likelihoods are often unavailable. We propose a simulation-based procedure that tests whether such a model fits the data and, when it does not, locates where it fails, without choosing a test statistic. The procedure splits the data in two and is formulated as a two-stage stochastic program. In the estimation stage, $θ$ is fitted on the first block by minimizing a Wasserstein distance between the data and simulations from the model. In the recourse stage, $θ$ is frozen at the fitted $\tildeθ$, and a finite set of representative noise values $\{\bar x_j\}$ is pushed through the fitted mechanism to give model atoms $G(\tildeθ,\bar x_j)$. The held-out block optimizes weights $\textbf{w}$ on the model atoms to best match its own distribution. The optimized weights are then compared with theoretical weights under correct specification. Since each model atom is the image of known noise values, the disagreement between optimal and theoretical weights points to the part of the noise law that is wrong. The split makes the scaled weights conditionally multinomial, yielding a calibrated Pearson test. We prove strong consistency of both stages under checkable assumptions and illustrate the procedure on a Gaussian location--scale family, the number of segregating sites under Kingman's coalescent, a Yule process, and an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck diffusion.

items.title: Testing the number of common factors by bootstrapped sample covariance matrix in high-dimensional factor models and errata
items.summary: This paper studies the impact of bootstrap procedure on the eigenvalue distributions of the sample covariance matrix under a high-dimensional factor structure. We provide asymptotic distributions for the top eigenvalues of bootstrapped sample covariance matrix under mild conditions.
