We validate the CH strategy empirically through a simulation study, and on 16 large-scale datasets from the M-series benchmark, showing how CH achieves competitive RMSE accuracy, while uniquely enabling parallel inference, targeted horizon querying, and interpolation and extrapolation across unseen horizons.

items.title: Decentralized Ranking Aggregation via Gossip: Convergence and Robustness
items.summary: The concept of ranking aggregation plays a central role in preference analysis, and numerous algorithms for calculating median rankings, often originating in social choice theory, have been documented in the literature, offering theoretical guarantees in a centralized setting, \textit{i.e.}, when all the ranking data to be aggregated can be brought together in a single computing unit. For many technologies (\textit{e.g.} peer-to-peer networks, IoT, multi-agent systems), extending the ability to calculate consensus rankings with guarantees of convergence and resilience to potential contamination in a decentralized setting, when preference data is initially distributed across a communicating network, remains a major methodological challenge. Indeed, in recent years, the literature on decentralized computation has mainly focused on computing or optimizing statistics such as arithmetic means using gossip algorithms. The purpose of this article is precisely to study how to achieve reliable and resilient consensus on collective rankings in a decentralized setting, thereby raising new questions, robustness to corrupted nodes, and scalability through reduced communication costs in particular. The approach proposed and analyzed here relies on the robustness guarantees offered by random gossip communication, which allows autonomous agents to compute a global ranking consensus using local interactions only, without coordination or a central authority.

items.title: Counting Under Disagreement: Dollar-Weighted Measurement, Selective Machine Labelling and Budgeted Human Review from Disagreeing AI Readers of Administrative Text
items.summary: We study AI-assisted measurement when one text label applies to many administrative records, the target is a monetary total, and the human readings that anchor the machines disagree. The testbed is 121,070 grant-purpose texts from US tax filings (799,675 records, \$126.4B), labelled by a rule-based classifier and three language models, with a designed sample of 651 texts read independently by three people under one codebook. We state exact conditions for a fixed-predictor difference estimator and for a cross-fitted predictor whose folds are assigned to the whole frame before sampling, under Poisson sampling, and assess the implemented fixed-size procedures by simulation: 8 predictors whose own totals span \$11.2-15.0B agree to within \$0.4B once rectified. Two rules that accept machine labels at a stated dollar-weighted error, weighted conformal p-values under a dollar measure and Learn-then-Test on the design estimate of the error, are evaluated on nested held-out folds and on re-draws of the design with synthetic truths; their error control in deployment is not established, and the count-based rule accepts no text under a dollar-drawn sample. In a replay that charges every human label, a two-phase review policy whose calibrator is fitted on its own first phase reduces the RMSE of the total by 28% at a budget of 100 texts relative to dollar-proportional sampling, while pure Neyman allocation fails with an uncalibrated predictor. Independent readers shift the estimated total by \$3.93B, 2.2 times the within-reader sampling interval, and institution-level intervals under-cover at every size. Every headline result is re-run under each reader. The results identify both the benefits and the limits of using learned predictions to decide what a person should verify.

items.title: Prediction Inference for Hybrid Models on Realized Volatility Forecasting
items.summary: GARCH-LSTM hybrid models have become increasingly popular in the volatility forecasting literature. To date, these models have almost exclusively focused on point estimation and accuracy measures such as RMSE and MAPE, while failing to assess the uncertainty of these point estimates. We approach this gap in two ways. First, we extend the existing GARCH-LSTM model by modeling the conditional mean with an ARMA structure. Second, we develop a forward bootstrap algorithm to build multi-step-ahead prediction intervals for future realized volatility. In order to address the notorious undercoverage of prediction intervals, we implement two solutions. One draws bootstrap innovations from the empirical residual distribution to mimic the fat-tail property of financial series. The other utilizes principles from conformal prediction to systematically extend the prediction interval length. We evaluate the methods in simulations with heavy-tailed and time-varying GARCH processes and in rolling-window forecasts of four U.S. stock indices from 2020 to 2025. The ARMA-based hybrid gives the lowest point-forecast errors in most settings, and combining both remedies with the mean-based hybrid yields intervals closest to the nominal level among competing methods.

items.title: Near-Optimal Sample Complexity of Deterministic Agnostic PAC Learning
items.summary: We study the problem of agnostic PAC learning under deterministic labels, where the examples are labeled by an arbitrary deterministic function, which need not belong to the concept class $C$. This model captures misspecification without stochastic label noise and lies between the realizable and fully agnostic settings. Prior work showed that, when $C$ has finite diameter $K$ and VC dimension $d$, deterministic labels can improve the sample complexity upper bound from the classical agnostic guarantee $O(d/\varepsilon^2)$ to $\widetilde{O}(K/\varepsilon)$, but left a large gap between upper and lower bounds. Our main result sharpens this picture. We prove that every class of VC dimension $d$ and finite diameter $K$ is learnable with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left( \frac{K^{1/3} \, d^{2/3}}{\varepsilon} \right)$, and we construct classes for which this bound is tight up to logarithmic factors. We also study the online analogue of this problem and show that the minimax regret is again partly controlled by the diameter of the class. Technically, our upper bounds are obtained via memorization-based learning algorithms that exploit the deterministic label structure.

items.title: Ratio-of-mediator-probability weighting for causal mediation analysis: estimation, extensions, and practical guidance
items.summary: Ratio-of-mediator-probability weighting (RMPW) estimates natural direct and indirect effects by reweighting mediator distributions across treatment conditions rather than modeling the outcome, thereby accommodating treatment-by-mediator interaction. This article brings existing RMPW methods together within a common estimation framework, incorporates a heteroskedastic normal model for continuous mediators, and extends two-step variance estimation to multiple parametric weight components. The framework is illustrated using a national health survey to decompose disparities in cigarette smoking by sexual-minority status and a randomized welfare-to-work experiment to examine pathways from program assignment through employment to maternal depressive symptoms. Targeted simulations evaluate model specification, alternative weighting strategies, treatment-selection adjustment, weight stability, variance estimation, and continuous treatments. Parametric RMPW performed well when models were adequately specified and weights were stable, but correct specification alone did not prevent unstable estimation from concentrated weights. Stratification-based weighting provided some robustness to model misspecification. Standard errors that treated estimated weights as fixed were unreliable, whereas two-step and bootstrap inference performed well under appropriate conditions. The results provide practical guidance for selecting weighting strategies, diagnosing instability, and conducting inference. The methods are implemented in the community-contributed Stata command mmwsmed.

items.title: Denoising data using convex relaxations
items.summary: We study the problem of denoising observations \(Y_i=X_i+Z_i\), where the latent variables \(X_i\) are sampled from a low-dimensional manifold in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and the noise variables \(Z_i\) are isotropic Gaussian. We propose a convex-relaxation estimator that first reduces dimension by principal component analysis and then projects the observations onto the convex hull of the projected latent manifold. We construct a statistical oracle that estimates its supporting hyperplanes from empirical Gaussian tail probabilities of the noisy sample. Under a lower-mass condition on the latent distribution, we prove finite-sample guarantees for the oracle and derive error bounds for the resulting denoiser. The analysis combines risk bounds for least-squares projection under convex constraints (due to Chatterjee) with entropy bounds for the manifold. We also verify the assumptions of the framework for a Cryo-Electron Microscopy observation model by establishing suitable covering number and Lipschitz estimates for the associated group action and imaging operators.

items.title: Strategic Causal Policy Learning with Manipulable Eligibility
items.summary: The standard rule in unconstrained causal policy learning is simple: treat individuals with nonnegative CATEs. But this rule can fail when treatment eligibility is strategically manipulable. After a policy is announced, individuals may change the covariates used for assignment without changing their underlying treatment effects. We study how such responses affect treatment allocation and welfare. Using an access-burden representation, we characterize strategic treatment and decompose welfare loss into missed beneficial treatment and harmful treatment. For linear CATEs and quadratic manipulation costs, we derive closed-form threshold corrections. When manipulation costs are homogeneous, a single correction recovers the ideal positive-CATE allocation. With heterogeneous costs, welfare maximization, pointwise safety, and minimax group welfare regret can favor different thresholds. Simulations illustrate these tradeoffs and examine the effects of estimating treatment effects and behavioral responses.

items.title: Causal Learning with Invalid Instruments for High-dimensional Imaging Responses
items.summary: Large-scale neuroimaging studies provide high-dimensional imaging phenotypes for understanding brain-related diseases and their causal relations with biological risk factors. While instrumental variable (IV) methods can address unmeasured confounding in such observational data, existing IV methods face significant limitations when applied to high-dimensional imaging data, particularly in handling large-scale data and leveraging the intrinsic spatial structure of images. To address these challenges, we propose High-dimensional Functional-imaging Instrumental Variable Estimation (Hi-FIVE), a novel framework for estimating spatially varying causal effects when a majority of the candidate instruments may be locally invalid. We first establish identifiability conditions under which the spatial continuity of the causal effect surface propagates identification from regions where valid instruments form a plurality into regions where they do not, provided that invalid-IV effects switch on non-smoothly. Motivated by this result, Hi-FIVE combines penalized multivariate splines over triangulations for the causal surface and region-wise penalties for spatially localized invalid-IV effects, under an anchor constraint that keeps at least one relevant instrument valid on every simplex. A distributed algorithm parallelizes the computation over simplices for two- and three-dimensional images. We study the asymptotic properties of Hi-FIVE, establish consistency and pointwise asymptotic normality, and construct bootstrap-calibrated simultaneous confidence regions whose finite-sample coverage is evaluated through simulations. Hi-FIVE is illustrated with an analysis of the effect of phosphorylated tau on FDG-PET imaging in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, interpreted under the stated IV assumptions.

items.title: Prediction-Powered LLM Ranking with Adaptively Collected Human Feedback
items.summary: Ranking large language models (LLMs) through human evaluations is essential for downstream decision-making. Because human feedback is expensive, evaluation platforms often collect it adaptively, prioritizing informative model comparisons using previously observed feedback. To further improve precision with limited human feedback, evaluators can draw on abundant unrated responses and relatively inexpensive LLM judges; however, judge bias and adaptive dependence challenge standard i.i.d. inference frameworks. We propose Prediction-Powered Ranking (PP-Rank), a framework that combines LLM-judge predictions with human feedback to improve precision while providing valid inference under adaptive sampling. Data-driven prediction weights minimize the asymptotic covariance trace within the proposed class. In theory, we establish asymptotic normality for general evaluation targets and simultaneous ranking inference. A joint martingale analysis handles dependence between adaptive human feedback and auxiliary data. We further derive a rule for reducing exploration that prioritizes lower-cost comparisons while matching a conservative variance bound, and characterize allocation limits for regular $\sqrt{T}$-rate estimation of pairwise means. Semi-synthetic experiments on UltraFeedback-Extended show improvements over human-only baselines in score estimation, confidence interval width, and ranking certification. Synthetic experiments demonstrate robustness to judge quality and adaptive allocation, while showing that PP-Rank can substantially reduce evaluation costs without sacrificing precision.

items.title: A unifying view of contrastive learning, importance sampling, and bridge sampling for energy-based models
items.summary: In the last decades, energy-based models (EBMs) have become an important class of probabilistic models in which a component of the likelihood is intractable and therefore cannot be evaluated explicitly. Consequently, parameter estimation in EBMs is challenging for conventional inference methods. This work is a review paper that brings together these different methodological contributions within a unified framework, highlighting the connections among noise contrastive estimation (NCE), reverse logistic regression (RLR), Bennett's acceptance-ratio (BAR) method, multiple importance sampling (MIS), and bridge sampling within the context of EBMs. Some of them are equivalent under specific conditions. This unified perspective clarifies relationships among existing methods and enables the development of new estimators, with the potential to improve statistical and computational efficiency. Furthermore, this study helps elucidate the success of NCE in terms of its flexibility and robustness, while also identifying scenarios in which its performance can be further improved. Our aim is to provide a self-contained and accessible treatment, with clear and straightforward derivations, that brings together these contributions within a common framework and makes the main results and their underlying ideas understandable to a broader readership. The contribution is twofold. First, this work serves as a comprehensive tutorial for researchers entering the field, introducing the fundamental concepts and derivations. Second, it offers a thorough review for experienced practitioners. The code used in the numerical experiments is available to support the reproducibility of the results.

items.title: Minimax Optimal Estimation of Transport-Growth Pairs in Unbalanced Optimal Transport
items.summary: Unbalanced optimal transport extends classical optimal transport to measures with different total masses, but statistical guarantees for estimation of the transport map and the growth map remain limited. We study unbalanced optimal transport with quadratic cost and Kullback-Leibler marginal penalties and argue that the natural target of estimation is a transport-growth pair. Consequently, we develop two estimators for the transport-growth pair under two setups: a nearest-neighbor estimator for transporting between general densities, and a kernel-based estimator for transporting between smooth densities. We prove that the kernel-based estimator achieves the minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor by deriving a matching lower bound on the minimax risk. Our main technical contribution is a reduction of estimation to a stability bound on the unbalanced optimal transport value. This bound controls the transport map and growth map risks through the duality gap of the true dual potentials for the estimated measures. These results provide a statistical foundation for estimation of the transport-growth pair in unbalanced optimal transport.

items.title: Disentangling Forced and Internal Climate Variability in Single Realizations using Dynamic Mode Decomposition with Control
items.summary: Separating externally forced trends from internal climate variability is a fundamental challenge in climate science, particularly when analyzing observational records that exist only as a single realization. We show that a single climate realization can be decomposed into forced and internal components by treating external forcing as a dynamical driver within a linear stochastic system, an idea grounded in pullback attractor theory. This addresses a central challenge for climate projection and for detecting and attributing the forced response. Existing single-realization methods rely on linear inverse models (LIMs), which ignore forcing, or linear regression, which omits dynamics. Here we introduce PullbackDMDc, a method grounded in non-autonomous dynamical systems theory and dynamic mode decomposition with control (DMDc), incorporating pullback attractor estimation to decompose a single climate realization into spatial modes and their associated forced and internal components, yielding a physically interpretable picture of the underlying dynamics. After testing on a synthetic system with a known forced response, we illustrate the utility of PullbackDMDc for Earth System Model (ESM) evaluation by applying it to near-surface air temperature and sea-level pressure from reanalysis and four ESM large ensembles. PullbackDMDc estimates the forced response with skill matching or exceeding established baselines and helps select forcing predictors against model-based ground truth. Its internal-variability components reveal that ESMs qualitatively capture interannual and decadal modes while exhibiting systematic differences relative to each other and to observations. Skillful forced-response estimation and a novel decomposition position PullbackDMDc as a practical tool for single-realization climate analysis and ESM evaluation.

items.title: Media Trading with Censored Auction Prices: A Stochastic Control and Reinforcement Learning Approach
items.summary: In real-time bidding, marketing agencies must balance campaign performance, transaction margins and the use of a finite advertising budget. A key difficulty is that market-clearing prices are typically observed only when bids are successful, so the information available for subsequent decisions depends on the bidding policy. We formulate this problem using a continuous-time stochastic control model with a latent price process. To construct a price signal, we consider parallel exploratory subcampaigns in which bids are randomized subject to an upper bound. Under a stylized cross-sectional sampling model, the resulting price estimator is consistent and satisfies a mean-square error bound of order $N^{-1}$, where $N$ is the number of exploratory observations. We then describe a model-based approach combining forward-equation calibration with Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman policy iteration and a physics-informed neural network, alongside an entropy-regularized actor-critic approach based on observable information in a model-free setting. Synthetic experiments illustrate the estimator and the computational procedures. The framework clarifies the decision and information trade-offs faced by the agency, while distinguishing full-information benchmarks and estimated-price policies from the genuinely partially observed control problem.

items.title: Deep Learning of Robust Market Making under Regime-Switching Order Flow
items.summary: Classical market-making strategies based on stochastic control, such as the Avellaneda--Stoikov and the Guéant--Lehalle--Fernandez-Tapia (GLFT) extension, provide closed-form quoting approximations, but rest on assumptions that break down at realistic microstructure timescales. One of them is that order flow is stationary, while empirical evidence points to the existence of regimes, possibly associated with algorithmic execution of metaorders. In our experiments, persistent directional flow makes stationary controllers unprofitable. In this paper, we develop a deep reinforcement-learning market maker (RLMM)---a Rainbow-style distributional deep Q-network which is calibrated and tested in a zero-intelligence limit order book. We find that, in the stationary setting, RLMM outperforms GLFT at comparable levels of profit and loss (PnL) dispersion. The stationarily trained RLMM is more robust to flow asymmetry than GLFT, but still suffers inventory saturation and large drawdowns under persistent directional flow. Training a separate RLMM under regime-switching flow, with a Bayesian flow-belief signal and a queue-adjusted quote exposure signal, restores positive mean PnL in our experiments. A final scenario-bandit step prioritizes low-return scenarios and improves performance under varying regime persistence and directional correlation.

items.title: Dynamic Scenario-Based Portfolio Optimization for Multi-Asset ETFs
items.summary: Portfolio outcomes may depend as much on trading restrictions as on how returns are modeled. We compared historical moving-window returns with conditional scenarios from ARMA--GARCH models and a Student-$t$ copula for 30 U.S.-listed exchange-traded funds. Matched mean--variance and conditional value-at-risk portfolios were evaluated under long-only and limited long--short bounds over 946 sessions. Historical portfolios had higher observed reward--risk ratios in most comparisons, but no paired difference remained significant after multiple-testing adjustment. Conditional scenarios did not consistently reduce realized downside risk. We distinguished changes in target weights from trades required to rebalance holdings after market movements. Relaxing the target-adjustment limit changed exposures, turnover, and some returns more than varying scenario count or seed in the examined tests. These findings suggest that assessments of conditional return inputs should consider portfolio constraints and trading requirements.

items.title: Verifiable Settlement and Pricing for Local Energy Markets: Architecture and Deployment on Hyperledger Besu
items.summary: We implement privacy-preserving local electricity exchanges using an automated market maker on the Hyperledger Besu network under QBFT consensus. The proposed protocol operator collects individual electricity positions off-chain and publishes aggregate supply and demand on the blockchain, where smart contracts compute market prices every fifteen minutes. Individual positions remain off-chain; Poseidon2 commitments and UltraHonk zeroknowledge proofs, generated from Noir circuits, verify aggregation, payments, and daily balance updates. The architecture retains community coordination while making financial execution independently auditable. Signed receipts and member-triggered recourse prevent unverified or partial settlement. In a ten-household experiment using simulated US residential profiles, daily settlement uses approximately 19 million gas and produces eight-member proofs in 2.4 seconds. Over four simulated days, local trading covers 34.4% of demand and reduces grid-only costs by 30.5% under assumed tariffs. Numerically computed __-Nash Equilibrium electricity profiles capture 83-88% of the social planner surplus.

items.title: TAPES: Terminal Adjoint-Propagated Error Scheduling for Financial Diffusion Samplers
items.summary: Financial diffusion samplers are often reused with a small number of function evaluations (NFE) inside scenario and risk pipelines, where numerical time-grid error can distort terminal quantities such as covariances, tails, and drawdown proxies. We study offline grid construction for a frozen probability-flow ODE: the score network, conditioning, Euler solver, report normalization, and deployment NFE remain fixed. TAPES (Terminal Adjoint-Propagated Error Scheduling) estimates signed local defects by Richardson comparisons, transports them through the remaining discrete flow and a terminal-report adjoint, and optimizes the squared norm of their sum before a capped direct refinement. We show that this transported signed sum is the first-order terminal-report error and quantify, under an aligned-defect model, the inefficiency of diagonal criteria. Across six budgets on a regime-switching simulation and chronologically held-out Mag7 contexts, TAPES gives the lowest design- and audit-report errors in all 24 dataset--budget--report rows within the reported five-pipeline panel. Cross-budget mean relative audit-error reductions are about 10--11% on Regime-SV and about 1% on Mag7, with Bonferroni intervals excluding zero; all displayed winners persist under a doubled-resolution reference, and a small Regime-SV Heun probe preserves the TAPES-first audit ordering. TAPES changes only the offline schedule and retains the prescribed deployment NFE; claims concern numerical fidelity to frozen generators.

items.title: Mean--Variance Portfolio Selection by Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning: Algorithms, Regret Analysis, and Empirical Study
items.summary: We study continuous-time mean--variance portfolio selection in markets where stock prices are diffusion processes driven by observable factors that are also diffusion processes, yet the coefficients of these processes are unknown. Based on the recently developed reinforcement learning (RL) theory for diffusion processes, we present a general data-driven RL approach that learns the pre-committed investment strategy directly without attempting to learn or estimate the market coefficients. For multi-stock Black--Scholes markets without factors, we further devise an algorithm and prove its performance guarantee by deriving a sublinear regret bound in terms of the Sharpe ratio. We then carry out an extensive empirical study implementing this algorithm to compare its performance and trading characteristics, evaluated under a host of common metrics, with a large number of widely employed portfolio allocation strategies on S\&P 500 constituents. The results demonstrate that the proposed continuous-time RL strategy is consistently among the best, especially in a volatile bear market, and decisively outperforms the model-based continuous-time counterparts by significant margins.

items.title: Accuracy Is Not Welfare: Evaluating AI Buyers under Strategic Price Complexity in a Synthetic Duopoly
items.summary: AI buying agents may alter sellers' incentives as well as consumers' decisions. In a synthetic duopoly, we evaluate price-comparison pipelines on a fixed menu and in empirical correlated-equilibrium games. Calculator assistance selects an optimal offer 84.00% of the time, versus 68.57% under verified-total disclosure, yet disclosure has a 20.14-unit higher consumer-worst equilibrium surplus. A frozen-strategy holdout comparison favors disclosure, while re-solving equilibria under scenario resampling produces a range spanning zero. These model-based results show why accuracy, loss severity, seller incentives, and welfare incidence require separate measurement.

items.title: On the continuity of martingale optimal transport in higher dimensions
items.summary: We investigate qualitative and quantitative continuity of martingale optimal transport under perturbations of both marginals in dimensions $d\geq2$. We assume that each pair of marginals admits a reference martingale coupling whose density relative to the product of its marginals is bounded above and away from zero, uniformly along the sequence. If the limiting target measure is not carried by a hyperplane, we prove continuity under $W_1$-convergence for continuous costs of at most linear growth, assuming only finite first moments. For Lipschitz costs, a uniform $p$-moment bound on the targets, $p>1$, yields an explicit stability estimate with exponent $(1-1/p)/2$; uniformly bounded target supports give exponent $1/2$. The proof constructs a correction of couplings with small martingale bias while preserving both marginals. Truncated moment corrections allow the target measure to have unbounded support. The construction also shows that every martingale coupling of the limiting marginals can be approximated in $W_1$ by martingale couplings of the approximating marginals. We also discuss counterexamples showing that neither the uniform density condition nor non-degeneracy of the limiting target measure can be omitted in general.

items.title: Optimal Trading Speed on Blockchain
items.summary: On blockchain-based exchanges, faster blocks weaken the priority-fee competition among arbitrageurs and shift rents from the block producer to them. Equilibrium liquidity peaks at an interior block speed; beyond a threshold, an active liquidity provider cream-skims and passive capital shrinks. Evidence from the Base Flashblocks upgrade, a tenfold block-speed increase, confirms the predictions. Priority-fee bids decrease sharply and arbitrageurs' net profit rises. The active liquidity provider rebalances faster, avoids toxic flow, and earns a higher profit. Pool depth falls and effective spreads widen despite closer tracking of external prices.

items.title: Novel Esscher concepts for informational risks and valuation in market models under random horizon
items.summary: This paper considers the setting constituted by the triplet $(S,\mathbb{F},τ)$. The pair $(S,\mathbb{F})$ is the initial model where $S$ is the discounted price process of risky assets (Stocks) and $\mathbb{F}$ is the ``public" flow of information that is available to all agents over time. $τ$ is an arbitrary random time, which might not be seen through the flow $\mathbb{F}$, and it represents a default time in credit risk and a death time of an insured in life insurance where mortality and/or longevity risks present serious challenges. For simplicity, we suppose $S$ follows a geometric jump-diffusion model with stochastic volatiles and $\mathbb{F}$ is generated by a Brownian motion and Poisson process. In this setting, we address how the Esscher densities and/or measures notions can evolves with the informational risk induced by $τ$. In fact, we introduce the notion of Esscher with degrees-of-freedom associated to the informational risks generated by $τ$. On the one hand, we give various and complete characterizations of these Esscher notions in our informational setting. On the other hand, we fully characterize the Escher-prices bounds, for vulnerable claims (claims built on the occurrence of $τ$), using constrained backward stochastic differential equations (CBSDEs for short hereafter) that appear to be novel as well.

items.title: TradeMech: A Method to Multilaterally Net Trades Without Altering Counterparty Exposure
items.summary: Financial markets such as bond, derivatives, and repo markets form networks of interdependent obligations. Existing multilateral netting methods typically trade off the extent of netting against preservation of counterparty exposure: central clearing reallocates exposure to a central counterparty, while trade compression may alter bilateral counterparty relationships. TradeMech is a mechanism for markets in which one or two homogeneous fungible objects are traded. The mechanism transforms a network of initial bilateral contracts into chains and cycles, nets the designated object multilaterally on those chains and cycles, and replaces initial contracts with multiparty contracts whose assigned trades remain fractions of the original bilateral trades. The construction achieves maximal multilateral netting of the designated object while preserving each agent's contractual profit and preserving the location of counterparty risk. When a party fails to pre-commit a required object, the affected assigned trade is recovered as a bilateral contract between the same original counterparties and the remaining assigned trades are re-netted on residual chains, so no new counterparty exposure is created.

items.title: Convergence rates for truncated and discretised signature expansions
items.summary: Linear expansions in Brownian Stratonovich signatures, which originate in stochastic Taylor expansions, are increasingly used to represent and model processes with memory. Their numerical use requires truncating the signature at a level $M$ and discretising the driving path along $N$ steps. Under a simple growth condition on the coefficients of the linear expansion, we establish strong and weak convergence rates for both approximations, uniformly in time. The strong truncation error decays like $(B^M/(M!)^\varepsilon)^a$ for some constant $B$, uniformly in $N$, where $\varepsilon$ measures the growth of the coefficients and $a$ the regularity of the test function; the weak error does not improve on it. The discretisation error is of order $N^{-a/2}$ in $L^p$, and $N^{-1}$ weakly for polynomial test functions, uniformly in $M$. All these rates are sharp for polynomial test functions, and $M$, $N$ can be chosen independently. We extend the estimates to errors in probability, on distribution functions and on risk measures, and illustrate them on stochastic delay equations, Volterra processes and option pricing in signature volatility models.

items.title: Breaking the Trend: How to Avoid Cherry-Picked Signals
items.summary: Our empirical results show a good fit with the theoretical Sharpe formula of a trend-following strategy depending on the parameter of the signal, which was derived by Grebenkov and Serror (2014). That empirical fit suggests that a mean-reversion process with only one time scale is enough to model the trend-following mechanism at the average scale of CTAs and that, as a consequence, a single simple EMA appears sufficient to capture the trend. Using a complex basket of different sophisticated indicators as signal therefore does not seem to be necessary and exposes to the risk of cherry-picking.

items.title: Market Impact Estimation via Causal Foundation Models
items.summary: When a trader executes a large order, the relevant question is not \emph{what will the price be?} but \emph{what would the price have been had I not traded?} Market impact is thus a causal quantity, yet classical models (Almgren--Chriss, propagators) regress price on flow, which is biased whenever informed flow moves prices through information as well as trading. We present a proof-of-concept \emph{Causal Market Simulator}: a continuous-time causal prior-data fitted network (PFN) trained on a synthetic market prior in which a hidden informational flow confounds the flow--price relation by construction, with confounding strength an exact per-episode knob. On this prior, the naive estimator's bias follows a closed form we confirm empirically (up to 68\% overestimation), while the PFN tracks the unbiased true-parameter oracle at high confounding. Its \emph{do-ablated twin}, the same model with the intervention inputs removed, collapses onto the pre-window mean. Zero-shot, the model responds at the ground-truth scale to metaorders in an ABIDES limit-order book (+0.38 pre-onset standard deviations against seed-replay counterfactuals), and its intervention response replicates on about 2,300 detected flow bursts in BTC/ETH/SOL perpetuals and 3,800 on Nasdaq equities, evidence consistent with, though not proof of, causal transfer. Off-prior the response degrades gracefully, and split-conformal recalibration repairs interval calibration. Transfer hinges on encoding the metaorder as added flow rather than a clamped price level, not on more training. A recurrent state-space variant closes the remaining shape gap: its impact accrues over execution duration where the transformer's stays flat, raising the correlation with measured metaorder impact from +0.68 to between +0.92 and +0.96, at the cost of weaker on-prior deconfounding that traces to the training recipe rather than to recurrence.

items.title: Global Seasonality Factor Investing
items.summary: We study seasonality as a factor for predicting risk-adjusted returns across global futures markets. We document five seasonality anomalies that, in aggregate, are pervasive across bond, commodity and equity markets. We demonstrate that each seasonality factor produces excess returns that are not reasonably explained by established global time series carry, momentum and skewness factors. We apply recent innovations in statistical learning and fit nonlinear seasonality models at the individual market level, thereby allowing each feature-market pair to express its unique seasonal prediction pattern. We discuss candidate economic rationales for the existence and persistence of each seasonality anomaly. Walk-forward out-of-sample testing demonstrates that fast-moving seasonal patterns, such as day-of-week and day-of-month, produce strong gross performance but with extremely high turnover, resulting in negative performance net of transaction costs. In contrast, slower-moving seasonal patterns, such as day-of-quarter, day-of-half-year and day-of-year, produce positive gross performance and, with the exception of day-of-quarter, positive net performance. An equal-weight ensemble of seasonality models produces an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio that is competitive with, and uncorrelated to, established global time series factor portfolios. Empirical results demonstrate that adding seasonality to a global factor portfolio increases the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio by approximately $30\%$ over the full evaluation period.

items.title: Idiosyncratic Market Effects in Global Time Series Momentum
items.summary: Time series momentum is a pervasive explanatory factor in financial markets whereby a market's recent historical average return positively predicts future returns. Recent applications of statistical learning augment the traditional linear model definition with a more descriptive global nonlinear factor model. We extend the work of \citet{MoskowitzNonlinear} and demonstrate that models fit at the individual market level exhibit response curves that are distinct from the global factor model. We highlight the heterogeneity of forward market returns as a function of time series momentum and provide a framework that enables each feature-market pair to express its unique prediction behaviour. Empirical results demonstrate that, despite substantially smaller sample sizes, fitting nonlinear models to individual markets is a robust and often overlooked modelling approach that can result in a marginal improvement in out-of-sample performance.

items.title: Parsimonious and Flexible Parameterizations for Realized Covariance Matrix Models
items.summary: Covariance models describe the dynamics of conditional covariance matrices as functions of past variances and covariances and are widely used to model the joint evolution of financial asset returns. Their specification faces two major challenges: the curse of dimensionality, whereby the number of parameters increases rapidly with the matrix dimension, and the need to ensure the positive definiteness of the estimated covariance matrices. Moreover, commonly used parsimonious parameterizations, such as scalar and diagonal specifications, fail to capture complex interactions among variances and covariances across assets and cannot accommodate the abrupt changes that often characterize financial markets. We propose a new class of parameterizations that reconciles parsimony with flexibility by allowing distinct, time-varying coefficients for each variance and covariance while requiring only a limited number of parameters. We derive sufficient conditions to ensure the positive definiteness of the resulting covariance matrices and assess the proposed approach through Monte Carlo simulations and an empirical application. The results show that the proposed models can capture complex dependence structures while preserving computational tractability.

items.title: Incomplete-market CAPM equilibria in continuous time
items.summary: We study continuous-time CAPM equilibria with general mean-variance preferences of the form $U(μ,σ)$, where $U$ is strictly quasiconcave, increasing in the mean $μ$ and decreasing in the volatility $σ$ of terminal wealth. Our framework accommodates both financial and productive assets with nontradeable endowments. We allow for equilibria driven by general semimartingales in the case of linear mean-variance preferences and by continuous semimartingales in the case of general mean-variance preferences. The key insight is a connection between mean-variance efficiency and quadratic utility maximisation. We first characterise quadratic equilibria through an explicit family of equilibrium price processes indexed by the aggregate risk tolerance. We then show that each agent's optimal mean-variance strategy corresponds to a quadratic optimum with an endogenously determined risk tolerance. This correspondence reduces the mean-variance equilibrium problem to a one-dimensional fixed-point problem, whose solvability we establish using fine properties of (dynamic) mean-variance hedging and a novel stability result for quadratic BSDEs with BMO growth at the origin. Finally, examples illustrate how unspanned stochastic-volatility risk interacts with aggregate endowments to affect equilibrium asset prices, and how nonlinear mean-variance preferences influence equilibrium risk tolerance and asset-price comparative statics.

items.title: A high-order recombination algorithm with adaptive scale selection for weak approximation of stochastic differential equations
items.summary: High-order recombination keeps weak approximation trees of diffusions small by a moment-preserving reduction of the measure on each patch of nodes. The weighted Litterer--Lyons (WLL) test of Ninomiya and Shinozaki sets the patch scale using a scalar \(λ>0\) chosen beforehand, whose appropriate value depends on coordinate units. First, the anisotropically weighted Litterer--Lyons (AWLL) rule selects the scale during recombination within a bounded factor of the measured increment amplitude. On a fixed set of nodes, expanding coordinate units leaves the AWLL patch-count bound unchanged but raises the WLL lower bound as a power until saturation. In Heston and shifted Stochastic-Alpha-Beta-Rho (sSABR) systems with initial price or forward rate 100, AWLL reduces the terminal supports of WLL with \(λ=1\) by factors of 137 and 1488 at comparable errors, but enlarges them at smaller Heston initial prices. Second, \(λ\) is extended to a positive definite matrix with a joint error bound for prices and sensitivities, a bound on the gain of its shape, and patch-count bounds. Third, the elimination stage of batched basis exchange requires \(O(J)\) arithmetic operations for \(J\) nodes at fixed moment rank and panel width, against \(Θ(J^{3})\) for the direct kernel update of Ninomiya and Shinozaki.

items.title: Gatheral's Conjecture: General sufficient conditions for refutation
items.summary: In this paper we give general sufficient conditions for a stochastic volatility model to be a counterexample for Gatheral's conjecture. The conditions, achieved by asymptotic properties of integrated variance derivatives and Wiener chaos expansions, show that a general class of rough volatility models are generally counterexamples to Gatheral's conjecture. For stochastic volatility models with Markovian variance, the conjecture fails under a relationship on the coefficients of the SDE defining the variance process. Particular examples are provided.

items.title: Least Expensive Standard Pensions
items.summary: The paper proposes generating annuity payment streams at far lower costs than those implied by traditional theories. For a given investment universe, this enables the design of a least expensive standard pension, providing accurate monthly payments of savings account units over a set period. Such a standard pension invests dynamically in the savings account and the equity market's growth-optimal portfolio to replicate riskless payments with high accuracy at the lowest possible cost. Since this mathematically grounded standard pension is reliable and, by orders of magnitude, less expensive than traditional pensions, it provides a unique opportunity to improve the health of pension systems and provide more benefits for retirees.

items.title: Conformal Risk Certificates for Portfolio Optimization Under Uncertainty: A Gated Reinforcement-Learning Approach
items.summary: Reinforcement-learning portfolio policies can optimize allocations from prices, covariances, and prior positions, yet they lack a calibrated, replayable mechanism for certifying that a proposed allocation respects a bounded risk envelope before execution. Regulators increasingly expect automated portfolio systems to provide exactly this kind of pre-trade audit trail, interpretable risk limit, and human-oversight mechanism. Gated Conformal Semantic Risk Control addresses this gap by separating return-seeking allocation from text-conditioned downside-risk verification. An instruction-tuned language model maps timestamped disclosures into schema-validated semantic risk states over macro, liquidity, earnings, and sector channels. These states induce correlated ellipsoidal factor-shock uncertainty sets whose conformal radii are calibrated by rolling finite-sample prediction over localized semantic nonconformity buckets. An asymmetric second-order cone gate then checks each raw PPO proposal against a certified worst-case semantic loss budget. The gate stays inactive for compliant proposals and intervenes only when that budget is exceeded. In walk-forward out-of-sample tests on nine liquid U.S. Select Sector SPDR ETFs, Raw PPO earns a 12.7% annual return while incurring a 4.05% semantic violation rate. Gated-CSRC removes all observed out-of-sample semantic limit breaches while retaining an 11.7% annual return. This 100-basis-point auditable safety premium is smaller than the yield loss imposed by unconditional hard projection, and exact McNemar testing confirms the compliance gain at $p < 10^{-15}$. Loughran-McDonald lexicon controls and time-shuffled text controls fail to reproduce this certificate.

items.title: Diffusion models for dynamic volatility surface generation and data-driven hedging
items.summary: We develop a diffusion-model framework for dynamic implied-volatility surface generation and evaluate its economic usefulness through data-driven hedging. The framework consists of two models. AD-Seq-Vol jointly learns the conditional evolution of the underlying asset return and the high-dimensional implied-volatility surface, generating adapted multi-period scenarios by sequentially updating the realized market history. AD-Seq-Vol-FT further incorporates option-market structure through post-training penalties for violations of static no-arbitrage conditions. Using daily SPX option data from 2000 to 2023, we show that the proposed models generate coherent surface trajectories while capturing both cross-sectional and temporal dependence. AD-Seq-Vol produces fewer and less severe static-arbitrage violations than the training data and the GAN-based benchmark, while AD-Seq-Vol-FT reduces these violations to nearly zero. We then integrate the generated conditional scenarios into an optimization-based hedging framework. Compared to a range of classical and data-driven benchmarks, the diffusion-based hedges maintain tracking errors near zero, substantially reduce tail risk, and exhibit particularly stable performance during the COVID-19 market disruption. These results establish Adaptive Sequential Diffusion Models as a promising class of market-consistent and economically useful financial scenario generators. Our code is available at: https://github.com/yinbinhan/volatility-surface-simulation.

items.title: Point-in-Time Encoders for Earnings Calls
items.summary: Text encoders turn earnings calls into vectors for search, for language models that answer from retrieved passages, and for forecasting models. A live retriever can use an encoder trained once on all available text, as finance retrievers are, but a backtest needs an encoder that read no text written after the date of each vector. To address this look-ahead bias, from 412,248 calls we train vintages under four pretraining recipes, with yearly cutoffs from 2010 to 2024, and each vintage reads only text dated on or before its cutoff. We then fine-tune each vintage on the question-answer pairs of the calls themselves. The vintages we train on calls alone, with 33.8M parameters, retrieve answers on held-out calls better than the general retrievers we tested in every test quarter. Their vectors also raise by about half the rank correlation between next-day returns and forecasts built from past returns and firm size. When each vintage continues the previous one, a later vintage retrieves better on earlier quarters than the vintage available at the time, and a point-in-time language model that answers from the passages the later vintage retrieves inherits the gain. The 2024 vintage of our families also forecasts earnings surprises better, although the interval of this gain includes zero on calls that no vintage read. It forecasts returns no better, so point-in-time vintages matter most for retrieval and little for forecasts of returns.

items.title: Deep Learning for Operator Maps in Optimal Liquidation
items.summary: We analyze the solution map of a optimal execution problem in which price dynamics are subject to a general transient impact kernel. Given the structure of the optimal trading strategy derived by Abi Jaber and Neuman in \cite{https://doi.org/10.1111/mafi.12465}, we show that the strategy is locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to the underlying model parameters governing temporary and transient price impact as well as the fundamental price process. Continuity of this map justifies the application of neural-net based approximations which take model parameters as inputs. We propose a method generating samples of the transient price impact kernel for the purposes of creating training data, and a method of projecting the kernel to a finite dimensional representation appropriate for input to a neural net, and a dimensional reduction based on the relationship between inventory and trade signal. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the trained neural net and use it to quantify the potential financial costs associated with misspecifying the transient impact kernel.

items.title: Fine-Tuning an Order-Flow Foundation Model for Sub-Second Forecasting
items.summary: Generative models have become the standard approach in language and vision. These models are typically pretrained first and then fine-tuned. Recent work demonstrates how to pretrain an autoregressive generative model on Level-3 order-flow data. However, to our knowledge, no one has fine-tuned such a model yet for downstream tasks. Here we first pretrain a 300M-parameter generative model on Level-3 order-flow data collected from two crypto exchanges, Bitstamp and Bitfinex. Then we fine-tune the pretrained model to predict the microprice return and its realized volatility. We show that our fine-tuned model outperforms classical baselines, such as gradient boosting on handcrafted features, in predicting microprice returns over sub-second horizons. Furthermore, the predictive ability of the model transfers zero-shot to assets it was never fine-tuned on. Due to the short-term nature of these forecasts, the predicted microprice moves are smaller than the bid-ask spread plus fees, so the natural applications are in execution and market making. These results indicate that a pretrained generative model can be turned into a competitive short-horizon price forecaster via fine-tuning.

items.title: Bandit Profit-maximization for Targeted Marketing
items.summary: We study a sequential profit-maximization problem, optimizing for both price and ancillary variables like marketing expenditures. Specifically, we aim to maximize profit over an arbitrary sequence of multiple demand curves, each dependent on a distinct ancillary variable, but sharing the same price. A prototypical example is targeted marketing, where a firm (seller) wishes to sell a product over multiple markets. The firm may invest different marketing expenditures for different markets to optimize customer acquisition, but must maintain the same price across all markets. Moreover, markets may have heterogeneous demand curves, each responding to prices and marketing expenditures differently. The firm's objective is to maximize its gross profit, the total revenue minus marketing costs. Our results are near-optimal algorithms for this class of problems in an adversarial bandit setting, where demand curves are arbitrary non-adaptive sequences, and the firm observes only noisy evaluations of chosen points on the demand curves. For $n$ demand curves (markets), we prove a regret upper bound of $\tilde{O}(nT^{3/4})$ and a lower bound of $Ω((nT)^{3/4})$ for monotonic demand curves, and a regret bound of $\tildeΘ(nT^{2/3})$ for demand curves that are monotonic in price and concave in the ancillary variables.

items.title: Supply Chain Propagation of Textual Signals: LLM Embeddings and Cross-Sectional Return Predictability
items.summary: This paper proposes a novel asset pricing framework that augments large language model (LLM) embeddings of annual report disclosures with supply chain knowledge graph (KG) propagation. Using FinBERT embeddings of 10-K MD&A sections for 255 S&P 500 firms over 2011-2025, two sets of return predictors are constructed: direct LLM embeddings and network-augmented embeddings, where firm-level signals propagate through inter-firm linkages. Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions reveal that the network-augmented factor (net_pc_5) carries significant return predictability with a Newey-West t-statistic of -2.64, even after controlling for momentum, volatility, and firm size. A long-short portfolio sorted on net_pc_5 achieves an annualized Sharpe ratio of 0.86 and a Fama-French five-factor alpha of 7.27% per year (t = 2.30). The predictive power survives out-of-sample tests, placebo experiments, sector-neutralization, and subsample analysis. The findings suggest that inter-firm network structure contains pricing-relevant information beyond firm-level textual disclosures.

items.title: Market Regime Council for Dynamic Credit Assignment in Multi-Agent LLM Decision Systems
items.summary: Multi-agent LLM decision systems for portfolio management still lack a principled way to assign credit across specialist agents, remain vulnerable to cold-start dominance under regime shifts, and offer limited transparency into how final allocations are formed. We propose Market Regime Council (MRC), an online credit-assignment mechanism over coalitions of specialist agents, with portfolio management as the downstream task. MRC computes exact Shapley credits across all single, pairwise, and Grand-coalition outputs for online agent weighting. Instantiated with N=3 specialist agents, at each trading period, MRC recomputes coalition-based Shapley weights from exponentially weighted performance histories, uses a Bayesian adaptive mixture to stabilize early periods, applies regime-dependent multipliers to adjust agent authority, and records each rebalance through a five-layer causal trace. Over 1,037 trading days across 13 crypto assets and five seeds, MRC achieves a Sharpe ratio of 1.51 and a cumulative return of 440.1%, ranking first on CR, SR, and IR among active baselines and attaining the lowest MDD among active methods. Ablation results show that the gains come from Shapley-weighted integration across coalition outputs rather than from any single stage in isolation. Code and demo data are available open source.

items.title: StakeBench: Evaluating Language Understanding Grounded in Market Commitment
items.summary: Existing financial NLP benchmarks often rely on labels supplied by outside observers, measuring how language is perceived rather than what speakers have committed to in the market. We introduce StakeBench, an evaluation framework for language understanding grounded in market commitment. StakeBench links 560,876 comments from 2,261 resolved markets to verified position, action, and market-odds records across Polymarket and Manifold. Supervision is derived from observable market behavior. Position sides, post-comment trading actions, and market-odds trajectories replace human annotation. Four diagnostic tasks test whether models detect market commitment, identify the revealed side, anticipate future action, and perform collective odds projection. Three commitment-aware metrics measure alignment with revealed preferences rather than perceived sentiment. Validity audits and explicit interpretation boundaries help distinguish observable commitment signals from latent belief and causal market-odds impact. Across 15 LLMs and 18 topics and platform settings, models partially recover position-side signals, with Directed Accuracy from 0.506 to 0.599, but show structural failures on later tasks. Ten of the fifteen models collapse to one or two action labels in future action anticipation, and no model consistently improves on the naive odds-direction baseline in collective odds projection. Model scale is not correlated with performance, finance-domain tuning does not improve revealed-side identification, and platform incentives strongly shape higher-order results. StakeBench is packaged with evaluation code and dataset under CC-BY 4.0.

items.title: Asian option valuation under price impact
items.summary: We develop a model for arithmetic and geometric Asian option valuation with external order flow and dealer execution costs. We first formulate it as a discrete model and then obtain its continuous time scaling limit. We derive an explicit geometric Asian option formula under a consistent price system and formulate the dealer's bid and ask through utility indifference with constrained stock trading. We identify sufficient conditions for finite reservation prices and prove absence of arbitrage under the dealer's stock trading rules. Increasing initial inventory lowers both the reservation bid and the ask in the cases studied. In the finite-step calculations, higher temporary costs and greater risk aversion widen the spread for both payoffs, with a smaller change in the midpoint of the quotes.

items.title: Nonzero-Sum Stochastic Exit Games with Singular Belief Dynamics
items.summary: We study a two-player nonzero-sum stochastic exit game with asymmetric information. Each firm chooses the time to exit a duopoly and, conditional on remaining active, when to exit a monopoly. The asymmetry stems from privately observed exit values, while profit flows are driven by a general one-dimensional diffusion. Allowing for exit from monopoly induces singular dynamics of the associated belief process, so we construct it as a limit of regular approximations. The underlying dynamics are not described by a system of SDEs, which requires a new mathematical approach. We construct a symmetric Nash equilibrium in which the duopoly exit is a hitting time of the belief process while the monopoly exit is described through the underlying diffusion. Our equilibrium exhibits novel phenomena: the market may be abandoned by both firms in finite time (market collapse), and firms with heterogeneous exit values may optimally exit simultaneously (clustering). These features are absent when monopoly is always preferred to exit.

items.title: Tabular Foundation Models in Financial Predictions
items.summary: This technical note introduces tabular foundation models (TFMs) to accounting research and evaluates their performance in one common benchmark task: predicting firms' next-year earnings changes. TFMs produce numeric predictions and learn in context, without post-release training or tuning, making them natural and easy to use for forecasting. The TFMs we study are pretrained on synthetic tabular data, so they avoid look-ahead bias from memorizing firms' outcomes. We compare Google Research's TabFM with a fine-tuned open-weight large language model developed in recent accounting research and with several tree-based models. TabFM is more accurate than all comparison models. It is also faster and less computationally intensive than the large language model. Several tree-based specifications produce predictions more quickly than TabFM, so choosing between them involves a trade-off between accuracy and speed. We conclude that TFMs have promise as a new tool for forecasting in accounting and finance. However, our evaluation is based on a single benchmark task, and no class of models is likely to dominate in all settings.

items.title: Making sense of rule 605
items.summary: The paper analyzes monthly reports of two companies: one market maker, Virtu, and one broker-dealer, SoHo, in the period between January 2021 and March 2024. The predictive power of standard methods for the probability laws of stock orders- linear regression and LSTM- is poor, despite their probability laws being relatively stable. However, the month-to-month correlations are highly stable and predictable. In this paper, we study the distributions of the sixteen datasets resulting from the 26 stock-trading parameters reported by brokerages under regulatory requirements.

items.title: Generative AI, Managerial Expectations, and Economic Activity
items.summary: Using generative AI, we extract managers' economic expectations from over 120,000 corporate conference call transcripts. The resulting AI Economy Score predicts GDP growth, production, employment, and wages five or more quarters ahead, beyond survey forecasts and other existing measures. Industry- and firm-level scores capture sector- and firm-specific activity, and a composite of firm, industry, and macroeconomic expectations further improves forecasting power and horizon. Predictability concentrates among historically more accurate, less biased managers, consistent with an information rather than a noise channel. Managerial expectations thus offer incremental insights into economic activity, with implications for macro- and microeconomic decision-making.

items.title: AWARE-FX: Auditable measurement of corporate foreign-exchange hedging disclosure
items.summary: Corporate annual reports describe hedging through transactional, policy, accounting, and explicit non-use language. This study presents AWARE-FX, the foreign-exchange application of the Auditable Weak-supervision and Aggregation framework, for constructing traceable firm-year disclosure measures. Professional-source retrieval, evidence-state rules, channel classifiers, and top-three aggregation link each score to supporting passages. The application covers 24,909 Hong Kong firm-years from 2008-2025 and 543,527 candidate snippets. Evaluation combines weak-label held-out tests, three-seed encoder comparisons, a 2023-2025 temporal test, calibration diagnostics, selective prediction, and a stratified 300-snippet audit coded by one researcher. The paired temporal tests do not detect statistically significant differences between FinBERT and ModernBERT. The negation-aware lexicon has higher broad-task audit F1 than strict-gate FinBERT and Qwen3-8B, demonstrating that learned models do not uniformly improve on domain rules. At 80% temporal coverage, retained-sample F1 increases by 0.050-0.077, although the study does not measure human review time or deployment impact. Reproducible Qwen3-8B results show substantial variation across evidence channels. Linked exposure associations provide exploratory external validation, with sensitivity to the multiple-testing family. The scores measure detected hedging disclosure rather than hedge notional or causal effectiveness. The contribution is an evaluated measurement workflow with inspectable evidence and explicit validation limits. Independent duplicate annotation and retrieval-recall assessment remain necessary for stronger reliability claims.

items.title: Diversification Across Predictors: Heterogeneous Ensemble Learning for Cross-Sectional Return Prediction
items.summary: Cross-sectional stock return prediction remains challenging due to extremely low signal-to-noise ratios, high-dimensional factor spaces, and non-stationary predictor effectiveness. Individual model classes exhibit complementary failure modes in this regime: neural networks overfit noise due to high variance, while linear models underfit nonlinear structure due to high bias. We propose a heterogeneous ensemble framework that extends the financial principle of diversification to the predictor level. Through a bagging procedure combining linear predictors with nonlinear predictors, each model functions as a distinct specialist whose prediction errors exhibit low cross-covariance, enabling error cancellation upon aggregation. We formalize this mechanism via bias-variance-covariance decomposition, establishing an exact mathematical correspondence between portfolio diversification and predictor aggregation. On CSI300 daily-frequency Alpha158 factor datasets, the proposed ensemble achieves a Rank IC improvement exceeding 13\% over standalone neural networks and surpasses tree-based state-of-the-art methods including XGBoost and Double Ensemble, as measured by both predictive accuracy and portfolio-based evaluation metrics.

items.title: Noise estimation of SDE from a single data trajectory
items.summary: In this paper, we propose a pathwise data-driven framework for model discovery of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) from a single trajectory, without requiring the ergodicity or stationary assumption on the underlying continuous process. By combining (stochastic) Taylor expansions with Girsanov transformations, and using the drift function's initial value as input, we construct drift estimators while simultaneously recovering the model noise. This drift is unique up to the fixed underlying Brownian sample path, in line with pathwise unique Rough-Smooth decomposition. This allows us to recover the underlying $\mathbb P$ Brownian motion increments for the observer path $ω$. Building on these estimators, we introduce the first stochastic Sparse Identification of Stochastic Differential Equation (SSISDE) algorithm, capable of identifying the governing SDE dynamics from a single observed trajectory without requiring ergodicity or stationarity. To validate the proposed approach, we conduct numerical experiments with both linear and quadratic drift-diffusion functions. Among these, the Black-Scholes SDE is included as a representative case of a system that does not satisfy ergodicity or stationarity.

items.title: INEUS: Iterative Neural Solver for High-Dimensional PIDEs
items.summary: In this paper, we introduce INEUS, a meshfree iterative neural solver for partial integro-differential equations (PIDEs). The method replaces the explicit evaluation of nonlocal jump integrals with single-jump sampling and reformulates PIDE solving as a sequence of recursive regression problems. Like Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), INEUS learns global solutions over the entire space-time domain, yet it offers a more efficient treatment of nonlocal terms and avoids the computationally expensive differentiation of full PIDE residuals. These features make INEUS particularly well suited for high-dimensional PDEs and PIDEs. Supported by a contraction-based convergence proof for linear PIDEs, our numerical experiments show that INEUS delivers accurate and scalable solutions for various high-dimensional linear and nonlinear examples.

items.title: Diversified-Risk-Perception Risk Measures and Portfolio Selection
items.summary: Traditional risk measures generally rely on a single probability model, potentially overlooking information from alternative models and leading to biased risk assessments. This limitation cannot be addressed by asset diversification alone in risk management. In this paper, we propose a Diversified-Risk-Perception (DRP) risk measure framework that integrates asset diversification and risk model diversification to provide a more comprehensive assessment of market risk while reducing reliance on any single model. First, we introduce a flexible exponential aggregation function to evaluate the risk of a portfolio, which accounts for the contributions of all loss components while placing greater emphasis on large losses. Second, we incorporate multiple risk models in the risk measure and optimize their weights based on their perceptions on the risk assessments. As a specific example, we introduce DRP expected shortfall (DRP-ES), establish its theoretical properties, and derive bounds quantifying its sensitivity to model parameters. Empirical experiments in the U.S., Chinese A-share, and South Korean stock markets show that trading strategies based on the DRP-ES achieve higher Sharpe ratios and lower maximum drawdowns than market benchmarks across different periods. Compared with asset diversification strategies based on individual probability models, the DRP strategy exhibits more stable and robust performance across different markets and periods. These findings suggest that the DRP framework can adapt to changing market conditions and improve the stability and effectiveness of portfolio risk management.

items.title: Evaluating LLM Research Agents as Tests of Return Predictability
items.summary: Researchers ask large language model research agents whether a forecasting model beats the historical-mean benchmark, a question that real data cannot settle. We evaluate the agent's verdict as a statistical test in runs of three commercial models and one open-weight model in simulated return series whose predictive signal, if any, is known. The commercial agents detect weak signals more often than an out-of-sample test, mainly because they accept weaker evidence: held to an agent's false-positive rate, a conventional in-sample test does as well or better. All four models claim predictability too often when no signal exists; the commercial agents also state miscalibrated probabilities and change their verdicts after a sentence about prior research. Magnitudes vary by model; excess false claims persist without a resampling artifact. Agent verdicts are informative but need a neutral brief, a decision rule fixed outside the agent and a sealed holdout.

items.title: Adjoint Kernel Sensitivity of the Rough Heston Characteristic Exponent
items.summary: Multi-factor approximations of rough volatility kernels affect the characteristic exponents used in Fourier-based derivative valuation. We derive an adjoint representation for the first-order sensitivity of the rough Heston characteristic exponent with respect to its memory kernel, with model parameters and the input variance curve held fixed. The Volterra--Riccati functional $\mathcal L_T(K,z)$ admits a local real-analytic extension, jointly in the kernel perturbation and the transform parameter. The Fréchet derivative of this extension with respect to the kernel in $L^1$ is represented by integration against a continuous sensitivity kernel $B_K(u,z)$, obtained from a backward linear Volterra equation and independent of the perturbation direction. This representation resolves the leading-order contributions of kernel perturbations across memory lags. On the structural kernel class, which contains the fractional kernel and its multi-factor approximations and has empty interior in $L^1$, the extension yields Hadamard directional differentiability and a first-order expansion with a quadratic $L^1$-remainder for all sufficiently close structural kernels, uniformly on compact subsets of the strip of transform parameters. The same sensitivity kernel yields multi-factor weight and decay-rate derivatives. Numerical experiments at multi-factor reference kernels assess the finite-resolution implementation and illustrate how the lag distribution of positive perturbations with equal $L^1$ mass affects the first-order response.

items.title: A Pricing and Hedging Framework for Infinite-Dimensional Financial Markets
items.summary: In this paper, we provide a comprehensive study of how the classical Black--Scholes-type market framework behaves in an infinite-dimensional setting. The asset prices are modeled by stochastic evolution equations in a separable Hilbert space. The evolution of the risk-free asset and the corresponding discounting operators are governed by a strongly continuous group of bounded linear operators. Accordingly, we consider contingent claims with Hilbert-space-valued payoffs, whose values are discounted through the corresponding operators. Within this framework, we investigate the pricing and hedging of contingent claims, deriving the corresponding Hilbert-space-valued Black--Scholes equations and establishing exact replication results for both strong and mild solutions. We also study the special case where the infinitesimal generator is given by $A=rI$, allowing for real-valued contingent claims. We further investigate no-arbitrage and market completeness, introducing a Hilbert lattice structure to formulate arbitrage and characterizing attainability through operator equations associated with martingale representations. We also establish asymptotic completeness through finite-dimensional noise truncations. We introduce geometric Brownian motions in Hilbert spaces and derive sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of an equivalent risk-neutral measure, together with explicit pricing formulas for some tractable examples. These results extend key aspects of the classical Black--Scholes framework to markets with infinite-dimensional asset-price dynamics. As a concrete application, the model can be interpreted as a segmented market consisting of a sequence of one-dimensional geometric Brownian motions.

items.title: Retrospective Analysis of Team-Following Trading Profitability in Pumpfun Meme Coins Using Funding Networks
items.summary: If the right token-creation teams had been known, how much could following them have returned, and what is left when only information available before each launch is used? We study ten separately recorded Pumpfun windows (April 2024 to September 2026), each reconstructed independently from real-SOL reserve states and finite-capital accounts that start with one SOL. Teams are directed funding groups ranked in hindsight. When every team exits at its own best reserve threshold, chosen in hindsight, the main account ends above one SOL in all 8 windows that have a qualifying team (1.10 to 11.32 SOL), but free cash exceeds one SOL in only 5, and marks of positions that never reached their threshold make up 17--94% of equity. If teams are recognised online, from tokens whose first hour has completed, 9 of 19 teams become identifiable only after their last launch; the remaining 10 end above one SOL in 10 cases, with free cash above one SOL in 7; funding links in this step still come from the full window, so even these results are not a fully realisable signal. A large model balance, a result above random cohorts that repeat the threshold search, and a statistical rejection in the selection-matched nulls (3 of 40 tests after Holm adjustment) are three different statements, and these nulls condition on the discovered funding graph, so they do not calibrate the whole selection procedure. Midpoint tests describe a further source of apparent opportunity. A detailed analysis of the best and the worst window, with every analysis parameter varied, shows that the worst result, which is close to break-even, rises several-fold with a stop rule or another funding-graph construction. The results are conditional retrospective model accounts, not executable profits, and not evidence of a causal effect of the SOL price.

items.title: Optimal execution in a fractional setting with reinforcement learning
items.summary: We consider the problem of optimal liquidation with linear market impact, as in the seminal work of Almgren and Chriss, but with an asset driven by a fractional Brownian motion. For $H \neq 1/2$, we observe that the deterministic solution given by Almgren and Chriss is no longer optimal. We develop a strategy to exploit the information induced by the correlation between price increments. The strategy is derived from a policy gradient algorithm, parameterized by a neural network, trained to maximise the CARA utility, for which our method allows for significant improvements.

items.title: JUBILEE: A Benchmark Environment for Off-Policy Evaluation in Debt Collections
items.summary: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the value a candidate decision policy would achieve, using only data logged by the policy already in production. In debt collections, unrecorded factors can influence both actions and outcomes. This paper presents JUBILEE, a benchmark environment built around a debt-collections simulator that generates million-loan panels with competing risks, rare recovery events, and hidden factors driving both outcomes and assignment. The evaluation includes an 80-run comparison of tabular and gradient-boosted estimators under two synthetic outcome mechanisms and a 190-run parameter grid. Independent policy simulations provide reference values with estimated Monte Carlo uncertainty for a synthetic reward score and for simulated cash. With hidden factors influencing action assignment, several tabular methods agree closely while underestimating the field-visit policy's score, an error that also appears with boosted models. Intervals from tabular doubly robust estimation usually contain the reference without hidden assignment dependence but mostly miss it when that dependence is present. Estimates from randomized decisions do not show the same large error, although their limited precision leaves policy choice uncertain. The decision consequences depend on how policy value is defined. The field-visit policy ranks last under the score and first under simulated cash, which excludes channel costs. Under cash, log-based estimators miss this best candidate in nearly every run with hidden assignment dependence in the paired study. JUBILEE supports reproducible study of these failure modes under specified collections mechanisms.

items.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing, Formalized in Lean 4
items.summary: The Fundamental Theorem of Asset Pricing states that a market is free of arbitrage exactly when it admits an equivalent martingale measure.
