We hence derive upper and lower bounds of hybrid functionals of the lifetime with respect to mortality rates, which are compatible with the observed life table at integer ages and the given financial market. We derive two sets of results under distinct assumptions. In the first, we assume that each mortality trajectory is almost surely consistent with all the tabulated one-year survival probabilities. In the second, we consider a relaxed formulation that allows for deviations of the mortality rates while still being consistent in expectation with the given reference life table. These distinct yet complementary formulations characterize the worst- and best-case contract values over all mortality processes that remain compatible with the observed life-table information and the financial market. The resulting bounds provide insurers with a practical and robust risk-management tool for assessing the impact of adverse mortality dynamics on variable annuities, quantifying the uncertainty arising from incomplete life-table information, and incorporating mortality model risk into pricing decisions.

items.title: Tempting the Agent: The Economics of Reputation without Persistent Identity in AI Agent Markets
items.summary: Reputation is a fundamental mechanism through which markets sustain trust when service quality cannot be perfectly assessed ex ante, constituting a form of intertemporal economic capital by attracting future demand. Its effectiveness as a disciplinary mechanism depends not only on past interactions but also on the persistence of the identity to which reputation is attached. When identities can be abandoned and recreated cheaply, reputational capital may itself become an object of opportunistic exploitation. This paper develops a dynamic economic framework to study when reputation is sufficient to discipline autonomous agents. We model reputation as capital attracting future economic activity. At each point, an agent chooses between operating honestly, investing in quality to preserve future gains, or executing a one-shot deviation to extract its reputation's value and restart from a penalized identity. Our analysis relates the temptation to opportunistic behavior to identity-reset costs, reputation persistence, demand sensitivity, and enforcement design, deriving comparative statics on optimal quality provision. Autonomous AI-agent operating on the blockchain are a relevant application: infrastructures such as ERC-8004, ERC-8183, and x402 combine reputation, identity, and payments in permissionless markets. Nonetheless, our framework applies to any environment where reputation generates future business and identities are replaceable.

items.title: Lineage-Aware Search Control for LLM-Based Evolutionary Factor Mining
items.summary: Formulaic alpha factor mining searches for symbolic expressions that transform market data into predictive signals. Recent LLM-based evolutionary factor mining methods use large language models as semantic variation operators. Under the conventional LLM-EA paradigm, stochastic variation and fitness-based selection can leave the search weakly directed and concentrated around a narrow set of structurally similar factors. We argue that these limitations arise because current methods mainly organize search at the individual and population levels, leaving lineage-level control underused. A lineage connects successive factor variants through evolutionary descent. We propose LineageEvo, which uses lineage in two coupled forms of search control: (1) lineage-conditioned LLM variation, which distills Lineage-Scoped Search Experience into operator-specific priors and fuses them with global operator priors, providing persistent, lineage-relevant guidance for LLM generation; and (2) lineage-stratified search allocation, which balances factor quality against lineage concentration by distributing the search budget across lineages during evolutionary search. Together, these mechanisms make semantic variation more direction aware and prevent branches from dominating the evolution, thereby promoting the discovery of predictive and diverse factors. We evaluate LineageEvo on CSI 500 and S&P 500 in terms of factor predictiveness, portfolio performance, search efficiency, and lineage- and expression-level diversity. LineageEvo achieves the strongest predictive performance on both markets, while LSPS produces a more balanced lineage distribution and a structurally broader factor pool. The results support lineage as a useful intermediate unit for controlling LLM-based evolutionary factor search.

items.title: Adaptive Entangled Neurons in the Brain and Natural Intelligence Simulations for Artificial General Intelligence
items.summary: Understanding the brain's mechanisms is crucial in neuroscience, particularly for simulating natural intelligence and advancing artificial general intelligence (AGI). Liu et al. (2024) and Deco et al. (2025) propose that quantum entanglement may underlie the synchronization of millions of neurons, introducing the Liu-Chen-Ao (LCA) hypothesis of entangled nerve fibers. However, directly testing this idea remains challenging. Here we employ a nonlocal many-body wave equation, introducing a generalized probability-wave framework to model collective behaviors among adaptive, interacting agents, particles, or neurons. This approach enables testable eigenmodes, offering an indirect means of examining the LCA hypothesis by observing patterns in collective trading behaviors. These patterns, rooted in behavioral psychology, are thought to mirror the internal brain's decision-making and underlying mechanisms. Our analysis of Chinese intraday stock market data shows that adaptive entangled game modes explain 82%-94% of decision patterns, sharply contrasting neoclassical finance predictions assuming independent rational agents. Additionally, 2-12% of actions adapt to news, events, and environmental changes, marked by rapid equilibrium shifts, while truly independent behaviors make up less than 5%. These results empirically support the LCA hypothesis and underscore the need to simulate the brain's mechanisms and generate adaptive, entangled modules for AGI. They also expose the shortcomings of conventional artificial neural networks (ANNs) that depend on vast, opaque parameters. By combining ANN-based AI with probability-wave-based entangled brain simulations, machine learning enables the creation of human-like processing units (HPUs). Such HPUs promise more efficient and robust AGI, particularly for embodied intelligence and robotics.

items.title: GROMM: Generative Risk-neutral Option Market Models
items.summary: We present a statically and dynamically arbitrage-free European option market model with smooth interpolation between option prices, based on the SANOS framework, and prove that its dynamics admit a unique strong solution. In spirit, it is a stochastic model for local volatility when the latter is used as a representation of a European option price surface, not as a pricing model. We illustrate the strength of our approach on S&P Index Option data from January 2022 to August 2025. We show that the model's initial state fits within bid/ask for more than 95% of relevant market option prices. We then train the model dynamics under $\mathbb{P}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ and show that the model is indeed free of arbitrage while fitting the dynamics of the market well. We also propose a range of BHW-tests to test for absence of arbitrage.

items.title: Rethinking Synthetic Scenario Realism: Compatibility, Not Fidelity, Drives Hedging Performance
items.summary: Deep hedging has emerged as a data-driven approach to optimizing hedging strategies. Since real market data are often limited, synthetic price paths play a crucial role in training these strategies. However, existing approaches primarily evaluate synthetic data generators based on statistical realism, while its relationship with hedging performance remains unclear. In this work, we introduce a decision-centric perspective on synthetic data for deep hedging through the notion of compatibility, which captures discrepancies in hedging risk between synthetic and real market environments. Theoretically, we establish an upper bound on hedging performance degradation in terms of learning error and a compatibility gap, and show that statistical realism and compatibility can structurally diverge. In controlled experiments, we demonstrate that the compatibility gap captures variations in hedging degradation across tasks even when generator realism is held fixed. Empirically, using real market data, we show that statistical realism does not consistently predict hedging performance, and that generator rankings depend on both hedging strategy classes and task structure.

items.title: (Early) AI Compute Asset Pricing
items.summary: Compute (computing power) is a scarce, capital-intensive input at the center of the AI economy. Compute capital expenditure and service flow already exceed 1% of U.S. GDP and are growing rapidly. The price of compute reflects uncertainty over AI adoption. The announced launch of compute futures turns this uncertainty into a tradable risk, raising questions on the pricing of a new asset class. We provide an early asset-pricing framework for compute. We begin by discussing the underlying compute rental market and its indexation. We then turn to pricing: 1) direct no-arbitrage links between futures prices and current spot prices fail due to the non-storable nature of compute, 2) synthetic futures prices from existing term rental contracts are likely upper bounds on true futures prices and, 3) upon financialization, futures prices will be investors' expectations of spot prices at expiration net of a risk premium. Using synthetic futures as stand-ins before the compute futures market launches, we construct the first compute futures return panel sorted by GPU generation and maturity. Our preliminary evidence is consistent with a positive compute risk premium, suggesting hedging pressure on the part of compute providers.

items.title: Strategic Index Reconstitution: Differential Games, Closed-Loop Equilibria and Mean-Field Dynamics
items.summary: We study a continuous-time, multiasset trading game around index reconstitution, in which opportunistic traders have heterogeneous beliefs about the future index constitution and interact through transient cross-asset price impact and instantaneous execution costs. Opportunistic traders build inventory based on their individual beliefs about the future index constitution before a public announcement, adjust their positions to the revealed composition, and unwind them against the indexer's prescribed rebalancing trades at the implementation date when the new index composition takes effect. Under a no-price-manipulation condition, we construct a subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium. Its affine feedback policies are computed from a non-standard matrix Riccati equation and linear ODEs whose number and dimensions are independent of population size. Under mean-field scaling, we construct a mean-field equilibrium and obtain quantitative convergence and approximate-Nash bounds. Numerical illustrations show that greater competition among opportunists dampens price swings around implementation and that opportunistic trading lowers the indexer's implementation shortfall unless price resilience is very low. Holding the average belief fixed, greater belief dispersion can increase gross trading volume without changing net aggregate opportunist holdings or price impact.

items.title: Dynamic Programming for Value-at-Risk Markov Decision Processes in Continuous Spaces
items.summary: Value-at-Risk (VaR) is a widely adopted quantile-based risk measure in practice, yet incorporating VaR objectives into Markov decision processes (VaR MDPs) remains a longstanding challenge. Recent work has derived dynamic programming equations for VaR MDPs in finite state and action spaces but left the case of more general spaces unresolved. This paper establishes, for the first time, the validity of these equations in continuous spaces, for both finite- and infinite-horizon settings. Such cases naturally arise in many real-world dynamic decision-making problems. As an application, we study an optimal execution problem with a VaR objective and demonstrate that our framework enables the characterization of optimal dynamic strategies, resolving an open question in the field.

items.title: A game-theoretic analysis of the market microstructure in decentralized exchanges with concentrated liquidity
items.summary: We study strategic liquidity provision in decentralized exchanges with concentrated liquidity as a mean-field game. Liquidity providers choose the width of their price range and when to rebalance it, pay a transaction cost at each rebalancing, and share the fees collected at each tick in proportion to their liquidity, so that each provider's income depends on the state of the population. We formulate the problem as a controlled continuous-time Markov chain on a finite state space. In an averaged version of the game, in which a rebalanced position is re-centered at a draw from the long-run law of the price, a mean-field equilibrium exists. Because each provider's share of the fees falls as competing liquidity is added, the equilibrium liquidity profile is unique. For the exact dynamics, with rebalancing at the range boundary and fast execution, we obtain closed forms for the optimal width, the value function and the stationary law of a position, together with a critical volatility above which provision does not pay. Free entry holds a pool strictly below this threshold, at a margin set by the rebalancing cost. The critical volatility is computed from the fee tier, traded volume, active-tick liquidity and price alone, with no fitted parameter. On two and a half years of hourly data from five WETH/USDC pools on Ethereum and Base, it tracks realized volatility. On the Ethereum $0.3\%$ pool the ratio of realized to critical volatility is less than one, and optimal value $w^*$ exists. On the standard Uniswap fee tiers the critical volatility coincides with the on-chain implied volatility of the pool.

items.title: DSINC beyond Heston: the 3/2 and other non-affine stochastic-volatility models
items.summary: This paper extends the damped-sinc (DSINC) method for American options beyond the affine Heston class to general one-factor stochastic-volatility models. We show that the collapse identity, which reduces the early-exercise integral to a single spectral integral, remains valid for these models. Damping between zero and one is admissible whenever the discounted spot is a nonnegative local martingale. An Itô transformation of the volatility factorizes the conditional characteristic function and identifies a natural coordinate for approximating the exercise boundary. The 3/2 model admits closed-form joint transforms in terms of Kummer functions, while uncorrelated SABR admits a Bessel representation. When a practical closed-form transform is unavailable, the required volatility integral is computed directly by solving one backward equation per frequency, without a grid in the log-price. Through a known change of volatility coordinate, this approach also accommodates correlated SABR. Tests on the 3/2, SABR, GARCH and lognormal-volatility models show agreement with fine finite-difference benchmarks to within one basis point of the strike. Computational cost is comparable to or lower than that of our finite-difference implementation, except for the slower Hankel implementation of uncorrelated SABR.

items.title: Understanding the Inner Workings of a State-Space Foundation Model for Limit Order Books
items.summary: Autoregressive foundation models offer state-of-the-art capabilities to simulate the market by generating the message flow of limit order books (LOBs). Yet, without understanding their inner workings, research directions are hard to narrow and practical use in real-world trading environments remains uncertain. This study therefore asks what these models actually learn about market microstructure. We find that, similarly to games where sequence models build an internal representation of the board, an 8.2M-parameter Mamba-3 state-space model trained autoregressively on the tokenized message stream of eight large-cap US equities learns an internal representation of the market and its dynamics. In particular, order-flow imbalance, a central driver of short-horizon price moves, is decodable at $R^2 \approx 0.59$, far above controls and baselines. This representation extends to unseen stocks, suggesting that these models learn general representations rather than ticker-specific patterns. The model also generalizes across metrics beyond order-flow imbalance: results hold across traded volume and volatility. Additionally, the representation is causally steerable: pushing the state along a feature's axis shifts the model's next-message beliefs as that feature implies, monotonically in dose, consistent with the emergence of a world model.

items.title: Speculative Imbalance Positions by Non-Physical Traders: Impacts on Electricity System Balancing in Great Britain
items.summary: The electricity system in Great Britain (GB) allows participants to deliberately produce or consume a different volume to their traded position and has incentivised this practice with a single imbalance price since 2015. In particular, non-physical traders (NPTs) often take an open position to imbalance without any intention to produce or consume power. However, new government proposals could restrict this practice due to concerns over supply-demand balancing feasibility and costs. This article presents the first empirical analysis of speculative imbalance positioning (SIP) by NPTs in the GB electricity system through its effects on imbalance volumes, balancing costs, the imbalance price, and associated settlement costs over the period 2021-2024. Our research uses party-level imbalance data in each settlement period to run counterfactual simulations of the electricity balancing mechanism without the aggregate NPT imbalance. Our results indicate that SIP by NPTs reduced the total net balancing volume required by 3.1-3.9 TWh (16-20%), reduced system imbalance standard deviation by 48-65 MWh (13-17%), reduced balancing costs by £347-396m (5.9-6.7%), and reduced supplier imbalance costs by £193-325m (65-75%) over the analysis period. These results suggest that consumer bills would have been higher without SIP by NPTs, since the extra costs would likely have been passed on to consumers through levies, although the potential for effects in the wholesale (primarily late-stage intraday) markets complicates this picture.

items.title: Arithmetic Models for Commodity Futures, Vanilla, and Calendar Spread Options
items.summary: We develop an arithmetic multi-factor stochastic volatility model for commodity futures and options. The arithmetic specification yields a low-dimensional Markovian representation of the futures curve and semi-closed-form pricing formulas for vanilla and basket options, including calendar spread options. These properties make the model suitable for large-scale empirical estimation. We estimate the model using an unscented Kalman filter on a panel of WTI crude oil futures, vanilla options, and calendar spread options spanning 2013-2024. We find that three stochastic volatility factors are needed to capture both the level and slope of the volatility term structure, and that hedges based on these factors remove almost all of the daily risk of a portfolio of vanilla options. Calendar spread options provide information about the dependence structure of futures prices that is not captured by futures and vanilla options alone. A model estimated without calendar spread options systematically overprices them by overstating the decorrelation between adjacent futures contracts. Including these options in the estimation brings the model's decorrelation close to the observed decorrelation, which removes the overpricing and improves their hedges, at only a small loss of accuracy in the pricing and hedging of vanilla options. Finally, we show that the arithmetic model fits futures and vanilla options better than its geometric counterpart and hedges the vanilla options slightly better.

items.title: Direct Inversion for Chi-Square Sampling, the Squared Bessel Process, and Applications
items.summary: In this paper we derive a new direct inversion method to simulate squared Bessel processes. Since the transition probability of these processes can be represented by a non-central chi-square distribution, we construct an efficient and accurate algorithm to simulate non-central chi-square variables. In this method, the dimension of the squared Bessel process, equivalently the degrees of freedom of the chi-square distribution, is treated as a variable. We therefore use a two-dimensional Chebyshev expansion to approximate the inverse function of the central chi-square distribution with one variable being the degrees of freedom. The method is accurate and efficient for any value of degrees of freedom including the computationally challenging case of small values. One advantage of the method is that noncentral chi-square samples can be generated for a whole range of values of degrees of freedom using the same Chebyshev coefficients. This property is especially useful in model calibration. The squared Bessel process is a building block for the well-known Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) processes, which can be generated from squared Bessel processes through time change and linear transformation. Our direct inversion method thus allows the efficient and accurate simulation of these processes, which are used as models in a wide variety of applications.

items.title: Amortized Neural Filtering for Calibrated Posteriors in Statistical Arbitrage
items.summary: Statistical arbitrage trades on an estimate of the state of a residual spread, and conventional practice discards the uncertainty of that estimate. We keep the uncertainty and use it in the trading decision. A Neural Filter Estimator (NFE) is trained on simulated paths of a mean-reverting process whose innovation law is selected by testing candidates against real residuals; once trained, it returns the posterior over the latent state of every spread in a cross-section in one forward pass. Three results follow. On simulated paths with known truth, every practical estimator, ours included, falls in one narrow band of accuracy well below an estimator given full information, so the posterior gains no accuracy over a point estimate; its contribution is a correct account of its own uncertainty. On Korean equities, net of costs, the conventional point estimate forecasts about a thousand basis points per holding period more than it realizes, and the amortized methods cut that gap by a factor of roughly two to eight. Sizing positions from the posterior on the same learned factors as the end-to-end Attention Factor Model matches the Sharpe ratio of those factors under the base rule within the period's noise, at no more risk.

items.title: Kernel-based collocation methods for Heath-Jarrow-Morton models with Musiela parametrization
items.summary: We study kernel-based collocation methods for numerical solutions of Heath-Jarrow-Morton models in Musiela parametrization. The methods are Euler-Maruyama approximations of finite-dimensional stochastic differential equations and can be used with standard Monte Carlo procedures for derivative pricing. We give a conditional mean-square error estimate under explicit stability assumptions on the differentiated cardinal basis over the full evaluation region required by the volatility functional. The estimate uses the spatial-radius exponent dictated by the squared-error calculation. Two finite-resolution examples illustrate the method for a Vasicek model and for caplet pricing.

items.title: Disclosure under Noisy Information Processing
items.summary: Capital markets process disclosures with noise. Adding this single friction overturns the standard characterization of costly voluntary disclosure. Firms may unravel to full disclosure despite strictly positive disclosure costs and, when unravelling fails, the model generically admits two equilibria rather than one. In the lower-threshold equilibrium, disclosure becomes more frequent as the cost rises and as reports become more accurate, falls with fundamental volatility when it is below the processing noise, but approaches full disclosure again when volatility grows large. These results help explain the mixed empirical evidence on the proprietary cost hypothesis and generate conditional predictions that distinguish high and low disclosure regimes. The model also explains why ESG ratings can be noisy, costly, and widely purchased, while still influencing market prices.

items.title: LOB-Impact Benchmark: Emergent Market Impact in Generative Limit Order Book Models
items.summary: Realistic market impact is essential for generative limit order book (LOB) models to serve as world models for trading agents. If a simulator misprices this mechanism, agents learn policies that are optimal in the simulator but wrong in the real market. Existing metrics assess generated streams purely through distributional comparison with historical data, leaving counterfactual response to an agent's own orders largely unexplored. Here, we show that market impact emerges naturally in neural LOB generators trained solely for next-token prediction. We inject execution-style metaorders into the generated message flow of five autoregressive models across five NASDAQ stocks and measure the response using estimators from the empirical impact literature, validated on baselines whose physics is known in advance. Our benchmark evaluates any message-level generator in three phases: free generation (reading order-flow persistence against price diffusivity); metaorder injection (yielding the impact law's exponent and amplitude); and a post-execution window (measuring relaxation). In addition, comparing each visible injection to a blind, simulator-only control isolates the model's learned response from standard book mechanics. For every model on every stock, we measure how the impact responds as a function of cumulative metaorder participation. Interestingly, we observe emergent impact in generative models of market data, with exponents in the range of 0.63 to 1.21, slightly above the traditional 0.5 of the square-root law of impact. In the family of models tested, we are so far unable to observe impact decay during relaxation. We tentatively attribute this to the still-short context windows of the models. We release the benchmark as open source to validate future generative models for market data.

items.title: Teacher Supervision, Fixed Representations and Calibration: Exact Risk Calculations for Candidate-Scoring Decision Models
items.summary: Candidate-scoring decision models return a probability distribution over a presented set of answers. Public documentation of one such system, Jev, and of an open counterpart, JevAny, describes three training ingredients that determine what these probabilities estimate: soft targets from larger models, a frozen pretrained backbone and temperature calibration. We analyze each ingredient in Gaussian surrogates where the finite-sample risk can be computed exactly. A student trained on teacher targets inherits the teacher's bias, which more student data does not remove and agreement with the teacher does not reveal. A fixed representation lowers the risk only below an explicit sample-size threshold. In a probit model the exact recalibration map is a temperature scaling, which removes all excess risk only when the teacher's coefficient has the correct direction and otherwise leaves a residual that calibration diagnostics do not detect. Under Luce's choice axiom, candidate scores are coherent across refinements of an event if and only if they aggregate by log-sum-exp. On 231,521 credit card complaints from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, where the decision is whether a complaint ends in monetary relief, a student trained on a logistic teacher's probabilities ends at the teacher's decision cost while a student trained on outcomes goes 8% below it, a 30B model read zero-shot remains worse than the teacher after recalibration, and that model departs from the coherence condition by 17.5 decibans. Pretrained representations reduce the labeled data required and calibration corrects the scale of the probabilities, but neither corrects a biased teacher, so the probabilities have to be checked against realized outcomes.

items.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Market Making on Prediction-Market Order Books
items.summary: A market maker provides liquidity by quoting prices to buy and sell an asset, earning the spread while managing inventory risk. We study market makers trained with multi-agent reinforcement learning on prediction markets, specifically Polymarket, whose thin order books pose distinct challenges. Three challenges underpin this research: adverse selection may cause a policy trained on real data to stop quoting; the consequences of a quote can arrive many steps after the action; and prediction-market L2 data does not identify individual orders needed for simulation. We address these challenges by reconstructing order-level LOBSTER-format data from Polymarket and training agents in JaxMARL-HFT on 417 real markets. We enrich the baseline market maker's observation space with the book and recent flow, redesign its actions and inventory controls, and propose a cooperative multi-agent decomposition into a quoter and a risk manager trained using recurrent Independent Proximal Policy Optimisation (IPPO) with RNN policies. We investigate reward shaping, particularly reward blending and post-fill markout, to mitigate credit-assignment difficulties between the agents. Our redesigned single-agent market maker quotes more frequently and incurs smaller held-out losses than the retrained JaxMARL-HFT baseline, although the contributions of jointly changed observations, actions and risk constraints are not separately identified. Decomposition alone performs poorly; careful reward design substantially improves the desk relative to the unshaped split and yields our best result. Models are evaluated on realised end-of-episode portfolio value on held-out markets. None establishes positive average portfolio value in periodic held-out evaluation, and each configuration was trained with one seed. The environment, data and protocol lay a foundation for makers that quote many linked markets at once.

items.title: Optimal Loss Allocation and Reflected Free Boundaries in Systemic Risk
items.summary: We study a singular mean-field control problem in which a central planner allocates losses generated by bank defaults to maximize terminal system health. Every generated loss must be borne by the surviving banks, without external capital. We prove that a cutoff, or "taxing-the-richest" rule is optimal for every non-decreasing concave terminal payoff, including the survival indicator. We construct the continuous-time optimizer by solving a time-discretized problem and passing to the limit, and establish its uniqueness in law for every non-constant payoff. The optimal flow is characterized by a novel reflected free-boundary problem. We establish well-posedness in a probabilistic solution class and prove positive-time smoothness of both the free boundary and the density of surviving banks. The main difficulty is the dependence of the limiting feedback on a moving support endpoint, which is unstable under Wasserstein convergence. We address this through stochastic-order comparisons, compactness estimates for the cutoff boundaries, and an augmented call-function formulation.

items.title: Probability-Weighting Functions for Normal Tempered-Stable Laws: Orthogonal Channels and Information-Theoretic Indices
items.summary: A probability-weighting function (PWF) maps objective probabilities into decision weights. We construct PWFs from changes in the distribution of returns rather than from a parametric family: with prior and posterior return distributions $F_{prior}$ and $F_{post}$, the PWF is $w(p) = F_{post}(F_{prior}^{-1}(p))$. Both distributions are normal tempered-stable (NTS), and the posterior differs from the prior along one of three channels, each isolated with the variance held fixed: scale, skewness and tail thickness. Around a symmetric benchmark with excess kurtosis 3, a 40% change in scale moves cumulative probabilities by up to 7 to 8 percentage points, a skewness of $\pm 0.5$ by 2 percentage points, and a change of $\pm 0.3$ in the tail index by about 2 percentage points. The three channels leave distinct signatures: the deviation $w(p) - p$ changes sign once, twice and three times, respectively. Three information-theoretic indices (a Fisher-normalized logit shift, a signed Jensen-Shannon divergence and a log-odds elasticity) summarize the distortions and avoid the endpoint singularity of the classical ratio $(w(p)-p)/[p(1-p)]$. Applied to NTS parameters calibrated to S&P 500 ETF daily returns over 2015-2025, the same channels produce distortions of 2 to 7 percentage points. Code that reproduces every figure and number in the paper is provided.

items.title: Branched Signature Model
items.summary: In this paper, we introduce the branched signature model, motivated by the branched rough path framework of [Gubinelli, Journal of Differential Equations, 248(4), 2010], which generalizes the classical geometric rough path. We establish a universal approximation theorem for the branched signature model and demonstrate that iterative compositions of lower-level signature maps can approximate higher-level signatures. Furthermore, building on the existence of the extension map proposed in [Hairer-Kelly. Annales de l'Institue Henri Poincaré, Probabilités et Statistiques 51, no. 1 (2015)], we show how to explicitly construct the extension of the original paths into higher-dimensional spaces via a map $Ψ$, so that the branched signature can be realized as the classical geometric signature of the extended path. This framework not only provides an efficient computational scheme for branched signatures but also opens new avenues for data-driven modeling and applications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework through two representative applications: rough volatility calibration and optimal execution.

items.title: Arbitrage-Aware Probabilistic Multi-Step Forecasting of Implied Volatility Surfaces: Joint Generation of Surface-Return Trajectories Using Latent Diffusion
items.summary: Implied volatility surfaces summarise the option market and are central to many financial applications. Probabilistic forecasting of their future evolution requires modelling two-dimensional geometry, temporal dependence, and predictive uncertainty while preserving economic admissibility. We propose a conditional latent diffusion framework for generating joint 30-step trajectories of implied volatility surfaces and underlying returns. An arbitrage-aware autoencoder learns a surface representation, while diffusion captures the evolution. Evaluated on SPX surfaces, the framework generates realistic probabilistic multi-step scenarios. Its predictive mean also outperforms persistence beyond the shortest horizons.

items.title: Regime-Aware Interpretable Ranking for Sector Rotation
items.summary: Sector rotation is a common decision in benchmark-relative portfolio management, where portfolio managers rank sectors for overweight and underweight positions. We formulate this task as ranking sector actions by expected future risk-adjusted active performance, measured with forward sector-benchmark Sharpe ratios. Such rankings should preserve temporal information, express model outputs through economically familiar signal characteristics, account for changes in signal relevance across macroeconomic environments, and capture dependencies among sectors. We propose RegimeRank, an interpretable sector-ranking model that represents fundamental and technical signals through expert-defined temporal characteristics, conditions them on learned macro factors via cross-attention, and models cross-sector dependencies through self-attention. Expected-gradient attributions identify the contributions of individual signal-transformation pairs, while macroeconomic and cross-sector attention maps provide diagnostics of the learned conditioning and relational structure. We evaluate RegimeRank on weekly S&P 500 data from 2002 to 2024 under combinatorial purged cross-validation, where it outperforms representative ranking and machine-learning baselines across multiple ranking metrics. Ablation studies support the contributions of latent macro states, regime conditioning, and cross-sector modelling, while attribution and attention analyses illustrate the temporal characteristics, macro states, and sector relationships underlying its rankings.

items.title: SHADE: Shrinkage via Halted Alpha-stable Denoising for Heavy-Tailed Probabilistic Time Series Forecasting
items.summary: Time-series observations are particularly susceptible to noise, and many real-world series have low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) together with heavy-tailed and time-varying disturbances. When Gaussian diffusion models are used for forecasting, reversing all the way to the zero-noise endpoint may yield an overly narrow and overconfident predictive distribution. We propose SHADE, an alpha-stable Lévy diffusion forecaster that reads out at a nonzero depth so that the residual stable kernel acts as distribution-level shrinkage. By decomposing halting risk into smoothing bias and estimation error, we develop a scale-calibrated halt for estimating the optimal shrinkage $τ^*$ and a context-amortized halt that requires no explicit noise labels. Gains concentrate in the extreme heavy-tailed regime $α\leq1.3$: Across synthetic noise settings, median CRPS improves by 21.7\%, while the NLL falls significantly; Cryptocurrency and foreign-exchange data provide further evidence of improved tail calibration in real-data implement. On near-light-tailed or high-SNR data, the model reverts to Gaussian diffusion or full denoising. SHADE maintains overall forecast error comparable to strong baselines while providing more honest tail uncertainty for heavy-tailed series.

items.title: DiSKO: Distribution Steering for Nonlinear Systems using the Koopman Operator
items.summary: This paper studies the problem of data-driven covariance steering for stochastic, nonlinear dynamical systems. We utilize Koopman operator theory to learn, directly from data, an approximate linear representation of the nonlinear dynamics in a lifted space of observable functions of the state. By exploiting this linear model, we design controllers for the mean and covariance of the underlying nonlinear system by utilizing linear distribution steering algorithms. To account for approximation errors in the learned dynamics and the ambiguity in the disturbance distribution induced in the lifted space, we formulate the problem as a distributionally robust covariance steering problem. Furthermore, we leverage a deep neural network (DNN) to simultaneously learn the Koopman observables and the linear model parameters, thus eliminating the need for manual observables basis selection while also reducing the dimensionality of the lifted representation. Additionally, we can promote desirable model properties, such as stability, during DNN training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework via numerical simulations.

items.title: Stability Despite Misalignment: Model Predictive Game Controllers with Objective Misspecifications
items.summary: Predictive control requires the controller to possess an embedded prediction model. In multi-agent control, this prediction model must consider the behavior that emerges from other agents' strategic decisions. Game theory offers a natural model for the emergent collective behavior of self-interested agents. Model predictive games (MPGs) are a class of controllers in which an agent iteratively solves a finite-horizon game to predict the behavior of a multi-agent system and synthesize their own control action. When all agents use the same game model to select their control action, conditions have been found that guarantee the closed-loop stability of the multi-agent system. However, when multiple agents implement their own MPG controllers, their respective game models may be misspecified due to inaccurate estimates or conjectures about other agents' objectives. This paper analyzes the consequences of these prediction misalignments on the system's behavior. We show that existing stability conditions for homogeneous MPG controllers do not extend to the heterogeneous setting, even when they hold for each agent's individual game. We provide sufficient conditions for the stability of multi-agent dynamical systems with heterogeneous MPG controllers adopting linear-quadratic (LQ) games. We also show that misaligned game models can destabilize a system that reaches stability when all agents share the same game model, using a financial duopoly simulation.

items.title: Generalized Gated Recurrent Neural Networks for Nonlinear System Identification
items.summary: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) networks are the two most widely adopted recurrent neural networks for black-box nonlinear system identification, yet they are invariably treated as mutually exclusive structural choices. To move toward a general framework that inherits the properties of both networks, we introduce the Generalized Gated Recurrent Neural Network (GGRNN), a unified architecture that embeds the exact GRU and LSTM network dynamics through homotopies between their respective gating mechanisms. Each homotopy continuously deforms one mechanism into the other, with a vector of homotopy parameters blending the contribution of the GRU and LSTM counterparts. Since benchmark comparisons report no consistent winner between the two architectures, the gating mechanism best suited to a given system is unlikely to coincide with either endpoint. We thus let each recurrent unit learn its own position along these homotopies, obtaining gating behaviors that neither endpoint can express. We pair the GGRNN with a two-stage training methodology: in Stage 1 we co-train all shared and network-specific parameters in parallel at the GRU and LSTM endpoint architectures, while in Stage 2 we freeze the network parameters and optimize only the homotopy parameters. Experiments on the Wiener-Hammerstein and Nano-Drone benchmarks show improved simulation accuracy over the co-trained GRU and LSTM networks on most output groups, and over the reference black-box baselines in nearly all comparisons.

items.title: Total Energy Shaping of Underactuated Systems via Gravity Compensation at the Desired Equilibrium
items.summary: This paper investigates total energy shaping of underactuated mechanical systems with gravity compensation evaluated at the desired equilibrium instead of throughout the online closed-loop operation. Within the interconnection and damping assignment passivity-based control (IDA-PBC) framework, sufficient conditions for local asymptotic stability are established in terms of integrability of a vector field and positive definiteness of an augmented potential energy. The approach is also combined with a reformulation of potential energy matching that replaces a nonhomogeneous partial differential equation with a homogeneous one and introduces an additional design term. Analytic constructions for the TORA system and a class of two-degree-of-freedom systems illustrate how the matching and integrability requirements can be addressed. The proposed control law avoids online evaluation of the configuration-dependent gravity term; offline controller synthesis and verification can still require knowledge of the gravity model.

items.title: Robust Control Design for LTI Systems with Sampling-Time Jitter
items.summary: Sampling-time jitter makes a sampled-data control loop time-varying, so standard LTI robust-control synthesis does not apply directly. This paper reformulates dynamic output feedback design under bounded, unmeasured sample-to-sample jitter as a robust-control problem. The exact zero-order-hold model is decomposed into a nominal time-invariant plant and a memoryless, time-varying uncertainty block with a norm bound representing the sampling-time jitter. As the block is memoryless, the operator small-gain condition for the time varying loop reduces to a standard robustness test with a matrix norm bound. It is shown that the same test also guarantees uniform exponential stability for every admissible jitter sequence. Embedding the decomposition into a generalized plant with performance channels serves two synthesis objectives with standard robust-control tools: Robust stability with optimized nominal performance through structured H-inf synthesis, and robust performance through mu synthesis with constant scalings. A numerical example shows that jitter can destabilize a control loop with a nominal H-inf controller, whereas both robust designs remain stable and the robust-performance design is less sensitive to jitter at the cost of nominal performance.

items.title: Control-Gibbs Distribution: Sampling for Optimal Control and Diverse Actions
items.summary: While conventional optimal control selects an optimal input sequence, probabilistic control assigns probability mass over all possible inputs and exploits a distribution of control sequences. Control distributions help enable exploration, capture diverse solutions, and solve deterministic optimal control problems. This work reviews an important probabilistic model for control distributions, the control-Gibbs distribution, i.e., the Gibbs distribution with an optimal control objective as the energy function. We point out its fundamental role in various probabilistic control frameworks, e.g., maximum entropy control, control-as-inference framework, model predictive path integral control, and energy-based models for control. This provides a model-central perspective to unify these probabilistic control frameworks. We also review the associated extensions of dynamic programming for computing closed-loop control distributions. To sample the control-Gibbs distribution, we consider projected Langevin sampling and develop non-asymptotic guarantees. The guarantees show the dual benefits of sampling the control-Gibbs distribution: obtaining diverse control solutions and solving the deterministic optimal control problem. We provide a numerical example where diverse arm trajectories are sampled from a control-Gibbs distribution.

items.title: Channel-Chart-Driven Antenna Activation for Energy-Efficient Cell-Free Massive MIMO
items.summary: Cell-free massive MIMO (CF-mMIMO) can provide uniformly high system performance across the coverage area through distributed cooperation. However, keeping all antennas active leads to high circuit and fronthaul power consumption. This paper studies energy-efficient uplink reception through antenna activation, where only a subset of distributed antennas is selected to serve the users. To enable network-wide activation with low signaling overhead, each access point (AP) maps its locally estimated channel state information (CSI) into a lowdimensional channel-chart (CC) embedding and forwards this representation to the central processing unit (CPU) instead of the full CSI. Based on the received embeddings, we formulate a binary antenna-activation problem for network EE maximization and propose three low-overhead strategies: (i) direct embeddingdomain activation using a proxy EE metric without CSI reconstruction, (ii) nearest chart-point CSI approximation, which estimates CSI from a reference chart database for greedy EE optimization, and (iii) decoder-based CSI reconstruction using a pre-trained autoencoder. The proposed approaches further enable a systematic comparison of antenna activation techniques in terms of achieved performance, computational complexity, and signaling overhead. Numerical results show substantial EE gains over the all-active baseline, with only a minor degradation in sum spectral efficiency and a significant reduction in signaling overhead. Moreover, the proposed greedy framework achieves EE performance close to that of the simulated annealing baseline, confirming its effectiveness for low-complexity antenna activation.

items.title: Integrating Sensing into Covert Communications: Opportunities and Challenges
items.summary: Covert communications aim to hide the existence of wireless transmissions from unauthorized adversaries. However, conventional designs based on blind interference or passive uncertainty can be ineffective in dynamic propagation environments. This article investigates sensing-empowered covert communications, where adversary and environmental information are used to guide transmission and jamming control. We show how sensing changes covert system design from passive concealment to state-aware decision-making, while also introducing new challenges related to exposure and resource consumption. We further discuss several intelligent sensing paradigms that extract task-relevant information with limited active probing. A case study in low-altitude wireless networks illustrates that sensing-assisted beamforming can improve spatial resource utilization and the reliability of covert data delivery in time-varying channels. Finally, several open issues are discussed to support more adaptive covert wireless systems.

items.title: CT-RespGeomLib: Deterministic reconstruction of CT airway masks into editable,port-matched lumen geometry
items.summary: Patient-specific airway modelling requires geometrically consistent lumen surfaces with identifiable boundaries and support for controlled anatomical modifications. We present CT-RespGeomLib, a deterministic framework that converts CT airway masks into two complementary representations: an editable assembly of semantically labelled pipe and junction blocks connected through canonical shared ports, and a fused lumen surface reconstructed from tapered implicit primitives with validated port-to-boundary loop correspondence. The parametric representation further enables localised modelling of airway stenosis and dilation without re-segmentation. Evaluated on 42 reference airway masks from ATM22 (15 cases) and AeroPath (27 cases), the framework produced 37 topologically accepted reconstructions, with a median port-to-loop distance of 0.123 mm across 2174 matched ports. Reconstructed and reference equivalent radii showed strong agreement ($R^2 = 0.976$), with a mean bias of -0.414 mm arising primarily from the circular, inscribed-radius representation. Controlled pathology modelling generated 40 variants across five patient-specific geometries, including 25-75% stenosis and 50% dilation at tracheal and main-bronchus locations. Prescribed radius changes were reproduced with a mean absolute ratio error of 0.0056, while the median 95th-percentile deviation outside the modified region was 0.111 mm. Downstream applicability was demonstrated through volume meshing and an OpenFOAM simulation with individually prescribed model-based resistance conditions at 62 outlets. Although additional surface preparation may be required for numerical meshing, CT-RespGeomLib provides a reproducible framework for CT-derived airway reconstruction, quantitative boundary validation and controlled geometric pathology modelling.

items.title: Survivability Guarantees for Delayed Serial Supply Chains under Demand Shocks
items.summary: When demand exceeds the maximum production capacity of a supply chain, it can be satisfied only for a finite time, determined by the inventory stored along the chain. Existing control methods ensure indefinite constraint satisfaction under bounded demand, but provide no guarantees on how long a supply chain can withstand a shock in which demand goes beyond production capacity. We address this gap for a serial supply chain with transportation delays and flow constraints. Under a specified flow policy, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions on the inventory distribution that guarantee a prescribed lower bound on the exit time from the set where demand is served. We use these conditions to compute inventory targets that minimize holding costs via a quadratic program. Then, we propose a two-mode controller that builds reserves under ordinary demand and depletes them during the shock. Simulations illustrate this approach.

items.title: A Modulation Strategy for Bidirectional Integrated Onboard and Wireless EV Charging
items.summary: Integrated electric vehicle chargers reduce cost by sharing power conversion hardware between the onboard charger (OBC) and the wireless charger (WC). A previously proposed dual active bridge (DAB)-based OBC/WC shares the rectification stage between the OBC and WC; however, the modulation required to realize its wireless operation has not yet been reported. This paper details a modulation strategy that enables the operation of the integrated OBC/WC topology. Differential-mode operation is used for the OBC, and common-mode operation is used for the WC. In OBC mode, the shared full-bridge produces differential-mode voltage for wired power transfer while ideally generating zero common-mode voltage on the wireless charging path. In WC mode, the same full-bridge produces common-mode voltage for wireless power transfer while ideally generating zero differential-mode voltage on the onboard charging path. The method preserves conventional DAB phase-shift power control and enables bidirectional power transfer in wired and wireless charging modes without additional contactors. Design considerations for the OBC transformer and WC coils are derived based on the resulting square-wave voltage amplitudes. Offline PLECS simulations demonstrate power tracking and decoupled charger operation at $\pm$7.4 kW. Hardware-in-the-loop simulations using a PLECS RT Box and an external Texas Instruments microcontroller further validate the proposed modulation method.

items.title: Improved Single-Input Space Vector for DC-Biased Sinusoidal Current Control in Battery Cyclers
items.summary: This paper presents improvements to the single-input space vector (SISV) concept for current control in a battery cycler based on a two-phase interleaved buck converter. The cycler is controlled to output a dc-biased sinusoidal current, enabling investigation of second-harmonic ripple effects on lithium-ion cell aging. A modified SISV generation scheme is introduced to track current references containing both dc and sinusoidal components, and an impedance-angle compensation method is proposed to decouple the d and q control axes without disturbing dc tracking. A dq phase-portrait visualization method is also introduced to evaluate transient performance for both SISV and proportional-integral-resonant (PIR) control methods. Simulation and experimental results validate dc-biased sinusoidal current tracking using PIR control and SISV control with different decoupling schemes. The phase-portrait framework allows for straightforward evaluation of transient performance for both SISV and PIR control methods and supports controller tuning to obtain desired trajectories. The results demonstrate the feasibility of SISV-based current control as an alternative to PIR control for battery-cycler applications. The proposed improvements support the development of battery cyclers capable of controlling both dc and sinusoidal current components.

items.title: Physics-informed structured learning of a class of recurrent neural networks with guaranteed properties
items.summary: This paper proposes a physics-informed learning framework for a class of recurrent neural networks tailored to networked systems. The approach aims to learn control-oriented models that preserve the structural and stability properties of the plant. The learning algorithm is formulated as a convex optimisation problem, allowing the inclusion of linear matrix inequality constraints to enforce desired plant features. Furthermore, when the plant exhibits structural modularity, the resulting optimisation problem can be parallelised, requiring communication only among neighbouring subplants. Simulation results show the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

items.title: Mode-in-Variance Participation Factors under Stochastic Excitation
items.summary: This paper investigates how the dynamic modes of a power system contribute to the stationary variance of its variables under continuous stochastic excitation. Using a modal decomposition of the covariance matrix, the variance of each state or algebraic variable can be resolved into components associated with individual modal responses and their interactions. These components are shown to correspond to within-mode variance and cross-modal covariance, respectively, and the corresponding normalized contributions are termed mode-in-variance participation factors (PFs). The proposed PFs can be used to identify modes governing the variability of important system quantities such as frequency and voltage, quantify the effect of modal interactions, and reveal control dynamics that can be targeted to reduce their stochastic variability. These capabilities are demonstrated through case studies based on the Kundur two-area and IEEE 39-bus systems.

items.title: A New Analytical Method and Interpretation of Loss-of-Load Counts
items.summary: This paper establishes the relationship between loss-of-load expectation (LOLE) and loss-of-load frequency (LOLF). We show why LOLE generally does not measure distinct-event frequency, mean event duration, or shortage magnitude. We identify conditions under which peak-based LOLE admits a frequency interpretation as the expected count of deficient daily peaks per horizon and distinguish this quantity from LOLF. We also derive an analytical formulation for frequency-and-duration indices that combines a convolution-derived generation probability-and-frequency model with chronological load changes. Under stationary generation, it uses the prescribed load profile directly, without constructing a separate load model or discretizing load magnitudes. Studies using generation and load data from the 24-bus IEEE RTS reveal different event frequencies and mean event durations at identical peak-based LOLE, motivating their separate assessment. Numerical comparisons demonstrate the accuracy advantage of the proposed analytical calculation over the conventional analytical implementations, quantifying the LOLF errors incurred by load discretization.

items.title: Adjacent Heat Transfer Effects Can Bias Savings Estimates When Controlling Only Part of a Multi-Zone Building
items.summary: Field demonstrations of advanced heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning control often operate a few thermal zones within a larger building and report savings for those zones alone. A recent theorem showed that this practice overestimates whole-building savings, because heat drawn from the neighboring zones is paid for by their equipment and is not counted. The error grows with the thermal conductance between the controlled and uncontrolled zones, with how much colder the controlled zones run over the test, and with the price of the heat their neighbors supply. For one controlled zone with one neighbor, a single thermal price, and slowly changing prices, the relative error reduces to the ratio of two conductances, a screening number that can be evaluated from the two conductances before a demonstration begins. This paper tests how far that reduction can be taken. A two-story house with one thermal zone per floor is simulated over a 90-day heating season in West Lafayette, Indiana, with receding-horizon model predictive control on the first floor and setpoint control on the second, under four combinations of electricity tariff (time-of-use or flat) and heating plant (heat pump or electric resistance). The exact correction from the theorem recovers the true savings in every case, and the full theorem, evaluated from the controlled zone's temperatures, the prices, and the building parameters, reproduces the measured relative error in every case. The conductance ratio bounds that error from above in all four cases, tightly under a flat tariff, within 3%, and loosely under a time-of-use tariff, where most of the controller's savings come from shifting load through the thermal mass rather than from lowering the temperature.

items.title: Transmission-Mode Multispectral Imaging for Estimation of Microcystis spp. Cell Concentration and ELISA-Equivalent Microcystin Concentration in Water
items.summary: Harmful algal blooms dominated by Microcystis spp. threaten freshwater systems through proliferation and microcystin (MC) production. Conventional measurements of cyanobacterial abundance and MC concentration commonly require laboratory processing, specialized instrumentation, or assay reagents. Because MC concentration cannot always be reliably inferred from cell abundance, complementary optical approaches for estimating both quantities are of interest. This study proposes and evaluates a transmission mode multispectral imaging (MSI) framework for estimating Microcystis spp. cell concentration and ELISA-equivalent MC concentration from culture derived dilution samples. A custom built MSI system acquiring twelve spectral bands from near-ultraviolet to near-infrared wavelengths measured transmitted light spectral responses. Following principal component analysis based dimensionality reduction, spectral variation was quantified using an aggregated Wasserstein distance descriptor for regression based prediction. Cell concentration estimation yielded $R^2=0.9819$ for calibration and $R^2=0.9754$ on held-out intermediate dilution levels, while ELISA-equivalent MC estimation yielded $R^2=0.9788$ for calibration and $R^2=0.9786$ on held-out intermediate dilution levels. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transmission-mode MSI as a dual output optical calibration framework for estimation of Microcystis spp. cell concentration and ELISA-equivalent MC concentration in water.
authors: K. A. D. S. A. Perera
A. D. S. N. P. Athukorala
H. A. D. R. P. Sirimanna

items.title: Asymptotic SINR Analysis of Linear Detectors in Uplink Massive NTN MIMO Transmissions
items.summary: This paper examines the performance degradation of receivers caused by imperfect channel state information (CSI), arising from training-based and semi-blind channel estimation techniques. We focus on the uplink of massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems operating in time-division duplexing (TDD) mode, considering the asymptotic regime where the number of base station (BS) antennas grows large while the number of users remains fixed. Leveraging random matrix theory (RMT), we analyze the asymptotic behavior of the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) under linear MRC and MMSE detection schemes. We derive closed-form approximations of the achievable rates, prove their asymptotic tightness, and validate their accuracy through simulations for systems of finite dimensions. Numerical results under realistic non-terrestrial network (NTN) conditions further demonstrate that semi-blind channel estimation enables MRC and MMSE receivers to outperform their training-based counterparts, while also quantifying the number of pilot symbols required to achieve a desired SINR level.

items.title: Quantum Network Flows That Solve Linear Equations
items.summary: We develop a distributed quantum network flow for solving linear equations from locally stored row data. Local pumping enforces each node's equation constraint, while neighboring registers interact through swaps. The node marginals obey an exact, closed flow combining consensus with local constraint enforcement. For consistent equations, all node states converge exponentially to a common state supported on the solution space; a unique solution yields full-network convergence to the product solution state. For inconsistent equations of full column rank, scaled encoding and readout recover the least-squares solution through successive large-gain and small-scale limits. For consistent systems, the marginal convergence rate is nondecreasing and concave in the swap gain, approaching a graph-independent limit for fixed local dissipators. Its leading finite-gain correction couples graph topology and row placement through the Laplacian pseudoinverse, enabling semidefinite optimization of edge rates under a fixed total swap-rate budget. For invertible systems, a dissipative HHL-type construction using the same pumping law provides a comparison of solution-state encodings, decay rates, and row-update locality under squared-row-norm pumping. Numerical examples are provided to validate the presented results.

items.title: FlatSeek: LLM-Driven Symbolic Discovery of Flat Outputs via Backward Data Generation
items.summary: Differential flatness enables efficient planning and control, but discovering explicit flat outputs for general nonlinear systems remains difficult due to the lack of general methods and supervised data. We propose FlatSeek, a framework combining backward data generation with task-specific large language model (LLM) training. By reversing the defining reconstruction of flatness, we generate system-flat-output pairs with known certificates, then fine-tune an LLM to propose symbolic flat-output candidates for unseen dynamics. On literature and synthetic benchmarks, FlatSeek outperforms both the traditional symbolic methods and the untuned reference models in flat-output discovery success, and uncovers alternative symbolic flat outputs not reported in the literature.

items.title: CODE-PIF: Convex/Deep (CODE) Multiview Pseudoinvariant Features for Multitemporal Multispectral Surface Reflectance Imagery
items.summary: Multitemporal multispectral surface reflectance imagery exhibits radiometric and spectral variability due to atmospheric effects, sensor differences, and actual surface changes, complicating the identification of pseudoinvariant features (PIFs). The SOTA DeepMGCCA captures nonlinear dependencies across acquisition dates, but similarity in its learned feature space does not directly establish consistency in the original reflectance domain. Meanwhile, we believe that the PIFs extracted by DeepMGCCA preserve essential structural characteristics, providing an effective prior to guide subsequent refinement. Therefore, we propose the CODE-PIF architecture, an unsupervised convex/deep (CODE) framework that refines the coarse PIF from DeepMGCCA using convex optimization. Specifically, CODE-PIF uses the data-fitting term to integrate reflectance deviations, correlation-weighted spectral angles, and temporal reference change information to promote radiometric and spectral consistency between predicted PIFs and observed data. Moreover, the regularization term uses a mathematically simple Q-quadratic norm to incorporate information from the coarse PIF estimate into the refined solution. The resulting convex optimization problem is solved using the ADMM optimizer, which decomposes it into simpler subproblems and provides convergence guarantees under standard assumptions. Experiments across four distinct ROIs show improved average radiometric and spectral agreement relative to DeepMGCCA.Averaged across these regions, the RMSE decreases from 0.0192 to 0.0164, PSNR increases from 35.91 to 37.44 dB, and the between-date spectral angle decreases from 3.77 to 2.97 degrees. Although structural similarity and Pearson correlation do not improve in every scene, the results suggest that using observed data helps select PIFs with more consistent reflectance values and spectral shapes across dates.

items.title: Structure-Preserving Learning for Nonlinear Nonholonomic Dynamics
items.summary: Learning the dynamics of mechanical systems subject to nonlinear nonholonomic constraints is challenging, as data-driven models may violate the underlying physical constraints, leading to inconsistent predictions. To address this problem, we develop a constraint-preserving learning framework based on the Lagrange-d'Alembert-Chetaev equations and tangency to the constraint submanifold, which together define an affine space of admissible accelerations. Using the kinetic-energy metric and the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse, we construct a metric projector and the corresponding Chetaev correction. Embedding this geometric structure directly into a Gaussian process prior ensures that both prior and posterior dynamics satisfy the acceleration constraints exactly. We characterize the resulting reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), derive an adapted-coordinate representation, and establish nonexpansiveness and consistency transfer. Numerical experiments on a three-dimensional directional flocking system with up to 50 agents demonstrate exact constraint preservation and robustness to constraint-incompatible observations.

items.title: ScrewSense: Mapping the Invisible - Anomaly Detection and Error Classification in Screwdriving Processes
items.summary: The growing volume of process data generated by screwdriving systems, combined with advancements in computing power, data storage, and algorithms, is facilitating the application of artificial intelligence in this field. Accurately detecting and classifying screwdriving errors is crucial for ensuring product quality, avoiding costly rework in manufacturing, and supporting sustainability by facilitating the maintenance, reuse, and recycling of screw-connected products. In this context, machine learning approaches offer a promising alternative to traditional monitoring techniques, such as window-based methods or envelope curves. This study examines the use of deep learning techniques for anomaly detection and error classification in screwdriving processes. The data corpus consists of multivariate time series capturing process parameters, such as torque and rotation angle. For anomaly detection, the embedding space of a vector quantized variational autoencoder was analyzed. In terms of error classification, four different model architectures were evaluated. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of anomaly detection and confirm that deep learning models can distinguish between multiple error categories beyond traditional binary classification. This extends the capabilities of conventional monitoring approaches, achieving accuracies of up to 100%. Additionally, real-world data material was examined in order to further demonstrate model robustness. Overall the results indicate strong generalization capability and highlight the practical potential of the developed models for use in industrial screwdriving processes, eliminating the need for expert knowledge in error identification and significantly reducing manual effort and analysis time.

items.title: MESH: Multi-receiver Evaluation of Spatial Hearing across Egocentric and Allocentric Views
items.summary: Spatial hearing in multi-receiver environments requires identifying who speaks, where they are, and how they move. Existing benchmarks evaluate spatial prediction, transcription, tracking, and distributed speech processing, but offer limited evaluation of whether speech signal remains associated with the correct physical source across receivers and motion. We introduce MESH, which evaluates this association through egocentric and allocentric views of shared acoustic scenes. The egocentric view uses local recordings and peer metadata, while the allocentric view combines synchronized recordings from multiple receivers in a shared 3D world frame. MESH contains nearly 40,000 questions across 13 static and dynamic localization and spatial transcription tasks. We evaluate eleven audio-model configurations and a language-model agent using specialist tools. The best static distance-estimation and dynamic direction-tracking accuracies are only 21.90% and 41.54%, respectively, while the lowest word error rates across four transcription tasks range from 59.15% to 73.10%. Ablation studies and additional experiments reveal that existing models are not yet able to effectively leverage peer information and struggle to handle multi-speaker and dynamic scenarios. These findings highlight the gap between access to distributed acoustic information and its effective use for spatial speech understanding. We release the dataset and evaluation code to support further research on collaborative and distributed spatial hearing.

items.title: RadarML: A Multi-Channel Over-the-Air Dataset of Common Radar Waveforms for ES Evaluation
items.summary: This paper introduces "RadarML", a publicly available dataset of modulated radar pulses recorded over-the-air across multiple semi-independent receiver channels. The dataset was generated using the UCL ARESTOR platform which is a Radio Frequency System on a Chip (RFSoC) based Software Defined Radio (SDR). The dataset contains a library of around two million waveforms with varying centre frequencies, bandwidths, pulse widths and modulations, with 1,000 examples of each signal variation per receiver channel. The goal of this dataset is to enable comparative analysis of radar modulation classification techniques on real data and stimulate research into multi-channel signal detection and modulation classification methods.

items.title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning
items.summary: Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture. MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability. A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction. Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers. These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.

items.title: Directionally Supervised Neuromorphic Protection for Distribution Systems Using Local Measurements
items.summary: Reliable protection under varying power system operating conditions requires rapid fault detection while preserving selectivity against external faults and non-fault disturbances. This requirement is particularly challenging in communication-free schemes, where relays must determine trip conditions solely from local electrical measurements. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a directionally supervised neuromorphic protection scheme that integrates disturbance-responsive leaky integrate-and-fire dynamics with a direction-dependent firing threshold to distinguish internal faults from reverse-direction events. The unified relay architecture combines local disturbance detection, directional discrimination, and spike-based trip generation without requiring inter-relay communication. Its performance is evaluated under grid-connected and islanded conditions using a ring microgrid and the IEEE 13-node distribution feeder. Across 240 evaluated fault scenarios, the framework achieves median operating times of 5.4--7.6 ms across the two networks, with 78% of cases operating within 10 ms and 95% within 20 ms. It also maintains protection security during load disturbances, while fault-resistance analysis confirms its response under high-resistance faults. Controller-hardware-in-the-loop (CHIL) experiments using an RTDS simulator and an external dSPACE controller demonstrate trip-command assertion in approximately 10 ms and 5 ms for the tested single-line-to-ground and three-phase-to-ground faults, respectively. The results establish real-time feasibility within the evaluated conditions and characterize operating-time variability across fault types and resistance levels for different network configurations.

items.title: Velocity-Free Funnel Control of Euler-Lagrange Systems: An Artificial-Delay Approach
items.summary: Classical funnel control keeps the tracking error within a prescribed, time-varying envelope by increasing the feedback gain as the error approaches the boundary. For mechanical systems, this guarantee typically relies on velocity measurements. We show that it can be retained for fully actuated Euler--Lagrange systems using only position measurements. The proposed controller replaces the velocity error with a difference quotient of the position error over a fixed delay, while preserving the classical unbounded gain. It requires no plant model, reference derivatives, observer, or filter states. The central challenge is to reconcile the averaging inherent in delayed feedback with a gain that can grow without bound near the funnel boundary. We resolve this by establishing an a priori bound on the gain along closed-loop trajectories, independent of the delay. This bound yields a computable delay threshold that guarantees tracking within the prescribed funnel and boundedness of all closed-loop signals. The threshold depends only on bounds on the inertia, forces, and reference. Simulations demonstrate tracking accuracy comparable to full-state funnel control and tolerance of delays substantially longer than certified. With quantized position measurements, the controller also requires substantially less torque than an existing derivative-free funnel controller.

items.title: Transferable Neuromorphic Protection for Distribution Networks
items.summary: Protection of converter-dominated distribution networks is challenging due to limited fault currents, operating-mode transitions, bidirectional power flow, and heterogeneous network configurations. This paper proposes a scale-invariant neuromorphic protection framework to enable transferable protection decisions across such networks. The framework integrates asset-based normalization, multi-domain disturbance representation, event-driven spike encoding, leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) dynamics, adaptive threshold regulation, and directional supervision within a unified mathematical formulation.
