Frontier DMs are also roughly ten times faster than the fastest LLM and can be over a hundred times cheaper. Together, these results suggest that DMs capture the heterogeneity of human behaviour better than LLMs and make large-scale economic simulations more feasible.

items.title: Solving Problems of Unknown Difficulty
items.summary: This paper studies how uncertainty about problem difficulty shapes problem-solving strategies. I develop a dynamic model where an agent solves a problem by brainstorming approaches of unknown quality and allocating a fixed effort budget among them. Success arrives from spending effort pursuing good approaches, at a rate determined by the unknown problem difficulty. The agent balances costly exploration (expanding the set of approaches) with exploitation (pursuing existing approaches). Failures could signal either a bad idea or a hard problem, and this uncertainty generates novel dynamics: optimal search alternates between trying new approaches and revisiting previously abandoned ones. I then examine a principal-agent environment, where moral hazard arises on the intensive margin: how the agent explores. Dynamic commitment creates a frontloading force, which can be counteracted by the presence of learning. The framework reflects scientific discovery, product development, and other creative work, providing insights into innovation and organizational design.

items.title: Aggregating treatment effects across multiple outcomes
items.summary: Researchers often aggregate outcomes to estimate treatment effects on abstract concepts, such as "crime" or "wealth." First, I document that principal component analysis (PCA), inverse variance matrix (IVM) weighting, and standardized averaging (SA) are commonly used but have unexpected shortcomings. PCA can assign negative weights, need not maximize precision, depends on an arbitrary sign normalization, and can have nonstandard asymptotics. Unlike SA, IVM can assign negative weights, but neither necessarily maximizes precision. Second, I develop a statistical decision-theoretic approach that uses mean-squared error to choose nonnegative weights while accounting for outcome quality. I revisit a study on social distancing.

items.title: Left-Digit Bias: Theory and Empirical Evidence from a Tax Salience Experiment
items.summary: Demand often drops sharply at whole-dollar prices. To explain this phenomenon, known as left-digit bias, we develop a random utility model in which consumers consider a good only if its price is below a heterogeneous attention threshold. Masses of consumers with integer attention thresholds generate demand discontinuities. When a tax is introduced, the model predicts a weaker demand response compared to rational choice for left-digit biased consumers. Using data from a tax experiment, we find that the model matches behavioral moments and partially identify the distribution of willingness to pay relative to thresholds. A weak demand response need not imply a low excess burden of taxation and understanding the specific mechanism is important for welfare analysis.

items.title: How Different are Different Differences-in-Differences? A Large-Scale Meta-Analysis
items.summary: I use AI-assisted replication to assess the empirical importance of negative weights in two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimation, analyzing 1,430 staggered-adoption specifications from 116 economics papers. TWFE estimates are highly correlated with modern difference-in-differences estimates, with sign reversals in 12.0-14.9% of comparisons and greater precision for TWFE. Hierarchical models accounting for estimation noise imply estimand correlations of 91-97% and a 0.7-2.4% probability of a statistically significant TWFE estimate opposing the modern estimand's sign. These findings suggest negative weights may be a less serious problem in practice and illustrate how AI can support systematic, large-scale empirical assessments of new econometric methods.

items.title: Efficient Equilibrium Computation in Colonel Blotto Games
items.summary: Colonel Blotto is a fundamental resource-allocation game in which two players divide their budgets across battlefields, and the higher allocation on each battlefield wins its value. The problem of computing an equilibrium efficiently has remained unresolved for its classical continuous version with arbitrary budgets and with values that may vary across battlefields but are the same for both players. We give a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme that computes an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$, and nearly linear in the input length for fixed $\varepsilon$. For sufficiently balanced budgets and battlefield values, we also compute exact equilibria in linear time.

items.title: Bang-Bang Correlation Sensitivity: A Local-to-Global Dichotomy for Correlation Preference
items.summary: Binary choice under risk can depend on how the alternative outcomes are jointly distributed. We show that in a finite outcome space, continuity, completeness, and betweenness impose a local-to-global restriction on this dependence: indifference between two alternatives with one common marginal distribution, however their outcomes are jointly distributed, implies correlation insensitivity for all lotteries supported on the same outcomes. In the correlation-sensitive case, these three axioms alone characterize correlation weighted utility, which combines statewise comparisons with a bilinear function of the marginal lotteries. In the correlation-insensitive case, an additional projective independence axiom yields Fishburn's (1982) skew-symmetric bilinear representation. Strong independence reduces correlation weighted utility to Lanzani's (2022) correlation expected utility representation. We extend the correlation-sensitive characterization to finitely supported lotteries on general metrizable outcome spaces. The resulting framework distinguishes correlation effects from departures from classical independence, and yields testable restrictions linking choices between identically distributed lotteries to correlated Allais behavior.

items.title: Correlation Probabilistic Sophistication
items.summary: We study binary choice under uncertainty when the comparison between two acts can depend on the joint distribution of their realized outcomes. This motivates correlation probabilistic sophistication (CPS), a subjective reduction principle that extends both probabilistic sophistication and Fishburn's nontransitive subjective expected utility. We show how simultaneous event exchangeability elicits a unique solvable finitely additive subjective probability and reduces binary comparisons of acts to induced joint laws. Under convex range, the induced domain coincides with the full finite joint-law domain, allowing the transfer of correlation-utility representations from risk and, under completeness and Strong Independence, correlation expected utility with a skew-symmetric comparison kernel. Under completeness and transitivity, CPS collapses to ordinary probabilistic sophistication. We further extend the framework to multiple small worlds, allowing correlation sensitivity to vary with the source of uncertainty.

items.title: Voting Biases in Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) Governance
items.summary: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) replace formal managerial authority with collective decision-making, by handing both proposal rights and token-weighted votes directly to community members. Yet, as in corporate votes, where management sets the agenda and its proposals rarely fail, DAO votes are strikingly one-sided. Using 127 281 proposals and about 51 million votes cast on Snapshot, the leading off-chain DAO voting platform, between 2020 and 2023, we ask which features of the ballot are associated with this support. We relate each choice's voting-power share to three observable features: its position in the list, whether its stance expresses approval, and whether the proposal author selected it. Each identifies one voting bias: position bias, approval bias, and author-selected choice bias. Author-selected choices show the strongest and most robust association, receiving a voting-power share 58.8 percentage points higher than non-author-selected ones, compared with 27.1 percentage points for approving choices and 7.7 percentage points for first-listed ones. About one third of the author bias comes from the author's own voting power; that advantage is smaller in the largest protocols and in proposals with higher participation. The results are robust across alternative specifications and outcomes. Our findings suggest that the agenda power that management holds in corporate voting persists even without a formal hierarchy, and that ballot design and the visibility of proposers' preferences are governance choices rather than neutral implementation details.

items.title: Search and Verification for Strategyproof Facility Location on Metric Graphs
items.summary: We study automated design of strategyproof (SP) mechanisms for randomized facility location on continuous metric graphs, with the objective of minimizing total distance. We develop methods for computing upper and lower bounds on the optimal approximation ratio achievable by SP mechanisms for a given graph and number of agents. For the lower bound, we propose a cost-preserving reduction to a finite domain that yields lower bounds for unrestricted SP mechanisms through linear programming dual certificates. For the upper bound, we introduce finite representations of mechanisms, called piecewise-linear attributions (PL attributions), that mix piecewise-linear deterministic mechanisms using affine weights on a triangulation of the report space. We show that for mechanisms represented by PL attributions, checking SP and an approximation guarantee reduces to finitely many quadratic nonnegativity tests over compact polytopes. With exact arithmetic and comparisons, each verification certifies the proposed property or returns locations where it fails. In addition, we introduce a strengthening of the incentive notion called strong strategyproofness. We show that for fixed component mechanisms and regions of a PL attribution, the strong strategyproofness requirement can be expressed by a finite number of linear constraints on the attribution coefficients. Using these theoretical results, we propose a heuristic procedure for computing an upper bound on the approximation ratio. We compute certified upper and lower bounds on several metric graphs and numerically evaluate the proposed search procedure. Lastly, we show that deterministic SP onto mechanisms on graphs are strongly strategyproof and admit PL attributions. Thus restricting attention to strongly strategyproof mechanisms admitting PL attributions loses no deterministic SP onto mechanisms.

items.title: Open-ended innovation arm-race in zero-sum games
items.summary: We discuss zero-sum games with open-ended innovation, whereby each player may introduce new strategies. The innovation process is modeled as a draw of new strategies form a distribution. It is argued that, when the cost of innovation is vanishingly small, this setting can lead to an everlasting innovation arm-race. In particular, the introduction of new technologies of the advanced player increases the marginal utility for technological innovation of the backward one, whereas innovation of the backward player discourages the more advanced one to innovate.
